en: The Second Part:
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa; Homage to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
May the four arms of Hari— dark as rain clouds, hardened by the striking of the bowstring of the Śārṅga, and serving as the pillars for the pavilion of the three worlds— protect you.
May the pair of lotus feet of Hari, reddened by the jewels rubbed against them by the crest-jewels of the gods, grant us our heart's desires.
Māndhātṛ said:
"O best of the twice-born, what fire consumes that terrible fuel of sin, whether dry or moist? You ought to explain this to me. (NarP 2.1.3)

O foremost of Brahmins, there is certainly nothing unknown to you in the three worlds— whether it be that which arises from the four-faced Brahmā or the threefold nature of reality— this is well ascertained.
Tell us: is the sin committed unknowingly or knowingly? Is it said to be dry or moist? Is it yet to be, or past, or present? NarP_2,1.5 //
"By what means would that ash of fire come to be? This is my inquiry. Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O tiger among kings, to that by which it may be so through fire. (NarP 2.1.6)
Indeed, his sin, whether dry or moist, is entirely consumed by these ashes.
Having obtained the day of Viṣṇu, that man who has his senses restrained,
becoming intent on fasting, should worship Madhusūdana.
Accompanied by his nurse and engaged in keeping vigil at night,
he purifies his sins just as a gambler recovers his wealth.
O King of kings, by the fire known as Ekādaśī, the fuel of sin—even that produced over a hundred lifetimes—is reduced to ashes. (NarP 2.1.10)
O King, there exists nothing for men so purifying as the day of Padmanābha, which brings about the destruction of sins.
O lord of men, sins remain in this body for as long as a living being does not fast before this auspicious [image] of Padmanābha. (NarP 2.1.12)
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day. (NarP 2.1.13)
O Lord, whatever sin has been committed by means of the eleven sense organs,
all of that shall go to dissolution through fasting on the Ekādaśī.
O King, there is nothing that destroys sin equal to Ekādaśī; even when observed under a pretext, it does not fail to reveal the Sun. (NarP 2.1.15)
For this [discourse] bestows heaven and liberation; it grants sovereignty and sons;
it indeed grants a virtuous wife and bestows health upon the body. (NarP 2.1.16)
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, O King, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara; neither the field of Kairava, nor the Revā, nor the Devikā [is equal to it]. (NarP 2.1.17)
O King, O lord of kings, by the merit of a single day of Hari, one reaches the abode of Hari without effort, even from the Yamunā or the Candrabhāgā. (NarP 2.1.18)
Having observed the vigil at night and having fasted on the day of Hari,
a man, liberated from all sins, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Indra among kings, he likewise rescues ten persons on his mother’s side, ten on his father’s side, and ten on his wife’s side. (NarP 2.1.20)
O Indra among kings, he would lead even himself to the city of Viṣṇu;
for this [gift] is equal to the wish-fulfilling gem, or even equal to a treasure-trove.
O best among the foremost of men, those people who have indeed taken refuge in the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) are like trees of desire or, rather, comparable to the words of the Vedas.
With arms joined in pairs, riding upon elephants,
adorned with garlands and wearing yellow garments, they proceed to the abode of Hari.
O lord of the earth, this power of the twelfth day has indeed been proclaimed by me; it is known as the fire that consumes the terrible fuel of sin.
Men devoted to dharma who desire abundant enjoyments as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth, should observe a fast throughout the day and night dedicated to Hari.
O best of men, that mortal who observes this day of Hari here with devotion does not enter the womb of a mother again—
whether he be burdened by much evil through desire or without desire— he goes to the infinite abode of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Twelfth Day," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
With reference to this very matter, the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest...
The sages questioned Sūta, the high-minded disciple of Vyāsa.
Thus questioned, O illustrious one, he recounted in great detail the majesty of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), as well as the rules for its fast.
Having heard those words of the Sūta’s son, O best of the foremost twice-born,
they also heard of the majesty of the Wielder of the Discus, which brings peace to the flood of all sins.
Again, O King, the citizens questioned the pure Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas:
"O giver of honor, you know the eighteen Purāṇas. (NarP 2.2.4)
By the grace of Kānīna, there is nothing—even in the Mahābhārata—that you do not know, nor indeed in the Purāṇas or the Smṛtis. (NarP 2.2.5)
Regarding the life of Raghunātha, which extends for hundreds of millions of verses,
a certain doubt arises within our hearts.
Your Honor ought to explain that in its true nature and in great detail:
should the fast be observed at the end of the lunar day, or rather at its very beginning? (NarP 2.2.7)
"Tell me regarding rites for the gods and the ancestors; there is nothing that you do not know.
Sauti said:
The end of the lunar day (tithi) is indeed to be observed as a fast by the gods, for it increases their delight."
The root of the lunar day (tithi) is declared by those who know the proper time to be dear to the ancestors;
therefore, one who desires the tenfold fruit of the tithi should indeed fast at its conclusion.
Indeed, those who desire merit should understand that the "root" [lunar day] is for the sake of satisfying the ancestors;
the second lunar day joined with the first, as well as the eighth joined with the seventh, must not be observed. (NarP 2.2.10)

O King, for those desiring virtue, pleasure, and wealth, the sixth and the eleventh [lunar days] should always be observed as joined with the preceding day, O best of the twice-born; likewise, the seventh [should be observed as joined with the preceding day].

The New Moon (Darśa) and Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa) sacrifices, as well as the anniversary day of a father's death—by avoiding these when they are overlapped by the previous lunar day, one falls into hell. (NarP 2.2.12)
"One shall incur the ruin of one's lineage and suffer misfortune as a king;
this, O brahmins, I heard in the past from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana. (NarP 2.2.13)

At the time of sunrise, whatever lunar day (tithi) may occur, even if it is brief, it should be considered as overlapping with the previous day; however, if it is extensive, it does not count without the sunrise.
For men, the lunar day (tithi) is considered to be that which exists at the time of breaking the fast or of death;
for rites concerning the ancestors, it is the time of sunset; and for the first contact [of the moon], it is declared to be the full [lunar day].
In that case, the lunar day (tithi) of the deity arising at sunrise should not be accepted;
rather, a wise man should daily verify the lunar day from an astrologer who contemplates the heavens.
O best of Brahmins, the moon and the sun are the measure of the lunar days;
those who know time understand it through their knowledge of the movements of the moon and the sun.
O twice-born ones, due to the fault of association with the east, those [women] are not fit for worship; therefore, men who know that avoid them during the four watches of the night.
Henceforth, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for bathing and worship;
one does not attain purity by day, therefore it is prescribed at night. (NarP 2.2.19)
Indeed, the entire daily ritual must be performed at the beginning of the night;
this is the rule I have declared for men observing the fast.
Furthermore, O best of Brahmins, when the twelfth day is short,
the rites of bathing and worship, accompanied by gifts, burnt offerings, and so forth, should be performed at the break of dawn.
On the thirteenth day, by breaking the fast, a man undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the earth, or even more than the merit of a hundred sacrifices. (NarP 2.22)
For this reason, O Brahmins, one should perform the bath at dawn accompanied by the libations to the ancestors, provided that the day of the twelfth lunar tithi has not been seen.
For this twelfth day, when transgressed by men, causes great ruin;
it effects the destruction of dharma, just as the Sarasvatī does for one who has not bathed.
Whether at the time of waning or waxing, or when the dawn has arrived, the meritorious Dvādaśī should be observed as a fast; one must avoid that which is overlapped by the preceding day.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O Sūta, when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs at the end of the preceding [day], how indeed should the fast be observed by human beings? Tell me. (NarP 2.26)
When the day of fasting is pierced by the preceding [tithi], and on the second day there is not even a slight portion of the Ekādaśī lunar day; (NarP 2.2.27)
"In that case, how is fasting prescribed? Tell me that, O son of Sūta.
Sauti said:
"O Brahmins, when the preceding [Dvādaśī] does not occur on the twelfth day..."

But when there is a conflict among many Brahmins who have come together and are disputing, the day following that fast is to be observed as the supreme day for me, born from the Sun and the Moon. (NarP 2.29)
The meritorious twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day;
likewise, this applies when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is pierced by the preceding day and the asterism Śravaṇa has arrived.
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) is meritorious for fasting on both fortnights;
this is the decision declared by me according to the conclusions of the scriptures. (NarP 2.2.31)
"What else do you wish to hear? Tell that to us.
The sages said: "O Sauti, tell us correctly and in accordance with reality the rule for the beginnings of the Yugas."
"For you, there is nothing that remains unannounced on the occasions of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti) and so forth.
Sauti said:
"The wise know that there are two white and two black [fortnights] which are the beginnings of the Yugas."
In the bright fortnight, [the moon] is to be grasped in the forenoon; in the dark fortnight, it is to be grasped in the afternoon.
The sun's course is enriched by the divisions of the day, and the transition [of the sun] is sixteen palas.
When the previous [half] has passed and the southern portion has elapsed, the northern is considered to follow;
however, at the time of the equinox in the middle, it is proclaimed as inexhaustible.
Having correctly ascertained the lunar day as proclaimed by the astrologer, the Brahmins, a fast must indeed be observed;
otherwise, one shall go to hell. (NarP 2.2.36)
A man who observes a lunar day overlapped by the previous one cuts away his merit;
it leads to the destruction of his lineage and the loss of his prosperity.
O best of Brahmins, even during a lunar eclipse, one should avoid Śivā on the tenth day;
just as one would discard the water of the Gaṅgā if it has been touched by a drop of liquor.

O best of the twice-born, one should avoid the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) that have been kept overnight, and one should abandon the eleventh day (ekādaśī), whether it be defiled by the tenth day or occurring on either of the two fortnights.

O best of the twice-born, that lunar day (tithi) joined with the previous one was formerly given by the Lord who wears the moon on his crest to the Dānavas for the sake of pleasing those great-souled ones.

O best of the twice-born, that wealth which is given at an improper time, to unworthy recipients, or that which is given even by those who are enraged, or that which is given without due respect; NarP_2,2.41 //
That which is given on a lunar day overlapping with the previous one is given to the Asuras;
likewise, that which is given by one who is impure from eating, or that which is given even to those who have fallen from their status.
Whatever is given to women, whatever is given without water,
and whatever is accompanied by boasting— that gift indeed goes to the asuras.
Therefore, O Brahmins, the Ekādaśī lunar day must not be observed when it is pierced [by the preceding or following day],
just as in ancient times a man who was the husband of a low-caste woman destroyed his merit and his ancestral offerings.

Whatever is given, recited, offered in sacrifice, bathed, or likewise whatever worship is performed for Hari on an intercalary lunar day (viddha-tithi) goes to ruin, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Just as women, proud of their youth, abandon an aged husband when afflicted by the god whose banner is a fish (Kāma),
so too do the wise always abandon one *vedha* for another lunar day (*tithi*) in order to increase their merit.

In the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, the second chapter, titled "Consideration of Lunar Days," the sages said: "Please explain in detail the ritual practice for the propitiation of Viṣṇu."
By which she attains satisfaction and grants what is desired. (NarP_2.3.1)
By what action may He—the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Master of the World, the destroyer of the entire mass of sins, and the one who encompasses all that is moving and unmoving—be pleased? (NarP 2.3.2)
Sauti said: O upholder of the earth, Hṛṣīkeśa is to be grasped through devotion, not by riches;
Viṣṇu, when fully worshipped with devotion, grants one's heart's desire.
Therefore, O Brahmins, devotion to the wielder of the discus should always be practiced;
for even by an ordinary person, when the Lord of the World is worshipped, He becomes the destroyer of suffering.
Just as one who is thirsty quickly attains satisfaction by means of water, so too, O Brahmins, a narrative that destroys sin is heard in this regard. (NarP 2.3.5)
Indeed, there was a dialogue between Rukmāṅgada and the sage Gautama;
King Rukmāṅgada was a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, endowed with forbearance.
Devoted to the one who lies upon the ocean of milk, intent upon the day of Hari,
that lord of the earth saw no one other than the Lord of Gods, Padmanābha.
Having taken up the drum for the purpose of warding off [evil], one should sound it on the day of Hari;
this applies to anyone who is more than eight years old but less than eighty-five years of age.
Indeed, that dull-witted man who today eats on the day of Viṣṇu is to be punished by me, executed, and banished from the city. (NarP 2.3.9)
Whether it be my father, brother, son, wife, or friend,
if they eat on the day of Padmanābha, they should be restrained like a thief.
"Give [the kingdom] to the foremost of the brahmins; bathe in the waters of the Jāhnavī!
Having heard my words, let him enjoy my kingdom. (NarP 2.3.11)
Day after day, O lord of the earth, during the bright fortnight of Viṣṇu—
and especially during the dark fortnight— he [should offer] upon a drum and a golden casket.
O best of the twice-born, when the king had thus proclaimed it throughout the entire land,
O brahmins, the roads were made congested by the crowds of people going toward Hari.
Whatever men meet their death within the realm of the king,
whether through knowledge [of the truth] or even through negligence, they go to the abode of Hari.
O twice-born ones, the world of Viṣṇu is certainly attained by human beings even if they observe the sin-destroying Dvādaśī under a pretext.
He who eats on the day of Hari incurs the sin of the earth;
he who does not eat on the day of Hari attains the merit of the earth. (NarP 2.3.16)
"A Brāhmaṇa must never be killed"—this is the Vedic tradition;
likewise, "one must not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights. (NarP 2.3.17)
O best of the twice-born, King Yama, the son of the Sun, was filled with embarrassment,
and Citragupta then grew weary of his work of recording deeds.
Having cleansed the stains arising from their past actions,
men indeed go in an instant to the world of Viṣṇu by means of their own duties.
All the hells became empty, devoid of sinful beings;
the path of Yama was shattered, scorched by twelve suns.
For all people, mounted upon Garuḍa, went to the abode of Hari;
even the worlds of the gods likewise became empty.
Sacrifices to the ancestors and gods, as well as virtuous acts such as visiting sacred fords and giving gifts, have fallen into ruin;
mortals know no other vow except for the single Ekādaśī-Dvādaśī.
When the celestial realm had become empty and likewise the hell realms were empty, Nārada went to Dharmarāja and spoke these words. (NarP 2.3.23)
Nārada said:
"O King, no wailing is heard in the courtyards of the hells;
nor is any record made of those who have performed evil deeds."
"This Citragupta stands like a sage, restrained by silence;
what is the reason that those sinners do not come to his house? (NarP 2.3.25)
"Overcome by deceit and hypocrisy, and likewise devoted to evil deeds"—
when these words had been spoken by the high-souled Nārada, (NarP 2.3.26).
King Vaivasvata, filled with a certain dejection, spoke;
Yama said:
"O Nārada, this king who is currently established upon the earth..."
For he is a devotee of Hṛṣīkeśa, the ancient Supreme Person;
O Indra among kings, he indeed awakens the people with a drum.
"One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived; for whatever mortals eat on that day, they indeed fall under my punishments. (NarP 2.3.29)
Out of fear of that, O best of sages, all people observe the twelfth day (Dvādaśī),
fasting on the Dvādaśī even under some pretext.
By observing the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), people indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution; they reach the abode of Hari.
"O best of the twice-born, by that king the paths have now been blocked for me;
indeed, the hells have been made empty, as have the worlds of the dwellers of heaven. (NarP_2.3.32)
O best of the twice-born, the writing of the scribe has ceased and the document has been wiped away by people through the greatness of the fast on the eleventh day.

O twice-born one, even those who have committed sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to the abode of Hari by fasting for a single day of Viṣṇu, without having to experience the fruits of their transgressions.
Thus, O Great Sage, I have become like a deer clad in saffron robes;
I am deprived of eyes, deprived of ears, like a twice-born man who has missed the twilight prayers.
O Brahmin, just as a man conquered by women or a eunuch who is the husband of a woman [is powerless], so too am I, having abandoned all desire, regarding such a state of being a world-protector.
"I shall indeed go to the world of Brahmā to make known my own suffering;
for a servant who remains in his duty is one who is free from worldly activity. (NarP 2.3.37)
"He who consumes the wealth of his master certainly goes to hell.
Sauti said: Having spoken thus, O Brahmins, Yama, accompanied by Nārada, [departed]. (NarP 2.3.38)
Accompanied by Citragupta, he went to the abode of Virañci, which is adorned with variegated seats;
there he beheld him seated, surrounded by beings both embodied and formless.
He is the refuge of the Vedas, the seed of the universe, the great-grandfather of all,
the self-existent abode of beings, known as Oṃkāra, and free from all taint.
The pure one, whose station is purity, the swan, the Brahman, marked by *darbha* grass,
being worshipped by various world-protectors and lords of the directions.
And with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, with the Vedas situated within their respective spheres, with the oceans in embodied form, and with the rivers and lakes; NarP_2,3.42.
Likewise, by those who bear bodies, by trees— especially the *aśvattha* and others—
and by ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth, as well as by mountains possessing embodied forms.
O twice-born ones, [it is measured] by days and nights, as well as by fortnights, months, years,
and by moments (kalā), units of time (kāṣṭhā), twinklings of the eye (nimeṣa), seasons, solstices, and ages (yugas).

Through manvantaras as well as kalpas, through the closing and opening of his eyes, through the constellations, yogas, and karaṇas, and through the full moons and the waning of the moon; NarP_2,3.45 //
The Lord of Gods, the purifier of dharma, is surrounded by pleasures and pains, by dualities, by gain and loss, by victory and defeat, and by truth and falsehood.
And the Grandfather is worshipped by men who are experts in ritual action and by those of noble lineage, through the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).
The pervasive Lord [is perceived] through natural transformations— tranquil, deluded, or exceedingly terrible—
and through the personified afflictions known as wind, phlegm, and bile.
And by Ānanda, the Soul of the Universe, having resorted to the supreme state,
was himself surrounded by beings even though they had not been mentioned, as the creator of the world.
Amidst those embodied evil words, harsh speech,
and the like, Saturn entered as if with shame, like a bride.
Looking down with his face cast downward, he pointed out Yama, who had entered along with Nārada, still within his own body. Seeing them both there, they were struck with wonder.
With eyes wide with wonder, they said to one another: "Could this be the son of Bhāskara who has arrived here to see the Grandfather, the god who created the worlds?"
"There is not a single moment when he, the son of the Sun, is inactive;
why has he come here so preoccupied? Is all well with the inhabitants of heaven? (NarP 2.3.53)
I consider this to be an extreme marvel, that this scribe, whose cloth has been wiped clean,
has arrived endowed with such great wretchedness.
Indeed, this cloth had not been wiped by anyone possessing virtuous qualities;
yet that which had neither been seen nor heard of is now clearly visible right here.
O Brahmins, while those beings were thus crying out, the son of the Sun, having fulfilled his command, fell before Brahmā.
"Like a tree whose roots have been severed, I cry out, 'Save me! Save me!
O Lord of Gods, I am humiliated because my painted cloth has been wiped away. (NarP_2,3.57)
"O Lotus-seated One, with you as my protector, I see myself destitute," he said,
O best of the twice-born, and then became motionless.
Then a tumultuous roar arose in the assembly hall,
which causes all the worlds, both mobile and immobile, to weep.

"Why is this Vaivasvata Yama weeping, afflicted by sorrow? Or rather, this worldly verse appears true to us: ||| NarP_2,3.60 ||| "The king of the dead does not weep for the sake of his own grief; rather, he weeps out of compassion for those who have committed evil deeds. ||| NarP_2,3.61 ||| "Having heard these words of the messenger, the King of Justice (Dharma) spoke these words to that messenger, O best of the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.62 ||| "O messenger, go quickly and bring here that wicked-souled one, the son of Virocana, who has committed such a great crime. ||| NarP_2,3.63 ||| "Having been thus addressed by the King of Justice, the messenger departed with haste and brought Bali, the son of Virocana, there. ||| NarP_2,3.64 ||| "Then, having seen Bali brought before him, the King of Justice, being compassionate, spoke these words to him. ||| NarP_2,3.65 ||| "Bali, you have performed many sacrifices according to the rules; why then do you grieve, O best of the Asuras? ||| NarP_2,3.66 ||| "O Bali, you have indeed performed hundreds of thousands of horse-sacrifices and other sacrifices according to the ordinances. ||| NarP_2,3.67 ||| "O Bali, you have given gifts to the twice-born; why then do you grieve, O best of the Asuras? ||| NarP_2,3.68 ||| "You have given gold, cows, garments, food, vehicles, beds, seats, and houses to the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.69 ||| "You have given land, elephants, horses, chariots, and various kinds of ornaments to the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.70 ||| "You have given villages, cities, towns, and various kinds of wealth to the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.71 ||| "You have given beautiful women, male servants, female servants, and various kinds of gems to the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.72 ||| "You have given palaces, towers, and various kinds of precious stones to the twice-born. ||| NarP_2,3.73 ||| "You have given all these things to the twice-born; why then do you grieve, O best of the Asuras? He who causes suffering to people is tormented before long;
for a man who has performed evil deeds does not attain what is auspicious.
Then, having understood the intention of the Creator regarding those people of impartial minds, Vāyu restrained their speech at that time.
Dispelling the fear of the son of Martanda, the all-pervading Lord, whose form is the universe and whose intellect is noble, slowly raised him up with his two well-developed arms.
He seated the agitated one, who was fleeing, upon his throne;
then he spoke these words to the son of the Sun, whose form was like the sky, while he remained in his body.
By whom have you been overcome? By whom have you been banished from your station?
By whom has the divine cloth—the garment of the world—been wiped away from you?
"Speak everything without omission; let this Kuśaketu speak.
O father, he who is the lord of all shall bring about your exaltation and remove the sorrow residing in your heart, even as the sun [dispels darkness]."
Thus addressed by the Wind-god, the son of the Sun-god then spoke to him,
looking at the face of the son of Kuśaketu and uttering his words slowly with a faltering voice.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Yama’s Journey to the World of Brahmā," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Yama said:
"Listen to my words, O Lord, Grandfather, Great-Grandfather."
O King, nothing is more grievous than death than the impairment of one's majesty.
O Lotus-born One, he who, being free from desire, does not carry out his duty,
will surely fall quickly into a blind well— that is, into hell.
O Lotus-seated One, that official who does not carry out his assignment while consuming the wealth of his master shall become a wood-worm.
O Lord of the Earth, that official who, out of greed, seizes wealth from subjects or from the king goes to hell for three hundred kalpas.
But he who, intent on his own interests, robs his master,
shall become a dull-witted rat in a house for three hundred kalpas.
But he who, having been an official, enjoys the food in his own house while his servants perform the work for the king, shall turn into a cat.
Therefore, O King, by your command, I shall govern the subjects according to dharma:
rewarding the doer of merit with merit, and [punishing] the sinner with sinful action.
O Lord, having investigated thoroughly by means of the treatises on dharma and other sciences, the sages [determined] for you who exist from the beginning of the kalpa until this very day.
Therefore, O Lord, by your very command, I shall now be able to act;
for I have been defeated today by King Rukmāṅgada.
O Lord of the World, out of fear of whom this earth, clothed by the oceans,
does not consume anything during the day of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins.
Having abandoned all dharmas, having abandoned the worship of ancestors, having abandoned the worship of gods, and [the practice of] bathing at sacred fords and so forth at night; (NarP_2,4.11)

O giver of honor, having abandoned both Yoga and Sāṃkhya, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, and having abandoned Vedic study and burnt offerings, one may commit numerous sins. (NarP 2.4.12)
Having fasted on the day of Hari, men indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu together with their fathers and likewise with their grandfathers.
Likewise, their fathers— the fathers of those ancestors—
as well as the maternal grandfathers and those who are the mother’s progenitors and so forth, all go there.
For even they have progenitors who were born before their own fathers;
yet this sorrow, O Lord, pierces my very vitals once again. (NarP 2.4.15)
"Having wiped away my writing, the ancestors of my beloved shall depart;
for it was from the seed of the ancestors that he was held in the womb of the nurse. (NarP 2.4.16)
Whatever action one person performs, that alone is experienced by that very person;
O Brahmin, the seed produced by a planter does not belong to anyone else.
He whose body is sustained by the funeral cake (piṇḍa) shall deliver both sides;
for there is no seed belonging to the wife, nor is the wife merely a bearer of the womb. (NarP 2.4.18)
O Lord of the World, how does her side attain the supreme state?
Through the greatness of the merit of my son-in-law, the pain in my head has vanished.
"O King, I have no need for such a command;
he who observes the fast of Ekādaśī would abandon me and go to Hari. (NarP 2.4.20)
Having uplifted his three lineages along with himself, O Lotus-born One,
he abandons my path and proceeds to the abode of Hari.
O Lord, a human being does not attain such a state through sacrifices,
nor through sacred fords, nor through gifts, nor through vows that are devoid of Viṣṇu.
O Creator, one does not attain that state by dying in water or even in fire,
nor by being destroyed through yoga, nor by falling from a precipice.
O best among the wise, one who observes the Vaiṣṇava vow attains such a destination as no other does; this which has been spoken is the truth. (NarP 2.4.24)
A man who, on the day of Hari, anoints his limbs with wood-apple paste and eats food free from desire for flavors—
even if he is a performer of wicked deeds— attains the world of the Upholder of the Earth (Viṣṇu) in a human birth.

Thus, having become hopeless on earth due to my lowly karma, I have come to the pair of your lotus feet; grant me the time for obtaining fearlessness through a mere request, O cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction!
May those evildoers—those humans who are destitute and bound by the hosts of my bhūtas with chains and rope-bonds—not exist; may they come into my presence and fall under my control.
But when the path, scorched by the heat of the sun, is broken by the hosts of Viṣṇus with their exceedingly powerful hands,
the entire multitude of people, having abandoned the *kumbhī* hell, proceeds to that abode of the one higher than the highest.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Words of Yama," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Yama said:
"The path of the Discus-wielding God has now been reached."
O you who are worshipped by the three worlds, [you are attained] by men through flawless conduct and movement.
O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World, I consider the world of yours to be immeasurable,
for it is not filled by the worlds, which are like the lotuses of all sentient beings.
O Grandfather, by the mere fact of dwelling in the abode of Mādhava, all—whether established in their own duties or engaged in improper acts, whether pure or even impure—are [purified]. (NarP 2.5.3)
Having observed a fast on the day of Viṣṇu, they go to his world by the king's command;
for he is indeed our great enemy, and especially yours.
O Lord of the worlds, he shall be one who is to be restrained; there is no doubt in this matter.
By him, the circle of the earth was ruled for a thousand years. (NarP 2.5.5)
Having assumed a four-armed form and mounting Garuḍa, he led immeasurable people to the realm of Viṣṇu, which is beloved by Hari.
If the Lord of Gods, who is dear to Mādhava, stands upon the Mādhavī [creeper], well-enclosed in yellow garments, wearing garlands, and adorned with beautiful earrings; NarP_2,5.7.
"By this, the entire world shall be led to Viṣṇu’s painless abode;
for this is the staff and this is the cloth, released from your two feet."
O Lord of Gods, that incomparable status as a world-protector was attained by King Rukmāṅgada; blessed is she by whom he was borne.
One born of a mother is superior in virtue for the sake of destroying all suffering;
for what is the use of a child being born who only causes distress to his mother?
"He who does not scorch his enemies like the sun in the month of Jyeṣṭha—
O God, such a mother has given birth to a son in vain, for she is truly the mother of a wicked child."
He whose fame does not flash forth like lightning amidst the clouds, and who does not uplift his father’s side through either learning or power; ||| NarP_2,5.12 |||
That disease born from the mother’s womb is produced upon the earth in the form of a son who becomes hostile toward virtue, wealth, and pleasure. (NarP 2.5.13)
He is called a matricide by the virtuous; his life is in vain, O Brahmā, for he has borne but one son, and that too a hero—of this there is no doubt.
"O Lord, it was by her that Rukmāṅgada was born for the purpose of cleansing the stain of the Mallas;
this [rule] has not been established on earth by any king whatsoever. (NarP 2.5.15)

"O Lord of the World, even in the Purāṇas I have never heard of the wiping of a cloth. Such as I am, I have never before seen anyone standing in the service of Hari at Kṣīrīśa, beating a most terrible drum and proclaiming the destruction of my path to liberation. (NarP 2.5.16)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of Yama," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said: "What wonder have you seen, or why are you so distressed?"
And the anguish felt toward virtuous qualities—that anguish ends only with death.
"Since the supreme state is attained by the mere utterance of it, why would a man not go there after fasting on that day of the Sun? (NarP 2.6.2)
For a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices;
one who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but he who prostrates to Kṛṣṇa does not return to existence.
What need has he for Kurukṣetra, or for Kāśī, or even for Viraja, on the tip of whose tongue the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside? (NarP 2.6.4)
A Brahmin who approaches a dog-cooker woman, especially one during her menses,
or who eats food cooked with liquor— should he remember Hari at the time of death, [he is purified].
Having abandoned the accumulation of sin born from eating what is forbidden and approaching those who should not be approached, he,
liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, attains union with Viṣṇu.
If liberation comes from the mere utterance of his name, why would it not come from fasting for him?
Even he who is praised is meditated upon as the Supreme Person.
If one should chant the name of the God and listen to Janārdana even in play,
that man shall attain equality with the merit of being purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā.
How can that dull-witted one govern us, the lords of the worlds, the progenitor, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who serves him day after day?
That you were not crushed by them, and that you were not bound firmly by them—that honor was bestowed upon us; yet you do not understand the truth of this.
The official who does not know the excellent devotees of the king on earth, though he may be joined with all possible effort, is instead punished by them. (NarP 2.6.11)

Those who are favored by the king, even if they have committed offenses, must not be punished by the official; for they, having achieved success through their master's favor, will surely bring the official to ruin.
O son of the Sun, how can those who have committed evil deeds and yet bow down to Janārdana be restrained by them on account of their childishness? (NarP 2.6.13)
"O Divākara, I shall provide assistance to you by means of devotees of Śiva, or devotees of Bhāskara, or my own devotees; however, I do not assist you through the devotees of Hari."
The Supreme Person is indeed the first of all the gods.
The subjugation of those who are devotees of Madhusūdana is not appropriate, even if they observe the Dvādaśī of both fortnights under some pretext. (NarP 2.6.16)
If they should commit an insult against you, O son of the Sun, I shall not be your helper; for if I were to become your helper, there would be an unrighteousness that would destroy my own body,
like a reversal from the most meritorious state of Brahman while traveling on the path with the devotees of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Words of Brahmā," in the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
"O dear one, I have obtained that which is beneficial for bowing at the feet of the Vedas along with [my sons].
O Lord of the World, I shall not again go to the end of my yoga."
While the king named Hāṭakāṅgada was ruling the earth,
that single best of deities arrived on the day of Hari.
"If you move from your composure, then I am your servant;
O Lord, he is my great enemy, for by him my cloth has been stolen."
"By feeding even a single lord of the earth on this day sacred to Kṛṣṇa,
I shall have fulfilled my purpose, just like one who offers the funeral cake at Gayā."
"From this day forward, those men by whom Hari, the Lord of Gods, has been remembered,
fasted, or even praised— by me they shall certainly not be restrained."
Those mortals who, even by means of deception, suddenly utter the name "Hari," they indeed become liberated from the path of the womb;
being liberated, those skilled ones do not enter my [Yama's] painted cloth-scroll, and they are honored by the hosts of the best of the celestial wanderers.
Sauti said: NarP_2,7.6.
For the sake of Vaivasvata’s task and with the desire to honor him, Viriñci,
the lord of gods who bears the auspicious mark of the lotus, paid him homage.
Having reflected for a moment, the Lord, adorned by all beings, assumed a form that was merely intended to terrify living creatures; so did the All-pervading One.
In that [lake], he brought forth a woman who deluded the world;
she shone, created by the mind of the Goddess, as the most excellent of all women.
She stood before him, adorned with all her ornaments; and seeing her endowed with such beauty and wealth, the Grandfather was struck with wonder.
Indeed, upon seeing these beings of his own who were deluded by desire,
Brahmā closed his eyes out of fear of committing a transgression.
With a mind still possessed by passion, and with eyes still possessed by passion, one might even think of or look upon one's mother or daughter. (NarP 2.7.12)
Whether it be a daughter-in-law, a brother’s wife, the wife of a preceptor, or a king’s woman—
even if one merely contemplates approaching a woman of the lowest caste (śvapacī)— he goes to a terrible hell.
For indeed, the merit accumulated over many lifetimes of any man who falls into agitation upon seeing these women becomes fruitless; it cannot be otherwise.
In such a situation, ten thousand merits go to destruction;
due to the destruction of merit, the sinner will certainly become a stone-dwelling rat.
Therefore, a wise man should not look upon these women with a lustful eye;
even the feet of one's own mother must not be touched by those who have reached the age of twelve.
Furthermore, for the purpose of anointing, a wise son should employ women who have passed their sixtieth year and are established in youthfulness through [the use of] oils. (NarP 2.7.17)
Whether he be old or even young, one should not wash the feet of a woman;
it is said that both will fall into the Raurava hell amidst heaps of glowing coals.
O King, that bride who reveals her uncovered limbs to her father-in-law shall be struck by his hands and feet and become food for worms; likewise,
that sinner who performs the washing of his feet with the hand of his daughter-in-law [shall suffer the same].
Whether it be bathing or even anointing with oil, for him too there is such a destiny:
he is devoured by needle-mouthed beings with black faces for the duration of a kalpa.
Therefore, a man should not look upon a woman, a daughter, or even a daughter-in-law with a lustful mind; at that very moment, the man falls.
Having reflected thus, he indeed formed a subtle insight:
"That this face appears auspicious, round, and elevated. (NarP 2.7.22)
"For this is merely a skeleton, covered with skin and flesh; it is composed of fat, marrow, and eyes shining with impurities, situated within women. (NarP 2.7.23)
This flesh upon her breasts has become excessively elevated,
while the triple-fold situated on her abdomen reveals its deepened curvature.
Furthermore, excessive flesh has been cast upon the path of the hips;
this secret is the opening for urine, wherein the three worlds are deluded.
Constantly defiled by the downward-voiding wind (apāna),
this flesh— already more loathsome than the interior of a bellows— is cast into the path of the genitals.
Just as wood that has been split in two is certain to be likewise [unstable], so too the shanks are surely divided in two;
filled with semen, bones, and flesh, how could they ever attain beauty? (NarP 2.7.27)
Tell me, what is the essence of embodied beings, whose core consists only of flesh, fat, and marrow?
What man would take delight in a body nourished by the impurities of feces and urine?
Having reflected thus in many ways with the eye of knowledge,
Viriñci composed himself and spoke to that woman who moved with the gait of an elephant.
O woman of excellent complexion, O lady of lovely limbs, just as you were created by me through my mind, so indeed have you become— inciting the madness of the heart.
Then, having bowed to the four-faced one, she said to him:
"O Lord of the moving and unmoving world, behold this state of universal fainting. (NarP 2.7.31)
He who is not infatuated by my form, who is disciplined and free from blemish—there is no such man in the three worlds who, upon seeing me, remains unaffected. (NarP 2.7.32)
"O Lotus-born One, from the very beginning, he does not fall into agitation;
no one who desires what is auspicious should engage in self-praise. (NarP 2.7.33)
Even a pure man goes to hell because of praising [others];
nevertheless, O Brahmin, praise should be offered for the sake of one's purpose.
"O Brahmā, I have indeed been created by you for the purpose of agitating someone;
command him, O Lord of the World, and I shall agitate him without a doubt. (NarP 2.7.35)
O Lord, even the mountain that supports the earth faints upon seeing me;
how much more so a human being, endowed with consciousness and capable of inhalation and exhalation?
And so it is stated in the Purāṇas regarding the description of gazing at women:
"It causes madness in men and destroys their difficult vows. (NarP 2.7.37)

A man remains on the path of virtue, masters his senses, maintains his sense of shame, and adheres to discipline only so long as these arrows of the glance—belonging to playful women, drawn upon the bow of their eyebrows, possessing dark lashes, and reaching the path of the ears—do not fall upon the heart to steal away one's steadfastness. (NarP 2.7.38)
Fie on the poetry of that dull-witted bad poet who equates the face of a woman with the moon!
Where in the moon are there the glances of a sidelong look made startling by the knitting of eyebrows, nor the smiles, the graces, and the frowns of anger? (NarP 2.7.39)
For even when drunk, O Lord, liquor causes delusion to a man of great discernment;
yet a young woman, whether merely remembered or seen, surely bewilders a man even more than wine. (NarP 2.7.40)
"O Great-Grandfather, you have created me for the purpose of deluding men;
therefore, O Lord of the World, command me: 'I shall delude the three worlds. (NarP 2.7.41)
Brahmā said:

"O Goddess, you have spoken the truth; there is nothing impossible in the three worlds for one such as you, O fortunate one with thighs like an elephant's trunk, who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut."
O woman of excellent complexion, that you corrupt my mind as well—
I have indeed taken that [corruption] well in hand by means of the goad of knowledge.
How then will you not captivate the hearts of the worlds?
O large-eyed one, it is true that your form is utterly enchanting.
"For I perceive the entire world, including the gods, as motionless;
O fair-faced one, accomplish that for which I created you."
In the city of Vaidiśa, O auspicious one, there was a king on earth named Rukmāṅgada,
whose wife was Sandhyāvalī, who was equal to you in beauty.
In her was born Dharmāṅgada, a son who excelled his father,
possessing the strength of ten elephants and a splendor like that of the sun.
He who is equal to the earth in patience, like the ocean in profundity,
blazing like fire in splendor, and comparable to Vaivasvata in wrath.
In renunciation he was like Vairocana, in his gait like the wind,
in gentleness equal to the moon, and in beauty like the god of love.
O fair-faced one, that prince, who was equal to Jīva and Bhārgava in statesmanship,
enjoyed the entire Jambūdvīpa as his sole domain, which had been inherited from his father.
By Dharmāṅgada, other continents were also conquered;
yet, out of shame before his parents, he did not experience the pleasure of women.
He who, though thousands of wives were obtained by him and then abandoned,
did not waver from his word even while at his father’s house.
O fortunate one, O lady of lovely smiles, he indeed beholds three hundred mothers of yours, all alike and radiant as gold. (NarP 2.7.53)
O lady of beautiful limbs, go to the presence of that king, who is devoted to righteousness and adorned with the jewel of a son, on Mount Mandara, the best of mountains.
There the king, indeed, having been carried away by his horse, will dwell;
and, O lady of beautiful limbs, deluded by your song, he will abandon the horse and turn back.
Having ascended the ridge of the mountain, he will come into union with you;
there, O Goddess, you must not speak of this meeting with the king here.
"O King, I shall become your wife; of this there is no doubt. O Lord, whatever I say must certainly be carried out by you. (NarP 2.7.57)
Deluded by your beauty, he will likewise act accordingly;
therefore, having bound him with oaths, seize him indeed by the right hand.
"O fair-browed one, after a few days have passed, you should say this: 'For when you are seen to be bewildered during sexual union, O lovely-limbed one. (NarP 2.7.59)
Then, laughing, he recalled the king’s former words: "O King, that oath which you made to fulfill my request. (NarP 2.7.60)
"Therefore, O protector of the earth, protect it; I believe the time has come for this.
When you had spoken thus, the king, being simple-minded, [consented] out of reverence for the truth. (NarP 2.7.61)

"I shall protect you, of this there is no doubt; tell me, what may I give to you?"—when these words have been spoken by you, O fair-faced one, you should say: NarP_2,7.62: "I shall protect you, of this there is no doubt; tell me, what may I give to you? When these words have been spoken by you, O fair-faced one, [you should say]."
O auspicious one, King Rukmāṅgada, the father of Dharmāṅgada, said:
"You must never observe a fast on the day of Hari."
O beloved, for one who does not enjoy his own wife—who is innocent and endowed with youth—there shall indeed be a fast for him on the day of Suratasra. (NarP 2.7.64)
"O King, that man of evil conduct who disregards the lunar festivals will certainly go to hell; for three nights I have been abandoned by you through your failure to observe the fast. (NarP 2.7.65)
"I am not able to remain even for a single moment without you;
indeed, when the time for the ancestral rites arrived, the twice-born were already seated. (NarP 2.7.66)
"If she asks for union, then she is indeed to be enjoyed.
Even though the king was thus being enlightened by your words, [he did not comply]. (NarP 2.7.67)
O lady of beautiful limbs, if you do not abandon the fast on the day of Hari, O King, then you must speak these supreme words. (NarP 2.7.68)
O Indra among kings, having severed your own head with your own hand using your excellent sword, place it yourself upon my lap, along with Dharmāṅgada.
O lord of the earth, if you do not indeed do this which is dear to me, you will go to hell when your merit is exhausted; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful woman, having heard your words, he will not harm his son who is as dear to him as his own life;
accepting the command of the gods of the earth, he shall enjoy his residence in the abode of Mādhava.

Then people will go, as before, to the presence of Yama, bound by the nooses of his servants; they will become inhabitants of hell according to the measure of their writing. Indeed, you have done well! // NarP_2,7.72 //
Now, if the glorious king, endowed with truthfulness, slays his own son,
he goes to the station of Padmanābha, which is worshipped by all the gods without exception.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Words of Brahmā to Mohinī," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Sauti said:
Having heard those words of Brahmā, that lotus-eyed woman—
He said, "Give me a name by which I may go to my home. (NarP 2.8.1)
"O Lord of the World, a father must bestow a name upon his offspring;
it is said that a name removes sin. Therefore, O Kuśadhvaja, please do so. (NarP 2.8.2)
Brahmā said:
"O beautiful one, since this entire world has been deluded by you,
O Goddess, your name shall be Mohinī, for it shall indeed possess [this] quality."
O fair-browed one, if he attains your company, which brings such happiness, he will truly come to possess right vision regarding the ten stages of existence.
Thus addressed, the woman of beautiful hips bowed to the one seated upon the lotus and,
watched by the immortals on the path, set out for Mount Mandara.
In the third moment, they reached the mountain peak,
which could not be fully encircled even by the serpent Vāsuki.
That ocean, which was formerly held by Hari, churned by the gods and dānavas,
and which measures six hundred thousand yojanas— may its depths become [the dwelling place] of that [serpent].
O Indra among kings, that great mountain which was not shattered when joined with the body of the tortoise as it fell, revealed the secret of the ocean.
O twice-born ones, from that mountain water flowed along the path of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
and by its friction against the bones of the tortoise, a great fire was produced.
O best of the twice-born, that place where the naked god dwells together with the elemental beings has never been seen by either gods or dānavas.
When a vast period of ten thousand years had passed,
he was the one who performed the rubbing of the armlet for the divine Wielder of the Discus.
For this is a temple of jewels, endowed with many minerals.
That great mountain is a place of playful recreation for the denizens of heaven, a cause of asceticism for the practitioners of penance,
an enhancer of delight for the celestial nymphs, and the source of precious gems and medicinal herbs.
At its base, it measures ten thousand leagues, and it extends that same number in width;
for as many leagues it rises in height, like a pillar supporting the three worlds.
Illuminating both the surface of the earth and the sky with its peaks made of gold and jewels,
it is there that the son of Kaśyapa, having gone, loses his brilliance and becomes devoid of rays.
Having attained a golden radiance, she whose limbs were like the form of gold herself eclipsed with her own splendor Mandara, who was the subduer of the sun's brilliance.
Accomplishing the king’s desire, she sat upon a divine stone slab of blue luster, extending for seven yojanas.
O Indra among kings, upon that stone stands the Kaulisha Linga;
it measures ten cubits in width and the same number in height.
Renowned as Vṛṣaliṅga, that supreme palace was like a cloud;
there, O best of the twice-born, the young women performed an excellent concert.
Joined with the lute-playing, she was the supreme remover of fatigue;
the beautiful woman remained close by that linga. (NarP 2.8.20)

O Lord of Kings, when that song— which was accompanied by melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) and rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), joined with the sound of the note *gāndhāra*, and increased the passion of love— was set in motion, [the world was moved].
O lords of sages, even the immobile beings felt a longing for him;
indeed, no song had ever been sung before that was so divine or non-divine.
The song issued from the mouth of Mohinī was enchanting to all living beings.
Upon hearing that song of the beautiful woman in that very form, the naked one,
overcome by passion and desiring to enjoy her, moved toward that enchanting girl, though he was ashamed at being seen by Pārvatī.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Mandā," in the *Mohinī-carita* of the latter part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Sauti said:
Now, Rukmāṅgada, the lord of kings, having enjoyed human pleasures...
Having worshipped the god Hara many times, who wears yellow garments; ||| NarP_2,9.1 |||
O brahmins, having placed their feet upon the heads of their enemies who were skilled in battle,
they made the path to Yama empty by conquering Vaivasvata, the Lord of Death.
When the path to Vaikuṇṭha had been completely cleared by men,
he summoned his son Dharmāṅgada at the proper time and spoke to him.
O son, protect this earth, which is filled with wealth on all sides,
through your valor, having made a firm resolve to abide by your own dharma.
If a son has been born who is capable, he who does not hand over the kingdom to him will undoubtedly lose both his merit and his fame. (NarP 2.9.5)
And that father who does not attain happiness through a capable son must necessarily be known as a sinner throughout the three worlds. (NarP 2.9.6)
A son who is capable of bearing his father's burden yet does not carry it is like one born from his mother as a double-tongued serpent, though devoid of venom.
He is a true son who becomes more renowned than his father on this earth,
illuminating everything everywhere like the sun with its own rays.
That son who causes his father to stay awake at night due to the sorrows born of the loss of his children goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
He who, honoring the word of his father, carries out everything at home,
attains union with the Divine (deva-sāyujya), being praised by those dwelling in heaven.
Thus, O son, for the sake of my subjects, I have been bound by duties upon this earth;
remaining engaged in their protection, I have neither eaten nor slept according to my own will.
"O son, while you were incapable, I did not obtain happiness, for I was intent on suppressing those who eat on the day of Viṣṇu. (NarP 2.9.12)
Some are established on the path of Śiva, some are settled on that of the Sun; others follow the path of Viriñci, and still others abide in that of Pārvatī.
Seated at evening and at dawn, they were established in the Agnihotra sacrifice—
whether a child, a youth, an old man, a pregnant woman, or a young maiden.
"Those who say, 'One who is diseased or even impaired is not able to fast,' should be refuted on all sides. (NarP 2.9.15)
Having awakened me many times with words spoken in the Purāṇas over many days, for the sake of the happiness of all creatures; (NarP 2.9.16)
Having restrained them, I keep them without food on the day of Hari; however, according to the perspective of the scriptures, I punish the ignorant scholars with corporal punishment.
Having been commanded, they were all made to fast on the day of Hari;
because of that, I have found no pleasure whatsoever while dwelling upon the earth.
O son, it is said that a king should not cause his subjects to suffer, whether from his own people or from others; rather, he should protect his subjects. (NarP 2.9.19)
For those imperishable worlds have been proclaimed in the Purāṇas as belonging to him;
therefore, O gentle one, I am established here for the sake of progeny, and never for my own sake.
"I desire to enjoy the pleasure arising from hunting and such activities;
O son, I never desire that which arises from drinking or gambling."
"O son, a king who is attached to these things goes to destruction before long. By your grace, O son, I shall now go under the pretext of hunting. (NarP 2.9.22)
Desiring to enjoy various mountains, forests, rivers, and lakes, as well as all pleasant objects of desire, he has placed his burden upon you. (NarP 2.9.23)
All this has been fully explained, which resides within my heart:
if you do it, there will be great fame; if not, there will be a stay in hell.
Dharmāṅgada said:
"I shall do all this; enjoy pleasures according to your heart's desire.
O father, I myself shall bear the heavy burden of your kingdom."
Indeed, no other duty has occurred to me except for the carrying out of your word;
for one who fails to fulfill his father's command, even while performing other duties, shall go to the lower realms.
"Therefore, standing with palms joined in reverence, I shall carry out your word.
When these words were spoken, the king became truly joyful.
Then Dharmāṅgada, having ascertained that the forest was filled with deer and desiring to depart, summoned his subjects and, having realized the true nature of the self, spoke to them.
"Appointed by my father for your protection and welfare, I, desiring righteousness in every way, must carry out my father's command. (NarP 2.9.29)
For there is no other law for a son than the word of his father regarding his subjects;
while I am the wielder of the rod of punishment, Yama is nowhere the ruler.
Knowing this, you must remember Him whose banner is Garuḍa;
Janārdana is to be worshipped through the practice of offering to Brahman.
For by completely abandoning the sense of "mine" and by that which is prescribed for your own caste, you will indeed attain imperishable worlds; of this there is no doubt.
For this path superior to that of the ancestors has been shown to you, O subjects;
may you be engaged in the practice of offering to Brahman and become experts in knowledge.
One must not eat on the day of Hari; this is the eternal path of the ancestors.
Indeed, I have declared this distinction to you for the sake of your establishment in Brahman.
And this [vow], from which rebirth is difficult to attain, must be practiced by those who know the truth;
that the day of Hari must be observed through fasting—this is the established rule.
Having conciliated all his subjects and comforted them again and again,
Dharmagada never slept by day nor by night.
Roaming everywhere through his valor, he makes the earth free of thorns;
the drum constantly resounds upon the head of the enemy, like a lion.
Without having observed the twelfth day (dvādaśī), worlds are abandoned by me;
therefore, O Lord of Gods, let Hari be meditated upon in all three types of undertakings.
He alone is the god who carries the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, he is Puruṣottama;
for he is the Lord of the worlds who exists in the sun, in the subtle ether, and in the creative emission.
Mādhava, who is established on the true path, should be meditated upon in this way by all men who desire dharma, pleasure, and wealth, even though he belongs to his own particular caste.
He alone is the enjoyer, and he alone is that which is to be enjoyed; he is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Furthermore, it is he alone who is fit for the employment in all ritual actions.
Thus did the best of Brahmins cry out upon the drum sounding like a thundercloud,
having thus obtained the Dharma from the father of Dharmāṅgada.
O twice-born ones, having learned that his son was indeed endowed with the proper rites and superior even to himself,
he spoke to his wife, who stood there like another Lakṣmī, filled with joy.
O Saṃdhyāvalī, I am indeed blessed, and you too, O woman of excellent complexion;
for a son born of us both shall be as white as the moon upon the earth.
"Liberation is heard of through the ears, but it has never been seen by anyone anywhere;
yet that liberation, which arises from a virtuous son, has been attained by us in abundance."
O lady of excellent hips, when a son is endowed with discipline, possessed of good conduct and heroism,
and full of prowess, the liberation of his father from the household is certain.

O lady of beautiful limbs, through the performance of auspicious and virtuous deeds, a father becomes "Śatānanda"— one who possesses a hundredfold bliss— by means of his son, for bliss is the very form of Brahman.
O Goddess, there is nothing equal to this in the world of the moving and the unmoving:
that a virtuous son takes up the burden and carries it for his father. (NarP 2.9.48)
Therefore, O large-eyed one, I shall go joyfully to the forest, accustomed to dwelling there to slay deer; wandering at my own will, freed from sin, for the sake of protecting people.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rukmāṅgada and Dharmāṅgada," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having heard her husband's words, that large-eyed lady spoke.
"O King, you have spoken the truth: there is no happiness greater than the joy of having a son. (NarP 2.10.1)
O Indra among kings, it would not be so here as the speech of the sages says;
for in this world, he who is called Viṣṇu is indeed supreme and equal [to all].
The burden consisting of the seven continents has been placed by you upon your son;
therefore, abandoning violence toward living beings, worship Janārdana with sacrifices.
Abandoning desire for enjoyments, serve the celestial river;
this is what is right, O sir, for the capture of a deer is not right.
O King, they know that for those who have sons, indulgence in sensual pleasures is like the scratching of a nail upon the heart of an aged woman.
Or else, O lord of the earth, worship Hṛṣīkeśa in your own home;
it is not fitting for you to be the slayer of blameless herds of deer.
Non-violence is proclaimed in the Purāṇas as the supreme dharma;
for one who lives by means of violence, dharma becomes futile.
Indeed, he who pursues violence, even while performing religious duties, makes those duties in vain. (NarP 2.10.7)
O King, the virtuous do not consume that which has been destroyed by others.
O King, these six kinds of killing of living beings have been declared by the wise.
The one who approves [of the act] is traditionally considered the first killer; the second is the one who provides confidence; the third is the one who serves as the vessel; the fourth is the eater;
the fifth is said to be the cook; and the sixth is the king who accepts the vessel.
For the wise know that dharma and adharma are always joined with injury.
O King, having entrusted the burden to his son,
the father— whose hair has turned grey and who has properly taken refuge in righteousness— does indeed commit no evil.
Abandoning this disposition arising from the slaughter of deer, for kings who behave like deer have perished by the hundreds, O King. (NarP 2.10.11)
Therefore, I consider that act to be indeed wicked wherein there is the slaughtering of animals;
for compassion toward animals is seen even among the virtuous who possess self-knowledge.
"I have indeed restrained you again and again out of a desire for your welfare.
To his wife who was speaking thus, the king spoke these words: (NarP 2.10.13)
O Goddess, I shall not roam through the forest with bow in hand under the pretext of hunting deer, while performing the clearing of the thorns [of my enemies]. ||| NarP_2,10.14 |||
"O fair-faced one, let there be a son for me among people, while I myself shall dwell in the forest;
for the subjects must be protected from wild beasts and bandits by the king."
O auspicious lady, subjects must be protected by oneself or by one's son;
for a king who fails to protect his subjects falls into ruin, even if he is righteous.
Therefore, O beloved, with the intent of protecting [you], I shall go to the forest,
having become free from worldly attachments, like the sun upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Having thus addressed her, the king mounted that excellent horse,
which was as radiant as the lord of the stars (the moon), faultless, and an ornament of the earth.
Equal to a celestial steed in form and equal to the wind in speed, the protector of the earth, having raised his right hand, bestowed it upon him. (NarP 2.10.19)
He is the giver of thousands of crores, the presser of the breasts of passionate women,
whose form is like an ashoka sprout, and from whom the vajra-hook grows forth.
Setting out, that protector of the earth, that best of kings, shook the surface of the world as he traveled through various regions and forests. (NarP 2.10.21)
Driven by the force of the wind, the elephants, chariots, and horses, along with the foot soldiers,
fell down upon the circle of the earth, rendered unconscious.
O King, having traveled across more than one hundred and eight yojanas, that monarch suddenly arrived at the supreme hermitage of the sages.
He entered the delightful hermitage, adorned with groves of plantain trees,
endowed with *aśoka* and *bakula* trees, and covered with *punnāga* and *sarala* trees.
With mātuliṅgas, kapitthas, dates, jackfruits and the like,
as well as coconuts, tālas, ketakas, and sinduvārakas.
With sandalwood trees, tamālas, sāl trees, pippalas, and campakas;
with betel nuts, pomegranates, and thousands of dhātrī trees.
It was densely covered with many nimba trees, as well as mango and lodhra trees,
which were bent down by ripe fruits and frequented by birds perched upon them.
Indeed, being accompanied by the wind of that very day, which was filled with the fragrance of flowers,
the king, beholding the sage, saw him possessing the brilliance of fire.
Having dismounted from his horse and seeing Vāmadeva, the best of the twice-born, who was surrounded by many disciples, he bowed down to him with reverence.
That sage, having been honored by the king with offerings of water for the feet and other honors, sat upon a silken seat and spoke with a joyful voice: NarP_2,10.30 //
Today my sin has been exhausted; the fruit of my past actions has been attained, having beheld your lotus feet while remaining steadfast in perfect meditation.
Having heard those words of King Rukmāṅgada and having inquired after his welfare, Vāmadeva spoke with great joy.
O King, O highly fortunate one, because my hermitage has been beheld by you, who are exceedingly meritorious and a devotee of Viṣṇu, it has become sacred upon the surface of the earth.
On this earth, what other caste can attain equality with that king by whom Vaivasvata Yama himself was defeated and broken? (NarP 2.10.34)
O King, having observed the sin-destroying Dvādaśī fast, the entire world has been led to the imperishable abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having restrained the subjects on earth through the four excellent means,
Madhubhid led those established in their own duties and those engaged in improper acts to his own abode.

O King, protector of the earth, even though he is a dog-cooker (outcaste), this devotee of Viṣṇu has come into our sight, though we were desirous of seeing him; indeed, he is superior to the twice-born. (NarP 2.10.37)
But even a twice-born man devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu is worse than a dog-eater;
O King, kings who are devotees of Viṣṇu are rare upon this earth.
A king who seeks to secure the fortune of the earth must not be a non-Vaiṣṇava; he who is not a devotee of Ravi (the Sun) may have devotion toward other gods, but he cannot be a true king. 2,10.39.
Just as a woman who is devoted to a lover abandons her husband,
so too does that king certainly commit such a transgression.
O Viṣṇu, you have performed the worship of Viṣṇu in accordance with the principles of justice, for the sake of attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and even wisdom.
"Therefore you are blessed, O King; we too are blessed by the mere sight of you.
To Vāmadeva, who was speaking thus, the best of kings [replied]. (NarP 2.10.42)
Bowing down, he who was by nature endowed with humility said:
"O best of the twice-born, I beg your forgiveness; O Lord, I am not such a person as you have described."
"O Brahmin, I am indeed not equal to the dust of your feet;
for in this world, the gods are never superior to the Brahmins. (NarP 2.10.44)
When the twice-born are well-pleased, a living being gains devotion toward Mādhava;
when they are angry, he becomes an object of their hatred. This which I have spoken is the truth. (NarP 2.10.45)
Vāmadeva said to him: "Tell me, O King, what shall I give you? There is nothing that should not be given to you who have now come to my home."
For on this earth, O protector of the earth, he who gives a drum on the day of Viṣṇu to prohibit the feeding of his subjects achieves his desired goal. (NarP 2.10.47)
Then the king, with palms joined in reverence, said to that brahmin:
"Everything has indeed been attained by me simply from beholding the pair of your feet."
"O Brahmin, a single doubt has persisted within me for a long time;
I ask it of you, the foremost of the twice-born, who shatter all doubts. (NarP 2.10.49)
By what meritorious deed did Trailokyasundarī become my wife, she who always gazes upon me with a look that exceeds even the god of love? (NarP 2.10.50)
Wherever the goddess of excellent complexion places her foot,
there the earth reveals hidden treasures.
O best of sages, her limbs, free from old age and devoid of wrinkles or gray hair, always shine like the splendor of the autumnal moon.
O Brahmin, even without fire, she indeed prepares food of six flavors;
whatever small amount of food she cooks, millions eat from it. (NarP 2.10.53)

O Brahmin, she who is devoted to her vows, whose nature is generosity, and who brings happiness to all beings, was not treated with contempt even by a word from one who was fast asleep. (NarP 2.10.54)

O best of the foremost of the twice-born, the son who is born from her shall always abide by my command; indeed, O most excellent of brahmins, he shall be my very own son upon the surface of the earth.
My son is devoted to his father and indeed surpasses him in the accumulation of virtues;
I am known throughout the surface of the earth as the lord of a single continent.
"My son has become superior, a protector of the seven continents, by whom, O best of Brahmins, the king's daughter was brought here for my sake. (NarP 2.10.57)
Renowned as Vidyullekhā after defeating kings in battle,
she was then [taken] by that lord, who was distinguished by his beauty and wealth.
Having conquered [the enemy] in battle within six months and rendered them all weaponless,
he went to the kingdom of women and defeated those women in combat.
From among those beautiful women, he brought eight excellent maidens;
having bowed down to me again and again, he gave them all to me.
Whatever divine garments and whatever jewels exist on the surface of the earth,
my son, as described by his mother, gave them all to me.
In a single day, having traversed the entire earth for many yojanas, he returns again at nightfall for the purpose of massaging my feet. (NarP 2.10.62)
At midnight, having massaged his limbs, he stands at the gate clad in armor,
rousing the servants whose senses are overwhelmed by sleep.
Likewise, O best of sages, this body of mine is free from disease;
my happiness is immeasurable, for my beloved wife is under my control at home.
There are indeed steeds and elephants, as well as infinite wealth and grain;
for every person on earth is a follower of my command.
By the power of what karma is this present happiness mine— is it that which was performed in this life, or likewise that which was performed in another birth?
O Brahmin, having reflected with your own intellect, tell me what my merit is.
Freedom from disease in the body, a beloved wife under one's control at home, prosperity, devotion to Nṛhari,
honor among the learned, and the capacity to give to the twice-born— I consider all this to be born of well-performed merit.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rukmāṅgada and Vāmadeva," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard those words of the king, the lord of sages, the possessor of great knowledge, [spoke].
Having reflected for a moment and understood the cause, he spoke to him.
Vāmadeva said:
"O protector of the earth, in former times you were born into the Śūdra caste;
you were overcome by poverty as well as by a wicked wife."
O King, by serving others and receiving wages for his labor,
he dwelt there for many years, tormented by suffering.
Once, O lord of the earth, you went on a pilgrimage to sacred fords due to the company of brahmins;
thereafter, you traversed all the holy sites.
Devoted to the service of the twice-born, you went to Mathurā, which is of a meritorious nature;
there, through the company of brahmins, you bathed in the waters of the Yamunā.
O King, listen to the story being told concerning the sacred ford named Viśrānti— the most excellent among all sacred fords— and the temple of Varāha.
And he heard from the Purāṇas the vow of Aśūnyaśayana,
the completion of which is ordained by means of four ritual breakings of the fast.
By performing which, the Lord of Gods, who resembles a rain-cloud,
the husband of Lakṣmī, the Lord of the World, and the destroyer of the entire mass of sins, becomes pleased.
O King, by returning once more to your palace,
you have made that meritorious dwelling a place where the bed is never empty, bringing supreme prosperity to your home.
O Great King, without performing this vow which destroys all sins,
one who enters the life of a householder would be as fruitless as a barren woman;
such happiness appears to me to be difficult to find in this world.
O Lord of the Earth, on the second day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, this meritorious vow, which removes birth, death, and old age, should be undertaken. (NarP 2.11.11)
O King, the Lord of the World, accompanied by Lakṣmī, should be worshipped here with fruits,
flowers, incense, and beautiful red unguents;
likewise, with gifts of beds, gifts of garments, and the feeding of Brahmins.
O King, all this that you have undertaken is exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
it is the fulfillment of that very same deed which was not left unfulfilled, O Lord of the Earth.
Now listen in detail to these meritorious [deeds] which you yourself have mentioned first.
"It is certain that [these things] would not come to pass if the Lord of the World were not pleased;
in a previous birth, O Lord of Gods, you worshipped Him while being free from worldly attachment."
O Indra among kings, since you worship Hari on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in this life,
O King, you will certainly and surely attain union with Viṣṇu.
O King, this most auspicious question of yours has been explained by me;
it is endowed with the source of all prosperities and serves to bring about the exaltation of one's kin.
"O protector of the earth, what else shall I give you here or do for you?
You are certainly worthy of everything; you are a devotee of Janārdana."
The king said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am eager to go toward Mount Mandara;
by your command, I desire to see the many wonders there. (NarP 2.11.18)
O best of the twice-born, having become light and abandoned his father,
he took upon himself the burden arising from the governance of the kingdom, which is difficult even for kings to bear.

"Therefore, having departed to live as I please, my son shall perform my duties. Having heard these words of the king, Vāmadeva spoke this: NarP_2,11.20: "He who acts according to his own will has departed; let my son perform that which was my duty. Having heard the king's speech, Vāmadeva said this.
For this indeed is the supreme duty of a son toward an eminent king: that he always lovingly delivers his father from suffering. (NarP 2.11.21)
And by carrying out his father’s word through the power of mind, speech, and body,
he obtains the merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī day after day.
"But having disregarded his father's word, if he should go to bathe in the celestial river (Ganges), there is no purification for that son; such is the Vedic revelation."
Therefore, O lord of the earth, go as you please; you have accomplished your purpose.
By the grace of Hari, that meritorious son has been born into your lineage.
When the sage had spoken thus, the illustrious one mounted his horse and departed with swift speed, like the Wind-god himself.
Beholding all the mountains, forests, and rivers,
as well as all wonders, lakes, and groves, the king of kings [proceeded].
In a very short time, he reached Mount Mandara,
having caused the White Mountain and Mount Gandhamādana to revolve as well.
Having passed beyond Mount Mahāmeru and beheld the Northern Kurus,
[he saw] that which resembles a hundred suns and is entirely covered in gold.
That region of the earth, strewn with mountains and adorned with many minerals, was being rubbed by the arms of Hari, causing golden sap to flow forth.
It was joined by many waterfalls, adorned with many caves,
filled with tens of thousands of rivers, and washed by the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā.
O King, there were groups of trusting young women, enjoying the pleasure of their lovers,
who were as large as jars, fully matured, and fragrant.
It was adorned with fruits produced by young women, as if by their breasts;
it was joined with the humming of bees and resounded with the song of the cuckoo.
Beholding the mountain resounded on all sides by the cries of many creatures, the king entered that great mountain.
Desiring to climb it out of curiosity, he searched for its growth along which path; as soon as he looked all around, he beheld the entire multitude of birds upon that tree.
Spreading forth, seized by the sound arising from the mouth of Vimohinī,
and rushing forward with speed, the king went quickly along with that very sound.
Into his ear also entered that deluding sound which had arisen from the mouth of Vimohinī;
deluded by it, he abandoned his mount as if being leaped over by Trivikrama.
In an instant, the king suddenly beheld the path along the mountain, which was charmingly sung of by the bewildered;
it stood upon the mountain, glowing like molten gold, appearing as if it were a sacrificial pillar fashioned for Kāma.
She was like the emblem of Śakra fixed in the sky, as if being worshipped for the sake of the world's progeny;
she was like the very embodiment of forbearance, and like a mass of beauty belonging to Rasā, the daughter of the mountain.
Like the shore of the ocean, she was endowed with beauty; he suddenly dragged her body, known as Rati’s bower, which rested upon the *liṅga* for the sport of the gods, before the Three-eyed Lord.
Standing there, manifesting the form of Vimohinī, he perceived the mental longing of the one who had performed that merit;
pierced by the arrow of desire for Vimohinī, the king fell down, utterly deluded.
His body seized by a violent fever, he quickly approached her;
Sunetrā beheld the spreading monarch with a sidelong glance.
Having set aside her lute, she ceased her singing and suddenly considered her task accomplished;
shaking the flocks of birds and beasts, she covered her cheeks and arms with her fine garment.

Leaving behind Hara, the most worshipful one with his excellent phallus, the goddess of noble conduct went to the side of the king, leaving behind her arrows that were charming with the sweet fragrance of her breath. (NarP 2.11.43)

The deluding woman, whose eyes were like lotus petals in the water, spoke these sweet and charming words to Rukmāṅgada, who was tormented by the arrows of love: "Arise, O King! I am under your power."
O King, why do you exhaust this body with fainting, when you, who regard even this great burden of the earth as a mere blade of grass, have beheld my enchanting form? (NarP 2.11.45)
