Why do you despair, O weak Gaurī? Remain submerged here in the mud!
You are steadfast; why do you mock yourself, whose conduct is noble? ||| NarP_2,11.46 |||
"O lord of kings, if you have a desire for my most charming and agreeable amorous dalliance, then,
having bestowed the gift prescribed by the true Dharma, enjoy me— who am skilled in the arts of love— as if I were your own slave-girl."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Vision of Mohinī," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When those beautiful words had been spoken by Mohinī, the king then—
Then, O Indra among kings, he opened his eyes which resembled hundred-petaled lotuses.
Stupefied by the sight of the enchantress, he spoke these words with a faltering voice:
"O girl, O you whose face resembles the full moon, many times before have I [seen such as you]. (NarP 2.12.2)
Such forms have been seen and experienced before, yet nowhere has a body such as this ever been seen,
like the form you bear, which bewilders the world.
O lady of beautiful countenance, merely by the sight of you, I was pierced by the arrows of the god of love and suddenly fell to the ground;
O Goddess, rendered speechless, I am utterly bewildered by your splendor.
O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, show me favor; I shall give you everything that resides in your heart.
For one whose mind is bound by love for you, there is nothing in these three worlds that cannot be given.
O beautiful one, this earth has mountains as her ornaments, the ocean as her garment, and the moon and sun as her eyes;
she has clouds for breasts, the sky as her well-bound body, and is devoid of groves, possessing a lovely nature.

O fair-browed one, I am the giver to you of Pātālaguhya—a land with many trees for its hair, possessing seven lower realms, bound with treasuries, filled with elephants and horses, delightful to the heart of the assembly, and endowed with cities. (NarP 2.12.7)
"O lady of beautiful limbs, I would give even my own self to you in union;
how much more so wealth, jewels, and the like? Be gracious to me, O enchantress! (NarP 2.12.8)
Having heard the king’s words spoken in sweet syllables, Mohinī then smiled, raised the king up, and spoke to him.
"O lord of the earth, I do not choose the earth together with its mountains;
whatever I shall determine at the proper time, that task should be carried out without hesitation."
"I shall serve you, of this there is no doubt; make a covenant with me.
The King said:
"O Goddess, whatever covenant by which you are satisfied, that I shall make."
My body has reached its tenth stage without union with you.
Mohinī said:
"Let your right hand, which performs many righteous deeds, be given [to me],
O King, so that I may have confidence in your word."
"You are a king whose character is rooted in righteousness, whose fame for truthfulness extends through the three worlds;
you would never speak an untruth at such a time, for this path has been established by worldly custom."
O King, as she was speaking thus, the lord of kings, the ruler of men, afflicted by desire in his heart,
replied to her with a very gracious mind.
O fair-thighed one, from my very birth I have never spoken an untruth, even in jest or during moments of play, O lady of beautiful voice.
Or rather, what is the use of these words consisting of syllables of conviction?
For here is my right hand, marked with auspicious signs, which has been offered by me.
O beautiful one, O fair-thighed lady, if you do not follow my word, then whatever good deeds I have performed since birth shall all be for your sake.
"For in the meantime, O lady, this Dharma was entrusted to me by you as my wife;
yet, because of your beauty, agitation has suddenly arisen within me."
I am the son of Ṛtadhvaja, the king named Rukmāṅgada;
born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, my son is Dharmāṅgada.
"O lovely-eyed one, having entered the dense forest under the pretext of hunting,
I then beheld in the woods the heart-pleasing hermitage of Vāmadeva."
The Sage spoke something there, and by that he was dismissed;
mounting his excellent vehicle, he came to see Mount Mandara.
Then, wandering with a mind full of curiosity,
I reached the best of mountains and heard the song that had issued from your mouth.
Drawn by that song, I have come into your presence;
and you, O lovely-eyed one, have entered the path of my vision.
Then, O Goddess, I fell to the ground unconscious and deprived of my senses;
but now, indeed, I am endowed with consciousness through the nectar of your words.
O deluder of the world, I consider myself as if born again;
you ought to show me favor by granting me an answer.
Addressed thus by the king, Mohinī spoke these words in reply:
"O King, I am born of Brahmā; I have come here for your sake. (NarP 2.12.27)
Having heard his fame, she, filled with desire, abandoned all the gods, led by Viśvaṃbhara, and went to Mount Mandara, the golden mountain. (NarP 2.12.28)
With their minds composed, they remained there devoted to ascetic practice, worshipping Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, with songs and offerings. (NarP 2.12.29)
O King, I consider the gift of song to be most dear to the gods;
it surpasses all other gifts and bestows an infinite state.
By whom Paśupati was pleased and who immediately returned the favor—
that very person I desired, you, the protector of the earth, has been found by me.
"You are pleased with me, O King, and I am indeed pleased with you. (NarP 2.12.32)
Having thus addressed him, that enchanting woman took the king’s hand with her moon-like face and swiftly raised him from where he lay upon the ground, as if she were the staff of Indra.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Making of the Agreement," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having raised the king up, Mohinī spoke these words.
Do not entertain doubt, O Indra among kings; know that the maiden is free from sin.
"O protector of the earth, marry me according to the rites prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras;
for if an unmarried maiden, O King, should bear a child..."
She gives birth to a Divākīrti, who is censured by all social classes;
the wise know that there are three such births from the womb of a Caṇḍāla according to the Purāṇa.
One [wife] was born from a maiden, a second was of the same lineage,
and a third, O bull among kings, was born of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa.
"For this reason, O King, marry me, a maiden.
Then, on that mountain, King Rukmāṅgada [married] her, whose sidelong glances were tremulous.
Having married her according to the prescribed rites, the king stood as if smiling.
The king said:
"O lovely-faced one, the attainment of the third heaven would not please me as much as this."
O Goddess, just as your arrival here on Mount Mandara is for our happiness,
I consider myself, O Goddess, to be even more superior than Purandara upon this earth.
"O fair-eyed one, having obtained you, the beauty of the three worlds, as my wife, I shall do whatever is agreeable to you; please command me."
"O young girl, will you take your pleasure right here, or in my palace, on Mount Malaya, on the peak of Meru, or in the Nandana grove? Tell me."
O King, having heard those sweet words of the monarch, Mohinī spoke these words of repentance, which increased his joy. (NarP 2.13.10)
O protector of the earth, the wounds from the side-glances of my co-wives will exist within your city;
how can I go to your capital? (NarP 2.13.11)
May no woman whatsoever on the circle of the earth ever experience,
until her death, the suffering born of a rival wife.
O protector of the earth, having obtained you and come under your control by my own will, I recognized that my husband had been made [unhappy] by the suffering arising from a rival wife. 13.13.
"I shall dwell upon this best of mountains, which is filled with many wonders;
for you, O Indra among kings, do not dwell anywhere without Saṃdhyāvalī."
In her absence, you will be sorrowful along with your son;
O King, through your suffering, my own suffering shall become immense.
"Wherever you find happiness, there I shall also remain;
wherever you take delight, O King, there for me is Mount Mandara."
For a wife must dwell even with a husband who is destitute of wealth;
they declare that Meru, composed of gold, is present wherever he is.
O Lord, that mountain where you take delight is called Manoratha;
it has been abandoned by its master and even avoided by its own father.
A woman who delights in taking refuge in the state of her father sinks into darkness;
even if she is devoid of all dharma, such a woman becomes a sow.
"I recognize this danger; how shall I dwell on Mount Mandara?
O Lord, you are my equal in both pleasure and pain."
Having heard those words of Mohinī, the king, his mind filled with joy, embraced the woman of beautiful hips and spoke these words: NarP_2,13.21 //
"You shall stand above all my wives;
do not harbor fear, O fair-thighed one, for it will lead to suffering. (NarP 2.13.22)
"O fair-browed one, you shall be dearer to me than life itself in my home;
come, O slender-limbed one, let us go toward the city for our happiness."
O beloved, staying there, enjoy pleasures with me according to your own desire.
Thus addressed by Rukmāṅgada for the sake of her own destruction, she— her face as fair as the moon,
adorned with the sound of tinkling anklets— set forth, trailing behind her the splendor born of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Bewildering of Mohinī," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, both of them set out from the mountain peak toward the surface of the earth.
They beheld many enchanting objects born of the mountain.
Some resembled coral, some were like silver,
some had the appearance of sapphire, and some possessed the luster of gold.
Some had the luster of the color of crystal, while others resembled yellow orpiment;
they attained a state of mutual union as if with all stationary beings.
Having reached the earth, the king indeed beheld the best of horses digging the ground with its swift hoof,
which was like a thunderbolt.
As he was tearing up the earth with his very sharp hoof,
a house-lizard indeed emerged from within that spot of ground.
O King, as she was emerging, torn by his hoof, the king, who was devoted to compassion, saw her being rent asunder. (NarP 2.14.6)
Crying out "Alas! Alas! for his beloved, the lord of the earth rushed forward with speed; then, with a tender leaf from a tree, [he covered her].
Having quickly removed her from his hoof, he cast her onto a bed of grassy turf;
then, seeing that Mohinī had indeed fallen into a swoon, he spoke to her.
"O lovely-limbed one, O lotus-eyed one, quickly fetch water so that I may sprinkle the house lizard that has fainted from being crushed. (NarP 2.14.9)
At her husband’s word, she quickly brought cool water;
with that, the king sprinkled the house-lizard who had been unconscious.
He regained consciousness, O King, from the sprinkling of cool water;
for the sprinkling of water is prescribed in all cases of injury. (NarP 2.14.11)
"Or rather, O King, a sudden binding with a wet cloth is beneficial. Having regained her consciousness, the iguana spoke these words. (NarP 2.14.12)
Beholding the king before her, afflicted by pain, she spoke slowly and softly:
"O Rukmāṅgada of mighty arms, understand my actions."
"In the beautiful city of Śākala, O Lord, I was indeed the wife of a brahmin;
endowed with beauty and youth, I was not very dear to him."
"O King, he who was always filled with hatred toward me and spoke harshly to me, yet hated no one else—he is my husband. (NarP 2.14.15)

Then, filled with anger because I had been deprived of the power of subjugation, I asked those women who were said to have been abandoned by their husbands: "O noble ladies, is there anyone [who can restore me]? (NarP 2.14.16)
"O King, they said to me: 'Your husband shall become submissive to us. Trust was produced in us because of the abandonment and insult of our husbands. (NarP 2.14.17)
"For our husbands have indeed been brought under our control by the medicines of renunciation;
ask her, O lady of beautiful limbs, and she will give you the auspicious medicine."
"You must not entertain any doubt; the husband will become like a servant.
Then, O King, having gone quickly at their word, I [acted]. (NarP 2.14.19)
As she was asking me, that palace was described by the men to her as being provided with a hundred pillars and endowed with beautiful white plaster.
Having entered that place, I saw a female ascetic (brahmacāriṇī) possessing great splendor,
clothed in a long garment whose color was like the glow of twilight.
Enveloped by long matted locks and endowed with radiance,
she was accompanied by attendants who fanned her very gently.
Holding a rosary in her hand, Bhagamālinī was reciting the mantra that brings all things under control, causes agitation, and produces immediate results.
Then, having bowed down and placed upon his feet my ring made of soft gold and endowed with extraordinary luster, I spoke.
Then, seeing the ring resting at her feet, she became joyful;
even without being asked, she realized that my husband had been insulted by her.
Then, O King, having been addressed by that female ascetic, I stood before her with a prostration;
she said, "This powder, endowed with protection, brings all beings under one's control."
"You must unite him with his husband and guard the sprout resting upon his neck;
thus your husband will become submissive and will not go to another beautiful woman."
Having taken the protective powder, I returned once more to my husband's house;
at nightfall, the powder mixed with milk was administered to my husband.
O best among the most excellent kings, when my husband had drunk the powder, I applied the protection to his neck; indeed, I did not hesitate. (NarP 2.14.29)
On that day, he became afflicted with consumption; day by day the lord grew emaciated, and worms were born in his private parts, arising from a wound and a malignant ulcer.
After a few days had passed, my husband, his vigor destroyed by the sight of the sun as if it were a lamp, spoke to me with agitated senses.
Crying out day and night, "I am your slave, O beautiful one!
Save me, who have come to you for refuge; I shall not go to another woman. (NarP 2.14.32)
O Lord of the Earth, having heard his weeping, she was struck with fear and reported everything to her [mother], saying, "How may my husband become happy? (NarP 2.14.33)
She also gave a second medicine for the sake of pacifying the burning sensation;
once that medicine was administered, the husband became healthy at that very moment.
The burning pain arising from the previous powder was pacified by that medicine;
from that time forward, my husband became submissive and remained obedient to my word.
In due course, I met my death and went to the torments of hell;
indeed, I was burned in a copper frying pan for fifteen yugas.
Having divided it into many minute fragments the size of sesame seeds,
she cast it down upon the earth with the remainder of a slight sin.
"O King, I am she who was turned by the son of Bhāskara into the form of a house-lizard;
I have remained here for ten thousand years in the past. (NarP 2.14.38)
Furthermore, O King, whatever young woman practices subjugation over her husband,
being of vain virtue and evil conduct, she is burned in a copper frying pan.
The husband is the protector, the refuge, the lord, the deity, and the very teacher;
how can she who is subject to his will ever attain happiness? (NarP 2.14.40)
She goes for a hundred lifetimes among the animal wombs, afflicted with worms and leprosy;
therefore, O protector of the earth, women should always carry out the word of their husbands.
O King, if you do not rescue me today, who have come to you for refuge, I shall enter once more a loathsome womb, burdened by sin. (NarP 2.14.42)
Indeed, by the gift of your well-performed deed born of victory,
you have observed the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī on this meritorious day of union.
At the confluence of the Sarayū and the Gaṅgā, which effects the destruction of sins,
there is the meritorious Pretaniryātanī, which grants one's heart's desires.
O protector of the earth, in whatever house Hari is remembered by men, he bestows the fruit of all sacred fords; of this there is no doubt.
O King, whatever has been given, recited, offered in sacrifice, or performed such as the worship of the gods—
all that becomes inexhaustible when performed on the day of Vijayā.
Grant me that merit which yields such a fruit as this:
fasting on the twelfth day and breaking the fast on the thirteenth. (NarP 2.14.47)

O protector of the earth, by practicing compassion, you have become the very embodiment of Dharma on this earth; through this fast, you shall obtain the fruit of twelve years of fasting. (NarP 2.14.48)
"Destroyer of the path of Vaivasvata, protect me who am deeply distressed!
Having heard the words of the house-lizard, Mohinī spoke these words: (NarP 2.14.49)
"O Lord, a person experiences the fruits of their own deeds, consisting of both pleasure and pain;
therefore, what need have I for this sinful and wicked wife of mine? (NarP 2.14.50)
O King, by means of spells, protective powders, and the like, a husband was brought under her control;
whatever is done for virtuous people, O King, shall result in fame and heaven. (NarP 2.14.51)
Whatever sin may have been committed by both [parties], it perishes when milk mixed with sugar is offered to the son of Kadrū (the serpent deity). 2,14.52.
Just as that causes the poison to increase, so too would it result in the commission of sin;
therefore, abandon this sinful woman and let us indeed go to the city.
"The self-welfare of those who are attached to the activities of worldly existence perishes.
Rukmāṅgada said:
"O daughter of Brahmā, why have you uttered such a statement?"
"O fair-faced one, this conduct does not belong to the virtuous. (NarP 2.14.54)

O lady of excellent limbs, those who bring happiness to themselves through evil deeds become tormentors of others; yet when they have fallen into calamity, they truly become instruments for the benefit of others.
The moon, the sun, the rain-cloud, the earth, fire, water,
sandalwood, trees, and the virtuous— these indeed exist for the benefit of others.
It is indeed heard, O fair-faced one, that there was once a king named Hariścandra,
who dwelt in the house of a caṇḍāla and sold his wife and son.
Fearing false speech, he went from suffering to even greater suffering;
yet, because of his truthfulness, the gods, led by Śakra, were well-pleased with him.
They invited King Hariścandra to choose a boon;
and by that truthful man, the gods led by Brahmā were addressed:
"If you gods are indeed pleased, you ought to grant me a boon."
For this entire city, along with its trees and reptiles, its children, elders, and youths, its women, and its four-footed creatures— NarP_2,14.60.
"Let my city Ayodhyā go to heaven even though it has committed sin;
taking upon itself the guilt of Ayodhyā, I shall surely go to hell. (NarP 2.14.61)
"I do not go alone, O tigers among the gods, having abandoned my people on earth; this which I have spoken is the truth. (NarP 2.14.62)
Knowing his steadfastness, that city, together with him,
went to the heavenly realm by the permission of Indra and the other gods.
That king, remaining in heaven together with his own city,
was honored even by the immortals while traveling in a celestial chariot that moves at will.
O Goddess, out of compassion, Dadhīci indeed gave the gift of his bones for the sake of assisting the gods, after hearing that they had been defeated by the Daityas. (NarP 2.14.65)
O lady of excellent limbs, in former times King Śibi gave his own flesh to a hungry hawk for the sake of a pigeon.
In former times, O fair-faced one, there was a king named Jīmūtavāhana upon the circle of the earth;
by him also, his very life was given to a serpent.
Therefore, O Goddess, a ruler of the earth must be compassionate;
for the rain-cloud pours equally upon the pure, the impure, and the auspicious alike.
Even a Cāṇḍāla or an outcast may gladden the moon with its own rays;
therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, take this lizard which is so deeply distressed.
"By my own merits, I shall rescue her, just as the son of Nahuṣa rescued his daughter-in-law by means of his grandsons.
Having thus spoken, he cast aside the deluding house-lizard and addressed her.
"Whatever merit has been bestowed by me upon you, born of my victory, go now to the worlds attained by Viṣṇu, with all your impurities shaken off. (NarP 2.14.71)
At those words, O King, she was suddenly adorned with divine ornaments and cast off that worn-out body born of a house-lizard.
Having taken leave of that king, she departed, illuminating the ten directions and appearing as if she were creating a parting line for the extraordinary footprint of Viṣṇu.
Since that which is accessible to yogis, radiant as fire, most excellent, worthy of worship, and become the supreme self—
that [light]— this daughter born of the king, like a lamp of fire, exists for the illumination of the world.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the House-lizard," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having liberated the house-lizard from her sin, the king, as if smiling, spoke.
Delighted, he said to Mohinī, "Mount the horse quickly."
And he could travel ten thousand yojanas in an instant, like Kṛṣṇa’s horse;
having heard those words of the king, Mohinī became languid with passion.
She mounted that horse, swift as the wind, together with her husband;
and the lady of the lovely smile spoke these words to her husband, the king: NarP_2,15.3 //
"O Lord of the Earth, impel this swift chariot toward your own city;
your longing to behold the face of your son has become insatiable."
"O best of kings, you are dependent on me; go wherever your mind desires.
Having heard the words of Mohinī, he set out toward the city. (NarP 2.15.5)
Beholding the trees, mountains, rivers, and most wonderful forests, as well as various kinds of wild animals, he was greatly delighted.
Villages, forts, as well as countries and auspicious cities,
diverse lakes, and most enchanting regions of the earth.
O King, having seen Vāmadeva’s hermitage before long,
the protector of the earth, stationed in the sky, paid his respects with great haste.
Once again the king proceeded with a horse swift as the wind,
beholding many lands endowed with wealth and grain.
The king reached the city of Vaidiśa and brought it under his own control;
having heard from his spies that the king was approaching, his son Dharmāṅgada [prepared for him].
Filled with joy, he addressed these words to his father and the kings:
"O best of monarchs, this northern direction is approaching its fulfillment."
"My father’s horse was seized by him, and his splendor has been stained by yours;
therefore, let us all go into the presence of the lord of the earth."
A son must not go directly in front of his father as soon as he has arrived;
he goes to a terrible hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
The twice-born experts in the Purāṇas declared that for a son walking face-to-face toward his father, there is the fruit of a sacrifice at every step. (NarP 2.15.14)
"Arise! Surrounded by you, I am going now to affectionately salute this god of gods, who is my deity."
When all the kings had thus spoken and offered their praises, the prince then went on foot for the distance of one *krośa* to meet his father.
Then, accompanied by a thousand kings, he who was like the god of love incarnate traveled a long distance and encountered the king on the road.
Having reached his father with affection, he then descended to the ground;
together with the kings, he then offered salutation with his head.
Seeing him fallen along with the kings,
the lordly king dismounted from his horse, embraced his son who had come together out of love, and raised him up.
Then the king, having firmly embraced his son with his well-developed arms and smelled the crown of his head, spoke to him thus.
Do you protect all your subjects? Do you punish your enemies?
And do you maintain the treasury, my son, with wealth acquired through righteous means? (NarP 2.15.21)
I trust you have bestowed upon the Brahmins a most excellent and enduring livelihood;
I trust your conduct is pleasing and that your speech is never harsh. (NarP 2.15.22)
I hope the cows are not milked at the house of a Cāṇḍāla, my son;
and I hope your sons always carry out the words of their father.
I hope your daughter-in-law follows the words of her mother-in-law, and that she occasionally attends to her husband;
I hope you do not look upon disputes with your son, O Brahmin.
I trust that the cattle are not obstructed in your realm by various kinds of fodder; and indeed, do you constantly supervise all scales and measures of food and other goods?
O son, are you not excessively oppressed by taxes for the sake of your family?
And does gambling, drinking, and such [vices] not prevail in your realm?
I trust that in your city, the people do not subsist on gifts of food of inferior flavor or on rags from others, nor do they live by means of fragmented speech. (NarP 2.15.27)
I hope that, having seen them yourself, my son, you protect the elephants and horses;
and I hope that you regard all your mothers without distinction.
"O son, I hope that men do not eat during the day on the day of Viṣṇu;
and I hope that a man devoted to the ancestral rites does not do so when the moon has reached its waning."
And do you always abandon sleep during the latter parts of the night?
For sleep is the root of unrighteousness; sleep is the increaser of evil.
Sleep is the mother of poverty; sleep is the destroyer of prosperity.
Indeed, a king possessed by sleep does not long rule the earth.
"Like an unchaste woman who always destroys both worlds for her husband,"—as he was speaking these words, his son addressed him with this speech: (NarP 2.15.32).
Dharmāṅgada, having bowed down again and again to the protector of the earth, said:
"O father, all this has been done; I shall carry out your word once more."
Sons who carry out the word of their father are blessed in the three worlds;
what sin, then, could a king commit who does not obey his father's word? (NarP 2.15.34)

If one should go to bathe in the triple-pathed river (Ganges) while disregarding the word of one's father, he does not enjoy the fruit of that sacred ford, provided he does not carry out his father’s command. (NarP 2.15.35)
My body is dependent on you; indeed, my life is dependent on you.
My dharma is dependent on you, and you are my supreme deity.
"O Lord, even by giving away the three worlds, a son would not be purified of his debt; how much less so by the gift of one's body, wealth, hair, and so forth? (NarP 2.15.37)
To his son who was speaking thus while surrounded by many kings, Rukmāṅgada embraced him and spoke these words again to his son:
"O son, you who know the dharma, what you have uttered is true. (NarP 2.15.38)
Indeed, for a son, there is no deity whatsoever superior to his father;
the gods turn their faces away from him who holds his father in contempt.
Therefore, my son, you have been held by me upon my head for the sake of protecting the earth;
having conquered the earth with its islands, which is filled with many kings.
This is the supreme happiness in the world; this is the certain state of heaven—that a son should become even greater than his father upon the circle of the earth.
Thus, my son, I have been made successful by you through the path of virtuous conduct,
as you have accomplished the task of subduing kings on this auspicious day of Hari.
Having heard those words of his father, the son Dharmāṅgada said: "Where have you gone, dear father, after entrusting all these riches to me?"
In what place has she, who possesses a radiance equal to ten thousand suns, arrived?
I think that the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) created her out of a sense of world-weariness.
"Among all the women in the three worlds, there is no such form as this for the protection of the earth; I believe she is born from the mountains, or perhaps she has arisen from the ocean."
"Or perhaps it is the illusion (māyā) of the Daitya Maya, existing in the form of a woman. Oh, how very skillful is the Creator by whom she was fashioned, O Lord!
For even a hundredth part of the tip of a hair's breadth of falsehood is not possible."
O Lord of the lords of the earth, this maiden, bright as gold, is indeed worthy to be your wife;
if my mother were such as this, what other man could be more fortunate than I?
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Father and Son," in the *Mohinī-carita* of the latter portion of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard the words of Dharmāṅgada, Rukmāṅgada spoke joyfully.
"O son, it is true that I have reached Mount Mandara with you."
In the past, O son, this young girl, the daughter of Vedāśraya, having made a firm resolve for my sake, performed severe penance on Mount Devagiri.
Fifteen days from now, I shall indeed depart for Mount Mandara, the best of mountains, which is endowed with many minerals, riding upon my horse.
There, I saw Sudarśanā standing upon his head, intent on singing to please Maheśvara, while carrying the sacrificial offering for Bala.
Then, pierced by the arrows of the Bodiless One like a deer struck by a hunter, I fell to the surface of the earth overcome by a swoon.
Then I was moved by this goddess of beautiful eyes,
and she chose me as her husband along with a certain request.
And I also made a vow:
"This large-eyed woman shall be my wife," and so she was placed upon the summit of the mountain.
Having dismounted from the horse onto the surface of the earth and then remounted it,
he arrived in your presence with haste within three days.
Beholding the mountains, regions, lakes, and likewise the rivers—
O son, this is indeed your mother, who increases your joy.
"Salute Cārvaṅgī as if she were your own mother.
Having heard those words of her father, the subduer of enemies [remained] mounted upon his horse.
Having fallen to the ground with his head, he spoke these words:
"Be gracious, O Goddess; you are my mother, my servant, my slave, and your son."
"Accompanied by many kings, O lord of the earth, I pay homage to my mother;
for she beheld that son of hers, having reached the ground, and was filled with delusion. (NarP 2.16.12)
And out of devotion to her husband, she dismounted from her horse and,
lifting up her fallen son, embraced him with both arms.
Then, embraced by his mother, he greeted her once again;
thereafter, she honored him with very beautiful garments and ornaments.
Having adorned and readied that best of horses once more,
the lotus-eyed one placed his foot upon its back.
O King, by that very same rite he caused his father to ascend after him;
then the son Dharmāṅgada, surrounded by the lords of the earth, departed upon the path of the sky.
Indeed, his hair stood on end with rapture upon beholding his enchanting mother,
while he himself was being praised with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Blessed is that son in this world whose many mothers are his father’s beloved and enchanting wives, ever newer and more beautiful.
He whose mother alone in this world is his father is the one who partakes in suffering;
what happiness can exist in the heart of a son when his father is in pain?
By bowing to a single mother, one enjoys the fruit of the earth;
by bowing to many mothers, my merit shall become vast.
Therefore, day by day, his merit will become even greater as he utters this single [verse],
surrounded by kings.
Having entered the delightful city of Vaidiśa, which was endowed with prosperity,
the king immediately set out on horseback together with Mohinī.
Then, having reached his excellent palace while being honored by the people, the king dismounted from his horse and spoke these words to Māhinī: NarP_2,16.23 //
"O Manoharā, go to the house of Dharmāṅgada’s son;
there he will perform service for you according to his virtue."
"Neither a friend nor even a servant shall perform service for you," her husband said;
and having been thus addressed by her husband, she set out for the house of her son.
She was seen by Dharmāṅgada as she was indeed going toward her own palace,
having abandoned the kings at her husband’s command.
"Stay here at your father's command, for I shall serve him.
Having spoken thus, he went and took hold of him with both arms;
when the fifteenth step was reached, he helped him down onto a couch.
It was made of gold with a silken cord, both soft and firm,
provided with a gentle covering, and adorned with jewels and gems.
Then, upon that floor inlaid with many jewel-lamps and radiant as the sun,
Dharmabhūṣaṇa offered water for washing the feet to Mohinī.
Indeed, because Sandhyāvalī was his preceptor’s wife, the prince did not look upon her;
thus, his mind did not become corrupted toward that enchanting woman.
Though he was delicate, he regarded that slender-limbed woman— whose thighs, hips, and breasts were full—
as ten thousand years old, and himself as only three years of age.
Having washed her feet, he placed that water upon his head;
bowing down, he said, "O Mother, I am a man of merit."
Having spoken thus, he himself, along with the men and women, performed the removal of her fatigue and joyfully united her with all enjoyments.
When the churning of the ocean had begun, the two earrings that dripped with nectar were obtained;
having defeated the Dānavas, they were brought to Pātāla by the embodiment of Dharma.
Vṛṣāṅgada himself placed upon the ears of Mohinī auspicious beads resembling the fruit of the dhātrī tree, numbering one thousand and eight.
A necklace made of bright pearls was placed upon the Queen's chest,
along with a golden *niṣka* weighing a hundred *palas*, adorned with ten thousand diamonds.
Then the prince gave his mother a light necklace and sixteen bracelets set with diamonds for both her hands.
Her armlets and anklets were priceless; they had been fashioned by men skilled in valuation for a price of ten million gold coins each. That prince [gazed upon them].
He gave to his father’s beloved wife two ornaments with the splendor of the sun;
and he also gave the girdle of Śarvāṇī, which possessed the brilliance of fire.
Having fallen from that [position] during the battle with Tāraka, she was terrified by fear;
while Kālanemi held the kingdom, it fell into the hands of Mūlapācana.
But that [bow] was seized by the Daitya Maya, the world-deceiver;
having slain that Daitya in Malaya, who was surrounded by ten million Daityas.
In that terrible battle lasting a year, for the sake of carrying out his father’s command,
he obtained the waist-thread that had been worn by the beloved wife of the king of the Daityas.
The king, his hair standing on end with joy, gave her to his father’s beloved wife,
who had formerly been the world-beautiful consort of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Her son was Sīmantaka, who possessed a radiance like that of lightning;
when the auspicious lady entered the fire together with her husband, [he was born].
Having thrown the hair-parting into the ocean, she was overcome with great sorrow;
but the Ocean, it is said, took up that pair of excellent jewels.
Then, gratified by his valor, Dharmāṅgada gave him [the sword];
delighted, he gave it to his mother, which possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns.

The row of teeth possessed the luster of the moon, and her ankles were hidden for the sake of enchanting people; indeed, the entire form of that woman with beautiful, wide eyes was visible from head to foot.
The king, out of extreme joy, considered himself more than successful among the gods;
"Aha! This large-eyed girl of beautiful form will ask for whatever it is, and that alone shall be given. (NarP 2.19.34)
In this beautiful and auspicious sexual union, I shall bestow upon her at the end my entire wealth;
even that which is very difficult to obtain, and what others would not give, I shall give to her, or even what is not to be given.

"Even though my life is not to be given away, O golden-hued one, if she should ask for it, I shall give it without hesitation; there is nothing that cannot be given to her, except for my son. (NarP 2.19.36)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Mohinī’s Love," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
And so it was for King Rukmāṅgada, who was thus infatuated by amorous passion.
Indeed, three and five years have passed away in happiness.
When his ninth year had arrived, the powerful son Dharmāṅgada,
having conquered five Vidyādharas on Malaya, the best of mountains, [ascended it].
He brought five auspicious jewels that grant all desires;
one of them was an auspicious giver of gold, possessing millions upon millions of virtues.
The second [tree] likewise bestows garments, ornaments, and so forth, worth hundreds of millions;
the third drips with nectar and restores youth.
The builder of the assembly hall was the fourth, the preparer of food the fifth, the giver of the celestial realm the sixth,
and the one who traverses the three worlds the seventh.
Taking those jewels in his mind, accompanied by the Vidyādharas and surrounded by the wives of the Vidyādharas whose eyes were filled with tears, he departed.
He paid homage at the feet of his mother and his father, Rukmāṅgada;
then, having offered five jewels at their feet, he spoke while bowing low.
"O Father, O Lord of the Earth, these five Vidyādharas were conquered by me in battle on Malaya, the best of mountains, with the Vaiṣṇava weapon."
"O best of kings, these have come to serve you along with their wives;
grant jewels to Mohinī for the purpose of adorning her arms."
For these indeed grant all desires and restore youth;
by wearing these jewels, those with decayed teeth become young again.
By your splendor, those who bestow garments, palaces, gold, the attainment of heaven, and even immortality have been brought under your control through a month-long battle.
"O King, these seven continents have been conquered by me with great difficulty; by your majesty, they have all been made to pay tribute. (NarP 2.20.12)
A year has passed for me while I was in the ocean;
O father, Bhogavatī, which is filled with nāgas, has been conquered by me.
I have also brought ten thousand Naga maidens there,
and I have likewise brought back a great many necklaces of jewels.
Furthermore, O dear one, I went to the great city of the Dānavas;
having conquered them, [I took] maidens who were beautiful and radiant.
I have brought three thousand and five [loads],
as well as one hundred million jewels, for the purpose of lighting lamps at the arrival of night.
O protector of the earth, as they were performing [the rites], those [beings] were brought to your palace;
from there, I went to the world of Varuṇa, situated at the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala).
"Intoxicated by the power of his vigor, he has gone there to serve the pair of your feet;
there he addressed the god Varuṇa, saying, 'Stay under the command of my father.'"
If you wish to live, O King Rukmāṅgada,
Varuṇa has arrived to fight, enraged by my words.
A terrible battle took place for a year in the subterranean realm (rasātala);
that lord of the waters was defeated by me with the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
He was not slain by the words of the women for the sake of preserving his life;
rather, ten thousand horses, swift as the wind, were given by him when he was defeated.
On one side are those white horses with a single black ear, possessing the luster of the moon,
who have lived for many years deprived of grass and water.
Placing a single maiden of beautiful form before me, well-adorned, Varuṇa gave her to me as a wife; that auspicious woman was also brought by me.
But the maiden was brought back accompanied by vast wealth;
O dear one, her abode is difficult to reach, for she is the sovereign of the three worlds.
"There is indeed nothing that has not been conquered by me through the service of your feet; therefore, arise and behold the prosperity acquired by your grace."
"And all my current prosperity, O lord of the people, is dependent upon you,
dear father, since you say that this fortune was acquired by me through your son."
It must not be given to the gods of the earth; he too would surely go to hell.
My son, a son must certainly not indulge in self-conceit.
A son who is like an axe or a sickle in the gathering of wealth increases his father’s accumulation of riches through his own valor. (NarP 2.20.28)
Taking up a fiery sickle, he cuts through heaps of grass;
like a cloth filled with air, he carries across one who has entered a boat upon the water.
Just as a wooden puppet moves by the will of a magician,
so too do these sons, endowed with splendor and strength, act through the vital power of their father.

Therefore, O best of the assembly of mothers, behold this beloved of Mādhava-deva who has been brought by me today; let her give or let her protect it according to her own will, for she possesses her own wealth.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The World Conquest of Dharmāṅgada," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Māndhātṛ said:
Having heard the words of his son, what did the lord of the earth do?
And she too, O Brahmin, was the enchanting Māyinī, the beloved wife of King Vidhi and the daughter of Brahmā.
This wondrous narrative you have related is like nectar;
it is especially meritorious and shatters all doubts.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard those words of his son, that bull among kings rose up with his beloved,
and he gazed upon those goddesses of prosperity.
O King, for a moment the monarch, who was devoted to Viṣṇu, was filled with joy;
and all those Nāga maidens, together with Vāruṇī, were likewise delighted.
Out of love for his son, he gave him to Dharmabhūṣaṇa as a wife;
the remainder, along with many jewels, was given to the wives of the Dānavas.
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, the king, his father, divided the wealth collected by Dharmāṅgada and gave it to Mohinī.
Having summoned his domestic priest at the proper time, the king said this to him:
"O Brahmin, let my son take the hands of all these women according to the sacred law."
"This prince has always remained steadfast in my word regarding the maidens;
at the auspicious moment of the wedding lagna, under a constellation that fulfills all desires."
"Having had the twice-born recite benedictions and having gratified them with cows, gold, and garments, perform the marriage of my son Dharmāṅgada. (NarP 2.21.9)
That dull-witted father who does not perform the marriage of his son in this world shall sink into a terrible, bottomless hell for ten thousand ages.
Therefore, a father endowed with righteousness should marry off his son;
for he by whom a son is established has truly established himself.
O Brahmin, when the marriage of a son— whether he be endowed with virtues or devoid of them— is performed, he shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
Indeed, a father desiring to fulfill his duty must arrange a marriage;
for what father would fail to unite his sons with wives and wealth? (NarP 2.21.13)
He should be known as no man at all, despised both in this world and the next;
therefore, sons should be provided with a livelihood and established together with wives.
"Listen to how those sons, being contented, well-honored, and happy, take their delight.
Having heard these words of the king, the brahmin who was his family priest—
Filled with joy and intent upon the marriage to Dharmāṅgada,
that youth, though desiring the pleasures of women, was restrained by his sense of shame.
Then, at his father's word, he took wives—
those enchanting Naga maidens— together with the daughter of Varuṇa.
The mighty-armed one married them all— women peerless in beauty on earth—
having wedded them according to the rites prescribed by sacred law.
With joy, he bestowed gifts of wealth, cows, and jewels upon the Brahmins;
having taken a wife, he then delightedly saluted the feet of his mother and father.
Then his son Dharmāṅgada said to Queen Saṃdhyāvalī:
"O Queen, by my father’s command, I have taken a wife."
"This is not in my mind, O Queen: that I was wedded by my father; for I shall indeed serve my wise and imperishable father. (NarP 2.21.21)
"I have no need for divine enjoyments, nor even for heaven;
my duty is to serve my father and you as well, day and night."
Saṃdhyāvalī said:
"Live long, my son; enjoy happily the pleasures that accord with your heart. By the grace of your father, may you be long-lived; gladden my mind, O my son. (NarP 2.21.23)
"O son, by you, a virtuous son, I have become truly blessed with offspring on this earth;
indeed, I now dwell within the hearts of all your co-wives."
Having spoken thus, and having embraced him and smelled his head repeatedly,
he then dismissed his son to attend to the administration of the kingdom.
Then, dismissed by his mother and having paid homage to his other mothers,
he remained steadfast in his father’s word and administered that entire system of governance.
He carried out the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous;
he traveled through all lands and observed all activities.
He conducted a monthly inspection of all affairs everywhere;
likewise, he oversaw the maintenance of elephants and horses and monitored the network of spies.
Day after day, the king conducted an inspection of weights and measures,
and he ensured the protection of men in every household.
Nowhere does a breast-fed infant, deprived of the breast, fail to weep; nor does a daughter-in-law, even when insulted, ever weep before her mother-in-law.
In some cases, a capable son did not have to beg his father for anything;
furthermore, no intermixture of castes occurred within their kingdoms.
The world does not find fault with the Dharma when its true nature is concealed;
yet a woman who has a husband should never be without her bodice.
In my kingdom, let there be no going out of the house for women;
let not a widow have her hair, nor let one who has lost her husband be hairless.

Let not one who is observant of vows, nor one who reviles constantly, nor one from the forest, nor one who dwells in the city, nor one who fails to give the common livelihood remain in my kingdom— let such a pitiless man depart.
Let no cowherd who longs for the city, nor one devoid of virtues yet acting as a teacher, nor a priest lacking scriptural knowledge, dwell here in my kingdom. (NarP 2.21.35)
For those two evildoers who produce indigo by over-sprinkling it with indigo dye, as well as he who manufactures liquor, shall both be banished. (NarP 2.21.36)
He who eats meat in vain, he who is fond of the flesh of the back, and he who abandons his own wife—there is no place for him in my kingdom. (NarP 2.21.37)
He who, abandoning Viṣṇu, the best of the gods, should worship any other deity, shall go to a pregnant young woman who has recently given birth; and he shall be punished and put to death by our men.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Phonetics," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
In this manner, Dharmāṅgada ruled the kingdom upon the surface of the earth.
O Indra among kings, by the command of his father, he was observing the day sacred to Hari.
O lord of the earth, there was no person whatsoever who was not established in dharma; there was no one unhappy, none without offspring, and none who was not prosperous.
O King, while that people was joyful and well-nourished, the earth itself yielded treasures; and the cows were like vessels that milked out their desires, with calves always satiated.
In every tree, there will be honeycombs the size of a *droṇa* measure;
and when the earth is delighted, there will be the production of all kinds of grain.
In an age rivaling the Kṛta-yuga, at the end of the Tretā and the Dvāpara ages,
when the rainy season had passed and the sky was clear within the house.
In places rich with ripe, fragrant śāli rice, gazed upon by the one born from a jar (Agastya), and where rivers flow with moderate currents on all sides; NarP_2,22.6 //
With *kāśa* flowers growing on the banks like the white hair of a woman,
the world was bright as the moonbeams, while the sun shone without excessive heat.
In that place, it was surrounded on all sides by kings who had come with great eagerness, accompanied by throngs of men and adorned by their ritual ablutions in the water.
At the time of Viṣṇu’s awakening at the end of the month of Āśvina, Mohinī, afflicted by the god of love, took her pleasure with that Teacher of the World at that very moment.
With her whole being, Sundarī served the king with various pleasures in the forests,
on mountain peaks, and at the confluences of rivers.
In various lakes rich with lotus flowers, on Malaya, Mandara, Vindhya, Mahendra, and the abode of the gods; 2.22.11.
On the Sahya and the auspicious Prāleya mountains, on the Diṅnāga mountain,
and on others such as Svargasthāna and so forth, [he established] the king.
O Indra among kings, she took delight in him day after day with her divine form;
and the king, having obtained that enchanting woman, abandoned all his duties.
Not even a most foolish king would neglect that vow of Viṣṇu, which cuts through birth and death, nor would he let a single day pass without it being observed.
The king abandons his play during the three days beginning with the tenth;
thus, while he was so sporting, a full year passed by.
O best among those who know the proper time, the auspicious month of Kārttika has arrived;
it is the month that bestows merit and brings an end to Viṣṇu’s sleep.
O King, whatever meritorious deed is performed by Vaiṣṇava men there indeed becomes inexhaustible and bestows the world of Viṣṇu. (NarP 2.22.17)
There is no month equal to Kārttika, no age equal to the Kṛta;
there is no dharma equal to compassion, and no light equal to the eye.
There is no scripture equal to the Veda; no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā;
no gift equal to land; and no happiness equal to a wife.
There is no wealth equal to agriculture, no gain equal to cows;
there is no austerity other than fasting, and no auspiciousness equal to self-restraint.
There is no satisfaction equal to that of the tongue; there is no other equal to a twice-born man;
there is no friend equal to dharma; and there is no fame equal to truth.
Sages know that there is no sovereignty equal to health, no god superior to Keśava,
and nothing in the world as purifying as the month of Kārttika.
The month of Kārttika is preeminent and is always dear to Viṣṇu;
indeed, he who passes this month, so beloved of Dāmodara, without observing vows, [is lost].
Excluded from all righteous dharmas, he falls into the womb of an animal.
Māndhātṛ said:
O Sage, having obtained Mohinī—who was possessed of enchanting power—in the month of Kārtika, how did King Rukmāṅgada enjoy her? Tell me.
Devoted to Viṣṇu and intent on sacred revelation, that most excellent of kings was the foremost among rulers;
what did that best of monarchs do during that most meritorious month?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having seen that Kārttika had arrived, which marks the awakening of Hari, the king of kings, being deeply infatuated, spoke these words to Mohinī. (NarP 2.22.27)
O Goddess, for many years I have enjoyed myself with you;
fearing your displeasure, I have never said anything at all to you anywhere. (NarP 2.22.28)
O lady of auspicious countenance, listen now to what I wish to say:
O Goddess, many Kārttikas have passed while my mind has been attached to you.
"No one born in Kārttika has ever observed a vow, with the single exception of the day of Hari;
therefore, I desire to observe the Kārttika vow. (NarP 2.22.30)
For those mortals who have passed the month of Kārttika without observing vows, their sacrifices and meritorious deeds, as well as their dharma originating from Brahmā, are in vain. (NarP 2.22.31)
Even those kings who were meat-eaters and excessively fond of hunting abandoned meat during Kārttika and went to the abode of Viṣṇu, O auspicious one.
For when a restriction is observed during the month of Kārttika regarding foods that are normally consumed,
the practitioner certainly attains the very nature of Viṣṇu.
"O woman of excellent complexion, let alone those gifts that require great wealth;
by giving even a lamp, which causes no distress to the heart, one shall go to heaven. (NarP 2.22.34)
O fortunate one, since even that [lamp] may be absent, one should always perform the kindling of another's lamp with a spirit of devotion; that is superior to all other gifts.
On one side are all gifts, and on the other side is the gift of lamps;
the awakening [of the Buddha] through the gift of lamps is said to be equal to the month of Kārttika.
It is remembered that this should always be performed with a spirit of devotion as being superior to all other gifts;
and having observed the lunar day of Kārttikī, one should offer it at the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu.
He who passes the month of Kārttika with vows, fasts, and observances is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt.
Having become a celestial deity dwelling in a divine mansion, he attains the supreme goal;
therefore, O deluding one, abandon your delusion toward me.
"Give me your command; at that time I shall perform the Kārttika vow, O lotus-eyed one, for I have ceased from the worship of your breasts."
"I shall indeed be a bearer of vows in the worship of Hari.
Mohinī said:
"Relate to me in detail the greatness of Kārttika."
"O best of kings, it is said that this month is a mine of all merit;
O high-minded one, tell me where it is specifically so designated."
"Having heard the greatness of the month of Kārttika, I shall perform whatever I desire."
Rukmāṅgada said:
O fair-faced one, I shall declare the majesty of this month,
by which you will be inspired to perform the worship of Hari.
In the month of Kārttika, he who practices the *kṛcchra* penance, or observes the *prājāpatya*, or fasts every other day, or even fasts for three nights; (NarP_2,22.45)
Or else, O woman of excellent complexion, having spent ten days, a fortnight, or a month [there],
a man goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
By eating but one meal a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for,
men attain this very earth, garlanded with islands.
Especially at the sacred site of Puṣkara and at Śaukara in Dvāravatī,
this month is declared to bestow devotion through vows, gifts, worship, and other such acts.
That day is meritorious, as indeed is the Bhīṣmapañcaka;
having observed Prabodhinī together with a ritual vigil, a man [attains great merit].
O lady of excellent limbs, even a man burdened by sins shall not remain in his mother’s womb on that day when he beholds the mandala.
Without Sāṃkhya or Yoga, he goes to the supreme state by beholding the auspicious Maṇḍala of Śaukarika on a Sunday during the month of Kārttika.
Upon seeing either the Kokavarāha [temple], one shall not be born again;
by seeing it, men obtain liberation from even the threefold evil.
O lady with tremulous eyes, one should likewise avoid the *maṇḍala* and *śrīdhara* [scents] at Kubjikā;
in Kārttika one should avoid oil, and in Kārttika one should avoid honey. (NarP 2.22.53)
In the month of Kārttika, one devoted to Viṣṇu should avoid meat; in Kārttika, one should avoid women; and in Kārttika, O Goddess, one should renounce flat beans.
One is instantly freed from the sin committed over a year;
however, by eating it even once, one enters a royal womb.
That evil-minded person who eats the flesh of a hog during the month of Kārttika is cooked in the Raurava hell for sixty thousand years.
Released from that [sin], he is born as a sinful village pig that eats excrement.
One should not eat the flesh of fish, nor that of tortoises, nor even that of deer. (NarP 2.22.57)
O Goddess, one becomes a caṇḍāla by eating meat during the month of Kārttika;
for Kārttika destroys all sins for one who observes even a small vow.
Initiation performed in the month of Kārtika cuts away the births of men;
therefore, one should undergo initiation with every effort in Kārtika. (NarP 2.22.59)
O fair-thighed one, everything performed by one who is uninitiated is fruitless;
a man devoid of initiation attains the womb of an animal. (NarP 2.22.60)
One should not perform the Kārttika vow at home, especially on the full-moon day of Kārttika;
for by performing the Kārttika vow at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a man goes to the abode of Hari.
Having observed the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
a man who gives auspicious water-pots in the morning goes to the abode of Hari.
For the completion of the year-long vows is traditionally held to occur in the month of Kārttika,
wherein the marriages of Viṣṇu are seen taking place within the lotus of his navel.
O woman of excellent complexion, there [in that place], four days are like one [day],
even without the time of the northern solstice and even without the purity of the astrological ascendant (lagna).

"Since in this month of Kārtika are seen such auspicious connections that increase one's sons and grandsons, I shall therefore perform the observance of a vow during this enchanting month. (NarP 2.22.65)
For the destruction of all sins without exception and for the increase of your pleasure, Mohinī said:
"Aha! The incomparable majesty of Kārtika has been proclaimed by you."
O Lord of the Earth, tell me the procedure for the completion ceremony of the Cāturmāsya vows, by which those vows may reach fulfillment.
"And let there be no deficiency in the vow that bears the fruit of merit.
The King said:
"O beloved, one who observes the *nakta* vow should feed a Brahmin with food of the six flavors. (NarP 2.22.68)
In the case of an unasked gift, however, one should cause a cow along with gold to be given;
he who abstains from meat should likewise give a cow together with a sacrificial fee.
During the ritual bath for Dhātrī, a man should offer curd and milk-rice;
O fair-browed one, when there is a vow regarding fruits, he should perform the gift of fruit.
If one renounces oil, one should give ghee; likewise, if one renounces ghee, one should give milk. If there is a restriction regarding grains, one should give śāli rice, or else that very same grain.
One who sleeps on the ground should give a bed provided with cotton wool and pillows;
a man who eats from leaves should give a vessel filled with ghee.
In silence, one should cause a bell or sesame seeds along with gold to be offered;
a meal for a married couple should be provided, together with a bed for both.
For the sake of fulfilling the vow, one should give a horse accompanied by a sacrificial fee at the morning bath; if there is no horse, one should give ghee and roasted barley flour.
One should give a mirror for the purpose of grooming the nails and hair;
one should give sandals when there is a need for protection of the feet.
Upon the renunciation of salt, a fragrant cow should likewise be given;
upon the relinquishment of meat, one should give a tawny cow with her calf.
O beloved, he who constantly offers a lamp in a temple during his desired vow [should offer] a lamp made of gold or copper, along with ghee.
One should offer an umbrella with a cloth to a devotee of Viṣṇu for the fulfillment of the vow;
one who observes a fast on alternate days should cause a linen garment to be given.
On the third night, one should give a well-adorned bed provided with gold;
on fasts of six nights and more, a palanquin accompanied by an umbrella.
One should offer a fat man with a horse-drawn carriage, or a goat and sheep;
for one who eats only once a day, a single piece of gold; and for one who subsists on fruit, a golden coin.
In the case of a vegetable meal, one should give a golden fruit combined with ghee;
and likewise for the renunciation of all juices, or even for that which is not specifically mentioned.
A silver vessel or even one made of gold should be given according to one's ability;
for if that which was prescribed is not given, or if it is not performed as stated, [the following occurs].
O fair-browed one, one should carry out the word of a Brahmin preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu;
for that man who, O auspicious lady, considers the word of a Brahmin to be in vain, [is lost]. (NarP 2.22.83)
Or if he does not give the sacrificial fee at all, he will certainly go to hell;
having incurred a deficiency in his vow, he is born as a leper and blind.
Established in the words of the gods upon earth are the celestial beings, the hosts of holy fords, and the sacrifices;
O fair-browed one, what wise man desiring his own welfare would transgress their word? (NarP 2.22.85)
This secret of the Dharma, endowed with truth, which was spoken by the Lord of Śrī to Virañci, has been revealed by me to you—
something not to be told to others, which bestows fruit and is the cause for the satisfaction of Mādhava.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Month of Kārttika," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Mohinī said:
"What you have spoken regarding fasting during the month of Kārttika is excellent."
The undertaking of vows and other such observances for kings has not been mentioned anywhere in the authoritative examples.
Except for the one [duty] belonging to the Brāhmaṇa in this world, nothing has been prescribed even for the Śūdra or the Vaiśya;
indeed, giving, protection, and warfare—the third—is ordained for kings.
Indeed, you must not undertake any religious vow if you wish me to be your beloved;
for even for a moment, O Indra among kings, I am unable to exist without you.
O Lord of the Vasus, how much more so for one who dwells there, radiant as the interior of a lotus; for you consider that fasting should be performed there for a number of months.
"In that regard, food should indeed be given to the high-souled Brahmins;
or else, let whichever wife is the eldest perform the vow and other rites.
When these words were spoken by Mohinī, Rukmabhūṣaṇa [replied].
He summoned his beloved wife, the auspicious Sandhyāvalī by name;
having been called, she arrived at that very moment before the king, who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
He was seated upon a divine couch, embraced by the arms of Mohinī,
and pressed against her breasts which resembled golden jars.
O Lord of the Earth, on the bed, the left-eyed woman, full of desire,
joined her palms in reverence and bowed her neck toward her husband.
Saṃdhyāvalī said to the king: "Why have I been summoned? What shall I do?
O beloved, I abide by your word, free from the misery of co-wives."
O King, for as long as you take delight with Mohinī, for that long my own pleasure increases; of this there is no doubt.
O King, that woman who becomes filled with sorrow due to the happiness of her husband shall become a female hawk for eight years— three and five.
"Give me your command, O Indra among kings; do not cause me grief by withholding my desire."
Rukmāṅgada said:
"I know your character, O beautiful lady, and I know your lineage;
for a long time I have been delighted by your words."
While he was enjoying himself for a very long time, many Kārttikas passed by;
yet, as he was infatuated with the pleasures of his beloved, the day of Hari did not pass.
Thus, having attained satisfaction through the enjoyment of desires again and again,
I have recognized this month of Kārtika, which brings about the destruction of all sins.
"O Goddess, O auspicious one, this daughter of Brahmā prevents me from undertaking the highly meritorious vow known as Kārttika."
"O woman of excellent complexion, you must by no means do anything displeasing to her;
instead, undertake my vow called *kṛcchra*, which withers the body."

Thus addressed by her husband, she who was of the color of fresh gold and possessed full breasts, spoke these words: "I shall observe a vow with my face turned toward the moon for the sake of your satisfaction. (NarP 2.23.18)

"O Lord of men and gods, I shall perform that very act by which fame and renown shall arise, and likewise happiness joined with glory shall be yours; O gentle one, for your sake I cast my body into the blazing fire."
"O protector of the earth, this is not right; indeed, I shall not kill my own son at your word. However, O gentle lord of men, I shall once again perform this rite of the vow. (NarP 2.23.20)
