By the power of destiny, knowledge, home, happiness, wealth, and lineage may come to be;
indeed, impelled by destiny, a person goes everywhere.
"O night-stalker, you yourself will certainly become his husband;
when fate has set the path, what can even a wise man do? (NarP 2.27.144)
Therefore, bring the brahmin who is staying here by the Śāla tree;
perform the marriage according to the prescribed rite with clarified butter, water, kuśa grass, and fire.
Even without *darbha* grass, water, or fire, according to the prescribed rule,
a marriage shall be fruitful through the word of a Brahmin alone.
"O Rākṣasa, if the Brahmin is not killed by your wife while the performance of the *homa* is still in progress, you shall devour him once that task is completed."
When these words had been spoken by the princess,
that Rākṣasa, his mind full of confidence and pride, went forth.
Overcome by desire, he stood outside in haste to bring him forth.
O Goddess, as he was departing, it is said that he himself sneezed;
his left eye throbbed, and likewise his garment caught and snagged.
But having emerged from the mouth of the cave without taking all of that,
he beheld his own broad-hipped woman, who was wearing a human form.
"I renounce you, a sinful Rākṣasa of cruel deeds, who seeks to establish a relationship arising from the union of wife and husband. (NarP 2.27.152)
"Attached to human women and a defiler of my body!"—
hearing those harsh words uttered by his wife,
the night-stalker, filled with jealousy and anger, rushed forward.
Raising his arms and opening his mouth wide, he set out to devour them both;
like a wind rising with great force, Kāla uttered words fraught with calamity.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāṣṭhīla," within the account of Mohinī in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Kāṣṭhīla said:
[I saw] a Rākṣasa running, resembling Yama, the Ender of Time at the close of an aeon.
Seeing him, that Rākṣasī, filled with apprehension, spoke to her husband: ||| NarP_2,28.1 |||
Hurl your gold-adorned spear, which resembles fire;
let this enemy of mine, who is dear to the naked ones (the Digambaras), meet his death!
At her word, my husband,
relying on his own prowess, released a massive spear toward the chest of the Rākṣasa.
Blazing, resembling fire, illuminating the ten directions,
with a face as sharp as divine rays, it resounded with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells.
With her limbs smeared with red sandalwood and adorned with red garments,
that Śakti, released from the hand of the Brahmin, fell upon his heart.
Having reduced the Rākṣasa to nothing but ashes, she departed into the sky;
meanwhile, the Rākṣasī, having struck down her own husband with the hand of a Brahmin, [remained behind].
With her hair standing on end from joy, she considered herself as one who had accomplished her purpose;
then the delighted Rākṣasī spoke to the twice-born man of auspicious eyes.
"Come, my beloved, enter this delightful cave at your pleasure;
enjoy together with me all pleasures, both divine and human."
"So be it," my lord of life then said to me with a joyful countenance;
thereupon, taking my beloved, I entered my cave with delight.
Without even noticing that it was the ashes produced from her husband’s body,
she pressed him against her with her two high breasts.
He showed him that slender maiden lying upon her bed;
she was dark-eyed with long outer corners, possessed lips like the *bimba* fruit, and had a complexion like gold.
O best of the twice-born, she was brought from Vārāṇasī to be his wife;
indeed, no sins whatsoever ever transgress her boundary.
They call that sacred field of Śakti a merit-bestowing place that destroys sin;
it is situated five *gavyūti*s from the abode of Tripurāri.
"O you, whose house mortals who die therein do not enter the womb again— lead this beautiful-eyed woman back to that ancestral home of yours."
"Sell all these jewels of yours, as well as your beds and seats, together with me, according to your own wish."
O Brahmin, for your sake that terrible Rākṣasa was slain by me;
infatuated by your beauty, he has been sent to the abode of Yama.
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, having placed your trust in me with your own self,
accept me, O large-eyed one— I who am devoted to you and can assume any form at will.
Having heard these words of the rakshasi, who was tormented by desire, my husband [spoke], O beautiful-eyed one, in the presence of the maiden, O auspicious lady.
But he, filled with apprehension, spoke these sweet words to that Rākṣasī: "O blessed lady, according to the treatises on ethics, women are not to be trusted. (NarP 2.28.19)
How is it that she who kills her husband when he is still a youth does not harm me,
for she is a woman passionately devoted to men, considering him superior to me in beauty?
Thus, O fair-faced one, I have placed my trust in you through a spirit of confidence.
"Whether today, or tomorrow, or in a fortnight, a month, or a year—kill me as you wish, O beautiful lady; I have sought refuge in you. (NarP 2.28.22)
In this very way you must act; no favor has been done for you today.
Your own self must be surrendered in every respect as the means for repayment.
"Since my husband was slain by you without hesitation for my sake,
therefore, O fair-eyed one, I shall say no further word to you."
Having heard those words of my husband, she said this:
"O Brahmin, the harming of one who trusts you would be equal to the killing of a Brahmin."
Even if you consider me thus to be a cruel ogress and a slayer of my husband,
nevertheless, how could I revile my husband, whom I have slain while he was trusting me?
For the course of Dharma is subtle; it cannot be understood in any way whatsoever by anyone—whether gods, daityas, rākṣasas, or others.
Some men, however, are skillful in contemplating the subtlety of Dharma. (NarP 2.28.27)
It is heard in the Purāṇas that some achieve the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) by means of this impermanent body; something regarding this will now be recounted.
In accordance with Dharma alone, the powerful Viṣṇu underwent manifold sufferings during the assumption of his ten incarnations.
Where is Śrīnivāsa Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, who laments for the sake of Sītā during such acts as being bound by the serpent-noose? (NarP 2.28.30)
"Where is the God of gods, the son of Vasudeva, whose form is pure consciousness and who transcends the entire phenomenal world?
Alas, what misery!"—thus he acted with tears, glances, and other gestures, performing the duties of a servant such as swallowing Arjuna.
O twice-born one, the activity of the Lord, who abides in accordance with dharma, is difficult to comprehend;
for Vyāsa himself— the son of Parāśara, the seer of reality whose form is the sacrifice, the divider of the Vedas—
was born from a seed that destroyed his virginity, was known as "the son of an unmarried woman," and later took another's wife.
Parivettā, Didhiṣū, Śantanu, Svaḥsaritpati, and the son of Didhiṣū, Vasu himself, were all subject to death through disputes with women. (NarP 2.28.33)
The recitation of the names of those Pāṇḍavas— who were born of a common womb as *kuṇḍas*, the sons of *golakas*— is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin.
That which those who meditate truly contemplate is the eternal embodiment of yoga.
Viṣṇu, who is devoted to the courtesan and provides instruction to Prahlāda and others;
Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of the asuras, the supreme deity of the gods of gods.
He is the destroyer of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, the supreme deity of the gods and the presiding divinity;
he is the destroyer of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, whose abode is situated in the palace of Svarṇākṣa.
The son of Jamadagni was himself perfected through asceticism, his sins burnt away;
he was a lord who performed the deeds of destroying the Kṣatriyas and committing the slaughter of embryos.
The twice-born Ṛṣabha, a yogi devoted to instructing the world,
became one who caused distress to the world while acting out of conformity with dharma.
Nārada, Nārada again and again, even repeatedly Nārada;
he is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, he is Nāra, he is Nara, he is devoid of pride, and he is immortal.
Gautama, Gautama, the brahmin devoted to the conduct of a cowherd, composed a treatise associated with subjects outside the Vedas and rendered service to the Vedas. (NarP 2.28.41)
Vasiṣṭha was born of Urvaśī, and Agastya himself was also a lord;
by whom [this] supreme Vāsiṣṭha scripture was [composed] for the sake of benefiting the world.
In whom the Purāṇas and the Vedas were formerly established and attained their final form;
he who was himself the preceptor of Rāmacandra, the Lord of All.
How did he, who was cursed by Gādhi’s son, come to enter the womb of an animal—
he who, being all-powerful, had subdued the Vindhya mountain, Vātāpi, and the ocean?
How can he, who is the giver of the dead, perform such a difficult task—
he who is the procedure itself, who is to be honored as a witness to ritual acts, and who is the venerable Grandfather?
And how did he,
who is Śiva himself, the bestower of auspiciousness, the Lord of Nature, and higher than the highest, cast off his body while deluded by Māyā?
How could he, who frequents the wives of gods and whose conduct is impure like that of a cemetery, be worthy of it?
Therefore, O twice-born one, the rules of right conduct must always be practiced according to the prescribed injunctions.
The best of the wise, who is not to be abandoned and so forth, being endowed with the cultivation of that [self],
shall attain the foremost peace, which is righteous and established in both ways.
Dharma is remembered as that which leads to liberation, and wealth has Dharma as its sole means;
therefore, I have accomplished Dharma, whose essence is the highest of all forms of wealth.
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall now explain to you the subtle course of dharma in this matter:
when my husband arrived, he was taking away his daughter. (NarP 2.28.50)
"Seeing you established in your own duty, there is indeed no fault in him at all.
But how was this maiden brought here by me? Thus was he questioned. (NarP 2.28.51)
Then he spoke a false word for the purpose of devouring me; having heard that, he bound me and himself remained there to watch. (NarP 2.28.52)
Those who say that in the state of husband and wife the wife is an obstacle to liberation should be known as not seeing the truth; for she is not an obstacle. (NarP 2.28.53)
A wife rescues her husband from sin as he falls into hell;
she is a wife who is like a creeping vine of karma that bestows further worldly existence.
"O excellent one, listen well for yourself to what sin there is in this:
even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat, a falsehood must never be spoken. (NarP 2.28.55)
One should practice truth alone, being directly established in dharma;
Brahmā is firmly rooted in truth, and the virtuous are likewise firmly rooted in truth.
"The entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, is ever established in truth;
one should speak the truth"—this is the word proclaimed in the Vedāntas. (NarP 2.28.57)
Truth is indeed the very nature of Brahman; we meditate upon that Truth.
O Brahmin, Truth is eternally auspicious and the bestower of auspiciousness.
One should not speak the truth regarding women, for untruth in such cases brings about one's own destruction and produces immediate conviction; hear now the reason for this. (NarP 2.28.59)

In such injunctions as "one should not tell a secret treasure to a woman," the prevention of faults is stated; that [injunction] generates a dharma which demonstrates the subtlety of dharma. (NarP 2.28.60)
Where the kusha grass, the twice-born, water, fire, the Vedas, the earth, time, the quarters,
and the gods serve as witnesses in marriages, that union is declared to be between husband and wife.
The rite of *samaṅgīkaraṇa* is prescribed for marriage;
it is ordained for the consecration of a woman and a man, as well as for a teacher and a disciple.
Therefore, the teacher and the disciple, as well as the bride and the groom, should recognize one another;
no difference between these two, even so much as an atom, should be perceived by one who possesses true knowledge.
Because the predominance of the husband or the wife conforms to their respective past actions (*karma*),
if there is ever the fault of a reversal [of roles], divine destiny (*daiva*) alone is the cause in this matter.
The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is dependent on destiny;
that destiny consists of the latencies of karma accumulated in previous births.
Practicing whatever has been attained, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, he conducts himself according to his own will; O Brahmin, the wise know such a person to be tranquil.
"Peaceful, of truthful conduct, yet a deceiver of the world—having understood him to be such as this, my husband was not struck down. (NarP 2,28.67)
"Purified from the sin of violating a maiden and having attained the destination of the virtuous through my favor, he has passed away, struck down by your hand."
"O best of the twice-born, though I knew the subtlety of dharma, I rendered service to my husband;
for in the protection of your life, O Brahmin, I found my own dharma."
Understand correctly from me what was attained by that dharma:
having entered the womb of a rākṣasī, I have indeed become the beloved of a rākṣasa.
But the Brahmin woman Kāmarūpā was born for the sake of Dharma;
she is a cow that milks the desires of Dharma, and contentment is her Nandana grove.
Knowledge is said to be the bringer of liberation, while craving is the Vaitaraṇī river.
My husband, who was falling into the Vaitaraṇī, has been rescued by me here.
And a favor has been done for her, O Brahmin, by her being placed in the house of one of the highest caste;
moreover, she shall remain an unattached wife in her father’s home.
"I am always the protector of you and of her, awakening you to the Dharma;
she who was previously your wife, O Brahmin, [is now] through my union."
"This beautiful-faced wife of yours shall become your companion; she too, having entered the state of an animal, shall be liberated through my grace. (NarP 2.28.75)
"O twice-born one, in a previous existence I was a woman named Kandalī, renowned as the most beautiful in the world, the daughter of the sage Aurva."
Through the power of my asceticism, a twin pair was born;
the man who was born with me has been subdued by me for the sake of dharma.
O best of Brahmins, by that very Aurva, I was given as a remnant to Durvāsas;
having obtained him as my husband, O lord of sages, I am indeed subject to the power of my past karma.
Delighting in quarrels, she was cursed by her husband and reduced to ashes;
due to a small remnant of sin, she entered the womb of a rākṣasī.
In that womb, I obtained this husband, the lord of the Rākṣasas named Gobhila, who was full of splendor; he has been struck down by you.
O best of the twice-born, in his earlier years he suffered from consumption;
you have begun the funeral rites for a certain princess.
But I, freed from the state of a rākṣasī through the power of my former auspicious karma, have been born as your companion.
"O Brahmin, I was made miserable by my husband long ago because of his abduction of a maiden;
then, O Brahmin, that sinful man was slain by me as my wife."
"Since you indeed trust me with your whole heart, therefore,
O lover, I shall protect you with my entire being."
This is your true oath, witnessed by the five elements;
it has been uttered by me here in the presence of the entire person.
O best of the twice-born, you never act otherwise than as agreed;
O giver of honor, you must abide by my word in all undertakings.
Having heard these words spoken by the Rākṣasī,
he accepted everything that she had then done.
Then that rākṣasī, having gathered all the wealth from the cave and assumed the form of a female elephant, placed my husband upon her back.
Accompanied by that large-eyed Ratnāvalī, she, filled with joy,
traveled by way of the sky toward Kāśī, O fair-eyed one.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāṣṭhīla," within the account of Mohinī in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Kāṣṭhīla said:
"O fair-browed one, thus that Rākṣasī, assuming the form of a female elephant..."
In three muhūrtas, they reached Kāśī, the temple of Viśveśa.
Having reached that city, the dark-eyed woman said to her husband:
"O beloved, this [news] is proclaimed to be an axe for the tree of sin."
O beloved, this Durodarī has been described as the gold of the six waves;
she quiets the seeds of karma for all and bestows the ultimate goal. (NarP 2.29.3)
For the ancient sages declare that the primordial station belongs to Viṣṇu;
liberation for anyone is never possible in a place that is not Vaiṣṇava.
O best of the twice-born, this city of Mādhava was formerly the giver of liberation to all beings and the destroyer of all sins.
Once, Lord Śaṅkara went to see the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the sole creator of all worlds, who was blazing with his own splendor.
Having gone there, Mahādeva paid homage to Brahmā, the teacher of the worlds, and stood before him, listening intently to the recitation of the Vedas.
Seeing the Lord of the World joyfully uttering the four Vedas through his four wonderful mouths, he then became filled with delight.
Then, having observed that fifth face of Brahmā to be so arrogant, the Lord of Beings became instantly filled with indignation.
O best of Brahmins,
the three-eyed Lord, born of wrath, cut off with the tip of his fingernail that bold mouth of his which was situated in the sky.
O best of the twice-born, that severed head remained attached to his left sprout-like hand; though shaken incessantly, it did not come off.
Brahmā, having become distressed, stood gazing at Sthāṇu;
Rudra, too, having become ashamed, departed with haste.
Although he strove in many ways, being distressed to cast off that head, he was unable to relinquish it; that was a great wonder.
Becoming agitated with anxiety, he remembered the one whose banner is Garuḍa;
and as soon as he was remembered by him, that Lord appeared swiftly.
O twice-born one, having seen that Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods of gods who is omnipresent,
the bull-bannered Śiva, deprived of his luster, bowed his head in prostration.
Observing that he was thus afflicted and terrified, Hari comforted the slayer of a Brahmin and spoke these words intended to bring him satisfaction.
O Śambhu, you have committed a sin in that you severed the head of Brahmā;
O Omniscient One, enjoy the fruit of that which was done by yourself for some time. (NarP 2.29.17)
One must inevitably experience the results of the deeds one has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
for indeed, O dear one, an unexperienced deed does not perish even in hundreds of lifetimes.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go, having seen you, Hara, so distressed?
My very life-breaths are failing me at the sight of your suffering. (NarP 2.29.19)
Whatever great sins there may be committed against the great,
it is my opinion that they are not equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
You, who are the teacher of dharma and the preceptor of the entire world,
being overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, are not able to remain even for a moment.
O Lord of the Gods, this most terrible slaughter, smelling of fish and afflicted by old age, pursues you with its tongue lolling, seeking to seize you.
Therefore, you should not remain in one place for twelve years;
you must wander for the sake of your own welfare and with the desire to destroy your sins.
Having wandered for twelve years through all the sacred fords,
washing his left hand while receiving alms in a skull-bowl, he [proceeded].
"O Lord of Gods, you shall attain purification from this most terrible sin.
Having been addressed thus by Viṣṇu, O Brahmin, Sthāṇu became omnipresent.
Having wandered for three years while washing his hands in the water for the sake of releasing his skull, he reached Badarikāśrama.
"O giver of honor, O Viṣṇu, son of Dharma, god of gods! Standing at the door for the sake of alms, give me alms," he said repeatedly.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, seeing Hara standing at the door, said,
"Accept alms," and extended his right hand.
Then, O best of the twice-born, seeing Hari prepared to give alms, Hara struck his right hand with his trident.
From the wound of that trident, three streams terrifying to the world,
twelve *prasthas* in length and of variegated colors, issued forth.
Then one stream of blood fell upon the skull;
a second reached her mouth, and then a third fell upon the milk.
The stream of water reached Śiva as the cause for Hara’s gratification;
having duly partaken of those streams for three years, Hara [attained his purpose].
Slightly pleased, O twice-born one, he went to the merit-bestowing field of Kuru;
having gone there, Hara became Sthāṇu and fell down upon that spot.
Magna in the waters of the Brahmahrada for three years,
after those three years had passed there, he emerged with half his body wounded.
He praised Viṣṇu, the Lord of gods who dwells in the secret cave of all, for a long time;
then the Lord of the world, being pleased, granted him a boon.
"O Hara, wander from here to Kāśī, visiting many sacred fords (tīrthas) repeatedly;
then, having bowed to Hari and circumambulated him in many ways," so it was said.
Traveling by stages on a pilgrimage, he arrived at the city of Avimukta;
having reached the boundary of Avimukta, Dhūrjaṭi appeared before his eyes.
He did not see that personified Brahmin-slaughter standing outside him;
then, recognizing that this sacred field of Viṣṇu destroys all evil,
he became composed and praised Mādhava, the adorable Lord.
Victory, victory to you, O Lord of the universe, O Viṣṇu, O treasure-house of the world’s bliss, O you who are to be known through the Vedas!
O Slayer of Madhu, O Nṛsiṃha, O you clad in yellow garments, O Lord Mādhava and others, seated upon Garuḍa!
O delighter of Vraja, Lord of Ramā, Lord of Rādhikā, fulfiller of all desires of the lords of the thirty gods, Kṛṣṇa!
O ocean of compassion for the best of deities, destroyer of distress, lotus-eyed sovereign, omnipresent Lord, Supreme Master!

O Śauri, who dwells on the ocean of the Kṣīroda lake, O wielder of the bow skilled in the act of lifting up the mountain, O you whose pair of lotus feet remove the impurities of the Kali age, O giver of the self, O Tortoise, O you who arose from Kaśyapa! NarP_2,29.41.
O Buddha Kalkin, who is like a forest fire to the dry grass of the world, who wears dark garments at the time when all sacrifices have ceased;
O remover of the fear of existence, who brings devotees under your control, the cowherd who uplifts those who prostrate before you, whose fame is merit! NarP_2,29.42.
O Rāma, who removes the burden of the earth, who is worshipped by the enemies of the Asuras, the Lord of Prakṛti, and the Master of the universe;
O Lord of all moving and unmoving beings resplendent with a multitude of virtues, who transcend the three *guṇas*, the eternal one worshipped at the very beginning;
O destroyer of Death for Your own people, whose feet are like lotuses, O beautiful Padmanābha!
O abode of the lotus and the water-lily, O destroyer of the god of love, O one worthy of worship by the Lord of the Three Worlds!
O remover of sin, O Raghunātha, Lord of the Yādavas, beloved of the Brahmins, Supreme beyond the supreme, most venerable one;
O wielder of the plow, destroyer of evil, salutations to you who pervade the three qualities and are proficient in the three times of the world! (NarP 2,29.44)

O sole performer of the deed of destroying the race of Danujas; O you who have mounted the sinless Lord of Serpents; O Death to Kaṃsa; O you whose eyes are the sun and moon; O you of bold exploits; O you who have dispelled the darkness; O you who resemble a fresh rain-cloud; O Lord of the earth! (NarP 2.29.45)
O Makha, O bearer of the sacrifice, O you who are bound by your mother, O lover of fresh butter, O Lord of the cowherd women!
You are the ender of Agha, Baka, Vṛṣaka, Keśin, and Pūtanā; you are the one who brought about the destruction of Triśiras, Bālin, and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
O destroyer of the fortress of hell, wielder of arrows and arms, Lord of the enemy of Tripura, served by Sudāmā and Mitra;
O ancient one whose lotus feet are a boat for crossing the ocean of existence, you whose majesty is manifest and whose arms are full! NarP_2,29.47.

O Giver of Boons, O Worthy One, may Your pair of feet— which bring happiness to many, which are worthy of auspiciousness, known through the Vedas, the abode of sacred revelation, peaceful, and pure— protect me, who have sought refuge in them and am afflicted by sin.
"Indeed, there is no other than You, the Ancient Person, who can grant me a goal; therefore, be gracious to me today. (NarP 2.29.49)
Thus praised with devotion by the god Śambhu,
Mādhava, who is affectionate toward his devotees, suddenly manifested as the Lord of the World.
Seeing him, Hara fell prostrate on the ground like a staff before Hari;
rising again, O best of Brahmins, he bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Hṛṣīkeśa said to that prostrate leader of beings:
"Choose a boon; being pleased by your hymn of praise, I shall grant it to you. (NarP 2.29.52)
Having heard those words of the Blessed One, the Lord of Beings, his soul tormented by the slaughter of a Brahmin, spoke thus to Hari, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
O wielder of the discus and mace, I desire to dwell in your field;
for even the sin of killing a Brahmin is seen to vanish once it has reached the boundary of your field.
O Garuḍadhvaja, show compassion toward me by means of the gift of land;
when I depart, the sin of killing a Brahmin will come after me once again.
"Established in your field, I shall receive worship throughout the three worlds";
having spoken thus, the bull-bannered god became silent before the God of gods.
"So be it," replied the beloved of the one born from the ocean of milk;
and from that time forth, O best of Brahmins, it has been called a Śaiva sacred field (kṣetra).
O best of the twice-born, the wise know this ancient field of Keśava, Mādhava, who was completely overcome by compassion.
The water that issued from his two eyes became the Bindu-saras;
by the command of Mādhava, the bull-bannered god bathed there.
As soon as Hari had bathed, that skull fell from his hand;
that sacred ford (tīrtha) attained fame by the name Kapālamocana.
Having given his own abode to the trident-bearer under the name Bindumādhava,
Śambhu remained there, established with a spirit of devotion.
But that which Brahmā and the other gods dwelling in heaven always behold—
resplendent like ten thousand suns and attended by those clad in the directions (the sky)— [he beholds].
O beloved, obstacles were created by the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for his service;
yet those who worship Śiva, though overcome by such obstacles, praise Viṣṇu.

For all the worlds are established here; O Brahmin, those who contemplate Kāśī as Śiva become entirely free from agitation through that contemplation of Śiva. All such devotees of Śiva (Śaivas) are thus undisturbed.
Indeed, they go to the world of Śiva, which is free from old age and death;
endowed with abundant merit, they dwell there free from disease.
O beloved of Kāśī, those who eat the remnants of sacrifice are endowed with prosperity;
for them, they do not praise bathing here, nor recitation, nor the worship of the gods. (NarP 2.29.66)

Nor, O best of the twice-born, can a man achieve his desire and certainly become one who has fulfilled his duty by means of charity alone, except by the single act of casting off the body— that is, by meeting death.
O Brahmin, this city, crowded with palaces, has now been reached;
it leads even to liberation for those who enjoy worldly pleasures, how much more so for those who observe their vows!
"Let this young girl, who was previously separated from him by that wicked Rākṣasa, be placed here in the palace of the Lord of Kāśī. (NarP 2.29.69)
O best of the twice-born, even this power is beneficial for a maiden who, observing her vows, seeks sexual pleasure for herself; such is the power of this sacred field.
In this world, actions— both auspicious and inauspicious, belonging to the past, present, and future, and performed with or without knowledge— are destroyed.
This city was indeed created long ago by Kṛṣṇa for the destruction of karma;
in it, mortals who have died undergo the fierce and infinite suffering of the torments of Yama.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Kāśī," within the account of the Rākṣasī in the story of Kāṣṭhīla, in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, concerning the life of Mohinī.
Kāṣṭhīla said:
Having heard those words of his wife, the Rākṣasī, which were consistent with righteousness—
From the back of the woman who resembled Karoṇu, a twice-born man descended together with a maiden.
When the brahmin had descended, that night-stalker became once again a beautiful woman,
with a face like the moon and full, elevated breasts.
Then, having reached her father’s auspicious city,
the maiden spoke to the city guardian who stood at the outer gate.
"Go to the presence of the king, my father, O lord of the city, and tell him that I have arrived at the jewel-hall which was formerly seized. (NarP 2.30.4)
O twice-born one, while she was lying on her bed in her own city, that jewel among women, the Ratnāvalī of King Sudyumna, was carried off by a Rākṣasa during the night.
"Furthermore, O father, she has returned alive and unhurt;
take heart and do not grieve for me at all."
O Indra among kings, I am unbroken, like the pure waters of the Gaṅgā;
likewise, I am the bringer of fame to you and the indicator of my mother’s virtuous character.
Having heard those words of the princess, the city guardian known as Abāhu arrived in haste into the presence of Sudyumna.
Having offered his salutation and being questioned, he spoke with respect to the king:
"O King, bestower of honor, your lost daughter has been found."
Known as Ratnāvalī, accompanied by her wife and son, she was seen by me standing outside the city; though she was perceived, she was not recognized.
"O Lord, impelled by her, I have come before you to inform you;
let her, who speaks with unbroken virtue, know that I have arrived. (NarP 2.30.11)
"One must honor my father; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having heard those wonderful words of the city guardian at that very moment, [the king]—
Accompanied by his ministers and his wife, the king, together with the twice-born, went forth;
having departed from the city, he established himself on the bank of the Gaṅgā outside the town.
He saw her, who had the form of the sun, accompanied by women and twice-born men,
adorned in her natural attire though she was fond of ornaments.
Having seen from afar her who resembled a fresh amlāna flower and possessed the brilliant luster of refined gold, the king approached and embraced her.
She too, filled with joy, embraced her father and bowed to him; then, having met with her mother, she was thrilled within, being herself delighted by her mother's joy.
The large-eyed lady addressed these words to her father, the king, after awakening him:
"I was sleeping in the jeweled chamber, surrounded by my female companions."
Having washed her head and rinsed her feet with water,
she lay upon her bed at midnight, contemplating union with her husband, when she was carried off by a *rākṣasa*.
Having taken me with him, he went to his own city on Mount Arṇava;
there, in a cave composed of various jewels, I was indeed established.
Remaining there, absorbed in thoughts of a means for marriage,
[he saw] this fair-browed woman of slender waist who stands there as his wife.
O King, this Rākṣasī, beloved of the Rākṣasas, assuming a human form,
acted through her application of intellect and power, like that of Śakra.
My own husband, a performer of cruel deeds, was slain by the hand of a Brahmin;
long ago, that mountain-dweller was reached by the god, O protector of the earth.
But this Rākṣasī, seeing her husband as a violator of dharma,
made an agreement with the Brahmin regarding their conjugal duties through her own action.
Deluded by his beauty, she, assuming the form of a female elephant, caused the Rākṣasa to kill her Brahmin husband in this manner.
"O King, having taken the wealth of the site and having placed me upon her back as well, she has come here to your palace to devour me. (NarP_2,30.25)
"O King, she has been protected from that non-demon by this demoness;
therefore, honor her with due respect along with her elder brother."
"Give this very maiden to me for this brahmin;
by sitting upon the same seat with him, he has become my husband. (NarP 2.30.27)
Indeed, it is heard in the Purāṇas and even in the Āgamas that the husband of a woman who remains on a single seat is he alone, and no other. NarP_2,30.28 //
"Seated upon her back with affection along with this twice-born man, he shall become my husband according to dharma; such is my thought. (NarP 2.30.29)
Therefore, O father, having consoled me according to the prescriptions of the scriptures and traditional teachings, give me to this brahmin; I shall not choose another husband.
Having heard those words of his daughter,
King Sudyumna then consoled the slender-limbed Rākṣasī, bowing before her with humility.
"O virtuous lady, this daughter of mine, fearing for her dharma, has come to you alone for refuge—
for the sake of whom my beloved husband was slain by you long ago."
"Therefore, O blessed lady, this daughter of mine has indeed been born dependent upon you;
she desires as her husband this very man whom you have chosen as your husband. (NarP 2.30.33)
"O night-stalker, O fair-eyed one, you have been entreated by me with prostrations and gifts; please grant your consent to assist my daughter. (NarP 2.30.34)
"By your word, let my daughter become the servant of the brahmin;
having abandoned the state of a co-wife, please protect my daughter."
"You are the mistress of my daughter, of my wife, of myself, of Madbala, of the people, and even of the city and the province; of this there is no doubt."
"For she shall remain ever steadfast in your word.
Having heard these words of Sudyumna, the night-stalker— NarP_2,30.37 —
Her companion approved with a pure heart and spoke to the protector of the earth, who was making efforts to give her away.
"O best of kings, since you have approached me with sincere devotion for this purpose,
let this woman become the second wife of this twice-born man."
And I, having performed worship in the temple of the god on the bright fortnight of Phālguna, together with all the Nāgaras, am to be honored by you. (NarP 2.30.40)
A festival should indeed be held for seven days, from the eighth day until the fourteenth,
accompanied by actors and dancers and abundant singing and instrumental music.
By worshipping me with offerings of liquor, meat, blood, and the like, they act thus toward you; for I am indeed always a bringer of well-being.
"O tiger among kings, may it be so; fulfill your own word.
Having heard those words of hers, King Sudyumna then—
She accepted everything that was said by her with affection;
and when the king had agreed to her words, the rākṣasī was satisfied.
He spoke with affection to the brahmin: "O best of the twice-born, take this auspicious princess as your wife according to the rites prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras."
"Having abandoned my envy of the large-eyed lady, I shall become her sister; for, at the word of the Rākṣasī, I have married the king's daughter here. (NarP 2.30.46)
Accompanied by much wealth, the Brahmin went to the city of Mahodaya,
having in an instant mounted a Rākṣasī in the form of a female elephant.
Then, O Queen, I heard that your husband had arrived,
accompanied by wealth and jewels, and joined by his two wives.
Then I was repeatedly rebuked with harsh words that pierced my very vitals by my circle of kinsmen, my parents, and my groups of friends.
How will you go to your husband, who is now surrounded by wealth and greedy for riches—
he who was previously abandoned by you when he was poor, as if you were deeply distressed?
"O fortunate one, it is said that the wealth of women inherited from their fathers is indeed fickle in this world, whereas that earned by their own husbands is stable."
How can one who has been insulted with harsh words ever speak to him again?
Even entry into his house will be difficult for him.
Even when you have gone there, O woman of evil conduct, your lying down with your husband will never bring you any happiness.
If your husband should seize you because of public scandal and the like,
he will never meet with you again, his heart devoid of affection.
In this world, there is nothing so sorrow-inducing as the meeting of two lovers whose hearts are far apart; it causes great distress. (NarP 2.30.55)
Hearing these various words spoken by my kinsmen,
I became deeply distressed, with my face cast down and my eyes filled with tears.
And I, deluded by former greed, did not honor her with my mind; I gave no bracelet to her hand, nor did I give her a waist-string. (NarP 2.30.57)
Nor indeed should she give an anklet by which her husband might attain satisfaction;
for in the worlds, the husband is proclaimed to be the master of both wealth and life.
That wealth has been stolen by me; what will be my fate?
How shall I go to his house, and how shall I speak to him again?
"How indeed can he, who was abandoned by me in my wickedness, return to me?"—
thus she reflected with a heart that was burning with grief.
Surrounded by her circle of kinsmen, the very delicate swing arrived,
shining with a moon-white parasol.
The ground was strewn with thick, soft skins of the *rāṅkava* deer, and the shoulders of men were draped over it;
those men, having approached me, spoke repeatedly in a gentle manner.
"You have been summoned by your husband; go quickly, filled with joy!
Your husband has arrived together with his wife, accompanied by wealth and jewels."
O fair-faced one, as soon as he had entered the house,
your husband dispatched messengers in haste to bring you back from where you were staying in your father’s home.
Then, O Queen, seeing that behavior of my husband, I was ashamed; I gave no answer at all to them, but remained established in silence.
Then, repeatedly exhorted by my circle of kinsmen and summoned with honor by my husband, I was told, "Go to his presence. (NarP 2.30.66)
O daughter, that wife who, having been summoned by her husband, does not go to his side,
shall become a female crow for fifteen births.
Having spoken thus and comforted me, they took hold of me with haste;
placing me upon a swing, those affectionate ones said again and again, "Go!"
Then those men, having quickly placed the swing upon their shoulders,
went to the city of Mahodaya, where my husband resides.
I saw his house, covered on all sides with gold,
and then provided with seats, foods, wealth, and garments.
Then that Rākṣasī queen and that daughter of the king both performed a prostration before me with love and devotion, O beautiful one.
Then, having been honored by them with affection according to my merit,
and being well-pleased by my husband’s words, I bathed, ate, and was likewise led away.
Then, after eight months had passed, her husband quickly summoned her,
embraced her for a long time with both arms, and seated her upon a couch.
Then, having summoned the night-stalking woman and the princess, he said:
"With devotion, you two must perform service at her feet."
"This is indeed your former wife and your elder;
therefore, at the word of their husband, they both grasped my feet."
"O fair-eyed one, having abandoned the jealousy born of the feeling of rivalry toward co-wives, my husband then summoned his servants and spoke these words. (NarP 2.30.76)
Whatever wealth I previously obtained from the side of the Rākṣasa,
and everything I received from the king when he gave me his daughter in marriage— [all that I give].
Bring all of that with a spirit of devotion without delay;
for this mistress has arrived, and you are but servants of her wealth.
At her word, O auspicious lady, the husband, filled with affection, then had all that wealth brought by his servants and delivered to her immediately.
There, the rākṣasīs beheld both the princesses as they honored them with ornaments and garments, while their own minds were filled with deceit.
Embracing me as I sat upon the couch, O lady of beautiful, pouting lips,
she witnessed that miracle of her husband’s surrendering his body and wealth.
Her words were full of joy, yet she pressed her breasts with her hand;
my life-breaths departed like a cow cut down by a sword. (NarP 2.30.82)
Then, directed by Yama, I underwent the torments of hell;
having passed through that, afflicted by extreme suffering, O auspicious lady, I became a wooden post.
O fair-faced one, I shall again enter the wombs of animals thousands of times—
that woman who does not provide her husband with wealth and even her own life.
She too will surely come to such a state; of this there is no doubt.
Knowing this, she should constantly protect her husband’s wealth and his very life. (NarP 2.30.85)
The husband, the mother, the father, wealth, life itself, the teacher, and the refuge.

A woman who, out of greed for wealth and her own body, burns herself along with her husband by means of many meritorious rites, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; yet she also undergoes the torment of a wretched womb in the realm of Yama.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Story of Kāṣṭhīlā," within the *Mohinī-carita* of the latter part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O lady of pure smiles, having heard those words of Kāṣṭhīlā, [he spoke].
He spoke very respectfully to her, who was named Sandhyāvalī.
O Kāṣṭhīlā, upon hearing your words, astonishment has now arisen within me:
how is it that you, who were seen by me, are going to such a loathsome state?
"By what action, O large-limbed one, might you obtain liberation from this contemptible womb? Tell me that, for I am indeed distressed upon seeing you."
"O auspicious lady, beholding your body—smooth like a lump of flesh and like fresh butter—there arises in my heart [this thought]. (NarP 2.31.4)
Kāṣṭhīlā said:
"O fair-browed one, you may give me even the entire earth for my sake;
nevertheless, I shall not be released immediately from this loathsome womb. (NarP 2.31.5)
O fortunate lady, listen as I describe that very great merit which grants a superior rebirth, by means of which I may be liberated from the bonds of karma. NarP_2,31.6.
And this month of Māgha is remembered as the best of all months;
in it, even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin cry out.
The month of Māgha is indeed difficult to obtain; human birth is difficult to obtain;
bathing at dawn is difficult to obtain; and service to Kṛṣṇa is difficult to obtain.
This day of Viṣṇu, observed as a fast according to the prescribed rite, is difficult to obtain;
for in the month of Māgha, the gods have cast their own splendor into the water.
Therefore, bathing in the waters during the month of Māgha is indeed especially purifying;
such a bliss-bestowing state could not be attained by heroes even in battle.
Whatever merit is obtained by those established in their observances through swimming at dawn,
that is declared to be the highest merit from bathing in rivers, lakes, and ponds.
Merit is not obtained through pleasures—such as water from wells or vessels heated by fire; rather, it is attained only through sufferings. (NarP 2.31.12)
Bathing for the sake of serving the Dharma is not for the purpose of bodily cleanliness;
nor is the tending of fire for the sake of oblations intended merely to dispel cold and the like.
Bathing is prescribed for as long as the sun has not yet risen;
indeed, when the sky is covered by clouds, one should pray to the sun as it is about to emerge.
In the absence of rivers and other such waters,
they know that water placed in a new jar and struck by the wind at night is equal to the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing.
O lady of beautiful hips, one who bathes in the month of Māgha never beholds an evil destiny;
there is no sin whatsoever that the Māgha bath would not purify.
Drowning in the Māgha month is superior to entering the fire;
while living one experiences suffering, but when dead there is abundant happiness.
For this reason, O blessed lady, the ritual bath in the month of Māgha is preeminent;
sesame seeds mixed with sugar should be given day after day.
O slender-waisted lady, oblations should be offered with rice mixed with *meghapuṣpa* flowers,
along with barley-meal and clarified butter derived from cows.
When the midday bath is completed, one should give food of six flavors to a Brahmin, saying:
"May the god Sūrya, the stainless form of Viṣṇu, be pleased with me."
He should offer garments and seven types of food to a pair of twice-born men;
thirty sweetmeats made of sesame and sugar should also be given.
Three parts of sesame seeds and a fourth part of sugar;
one who knows the ritual procedure should offer these, along with betel leaves and other enjoyments, with devotion and water.
In a river, he should bathe facing the current; elsewhere, facing the sun.
Having invoked the holy fords (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā and others from his water-pot, he should bathe.
Whatever sin has been produced over many births, whether committed through knowledge or ignorance— may that evil be destroyed by your splendor in a thousand ways.
O Divākara, Lord of the World, Maker of Light, homage be to you!
O Acyuta, make this Māgha bath of mine complete.
O lady of excellent hips, one who bathes at sacred fords (tīrtha) obtains meager fruit, whereas one who bathes during Māgha attains the supreme state;
through bathing at sacred fords one goes to heaven, but through the Māgha bath one reaches the highest station.
That Ekādaśī which occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when joined with Sunday, is the destroyer of great sins.
Even without conjunction with the asterism [Puṣya], that Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight utterly consumes the sins of men,
just as a wicked king destroys his own realm.

Just as a bad son ruins a family, as a bad wife ruins her husband, as unrighteousness ruins righteousness, and as a bad minister ruins a king; so too does [a bad friend ruin a friend]. // NarP_2,31.29 //
Just as ignorance is countered by knowledge, impurity by purification, falsehood by truth, and contradiction by consistency; so too [is sin destroyed]. // NarP_2,31.30 //
Heat is to cold as misfortune is to fortune; evil is to fame, and pride is to austerity;
just as the tastes [are to] great diseases, so too is faith to a mere convention.
Likewise, the twelfth day (dvādaśī), when properly observed, destroys a multitude of evils:
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife.
The day of Hari quickly destroys these great sins;
yet Puṣkara does not pacify them when they are all combined together.
Nor is it the Naimiṣa forest, nor the sacred field known as Kuru;
O Goddess, it is not Prabhāsa, nor Gayā, nor the Revā, nor the Sarasvatī.
Neither the Gaṅgā nor the Yamunā, nor Prayāga nor Devakā;
neither lakes nor other rivers, nor even fire-offerings, gifts, and austerities [can equal it]. (NarP 2.31.35)
O fair-browed one, no other meritorious deed is clearly taught in the Purāṇas for the destruction of the multitude of sins, except for the single day of Hari.
O Goddess, by observing the fast even once, heaps of sins are destroyed;
on one side is the gift of the entire earth, and on the other is a single day of Hari.
No day is equal to Hari’s day as proclaimed by Brahmā;
for on that day, the Lord assumed the form of a boar and became Hāṭaka.
Having placed it upon a new vessel made of auspicious copper on top of the jar,
it should be provided with all kinds of seeds and covered with a white cloth.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with offerings of gold, excellent lamps, and floral ornaments, the observer of the vow should perform a ritual vigil.

In the morning, one should give that [image], together with its pedestal and its enclosure, along with the offerings of food (naivedya) and all its accessories, to a Vaiṣṇava brahmin who maintains a family.
And afterwards, having fed the twice-born, one should perform the breaking of the fast surrounded by friends;
when this is done, O lady of beautiful hips, one is never born again anywhere.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over many births, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly—
all that goes to destruction, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
O auspicious goddess, I have described to you the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) according to the scriptures; it is that very one which was previously observed by you in another birth.
She whose incomparable prosperity exists and will endure shall always bestow happiness upon you, her husband, and your son.
If you should respectfully give me even a fourth part of that [merit],
then, being pleased, I shall go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O beautiful one, give me a fourth part as the means for purifying whatever sin born of the seizure of wealth has been committed by me. (NarP 2.31.47)
She who deceives her husband even by means of her life or her wealth,
having passed through a hundred births as a worm, is born as a Pulkasī.
O proud woman, that evil-minded wife who does not grant wealth and sexual pleasure to her husband when he asks for them will certainly be reborn as a wooden post.
If you have compassion for me, grant me a fourth part of the merit arising from this twelfth day, for the sake of purifying that sin. (NarP 2.31.50)
Having heard these words of Kāṣṭhīlā, O fair-eyed one,
she took water in her hand and bestowed merit upon her.
"By the merit of even a fourth part of the fast I previously observed on Ekādaśī, let this Kāṣṭhīlā be liberated. (NarP 2.31.52)
"Truly, truly, I have spoken this from the sins committed in a previous birth.
When these words were thus spoken by me, she who possessed a radiance like lightning [appeared]. (NarP 2.31.53)
She was seen standing in a celestial chariot, proceeding toward the realm of Viṣṇu;
for in this world, the husband is indeed a deity, and he must not be deceived by his wife.
"If you desire an auspicious destiny through both body and wealth, then speak it; I shall grant whatever you desire for the sake of your husband."
O lady of beautiful countenance, wealth, body, son, or whatever else there may be—what other deity is there in this world for women besides their husband alone? (NarP 2.31.56)
Or for his sake, O fair-eyed one, one may sacrifice wealth or even life;
such a person is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for more than a hundred times ten million kalpas.
Having seen her husband summoned as a witness before the fire and other deities, Niṣṭhurā, the daughter of a twice-born man, was joined with terrible calamities;
though entreated, she did not give her husband his wealth, and by that very sin, she became a worm.

"O you of wicked form, O slender maid, having recognized this as beneficial and true for my husband, I give it all to you while I still dwell in my father's house in my maidenhood; accept it all, O fair-browed one. (NarP 2.31.59)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of Māgha," in the *Kāṣṭhīlopākhyāna* within the *Mohinīcarita* of the latter portion of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having heard the words of Sandhyāvalī, Mohinī, the daughter of Brahmā, [spoke].
Intent upon her own task, Mohakaraṇḍikā spoke.
If you understand the course of righteousness and unrighteousness in this way, O auspicious lady,
you have been a giver of even wealth and life for the sake of your husband.
Then I shall beg for wealth, O auspicious lady, which is dearer to me than life itself;
give me the head of my son, which is more cherished by my heart than anything else.
"If he does not take food when the day of Hari has arrived,
then your husband, the king, shall seize a sword in his own hand."
His head was beautiful with the armlet of Dharma, auspicious like the orb of the moon,
devoid of facial hair, and adorned with two earrings.
"O fair-eyed one, cut it quickly and let it fall upon my lap;
or else, O blessed lady, do whatever must be done so that he does not eat this food."
On the day of the god Mādhava, which destroys the multitude of sins;
having heard those bitter words of that Mohinī, [he spoke].
For a moment the goddess trembled like a plantain tree afflicted by the cold;
then Sandhyāvalī, that woman of excellent complexion, summoned her fortitude.
Smiling, the fair-faced woman spoke these words to Mohinī:
"O lady of beautiful brows, indeed, verses uttered by her are heard in the Purāṇas."
Those [observances] connected with the twelfth day (dvādaśī) bestow heaven and liberation;
one should abandon wealth, abandon wives, abandon life, and abandon home.
One should abandon a country, as well as a king; one should abandon heaven, a friend, and a teacher;
one should abandon a sacred ford, one should abandon dharma, and one should abandon that which is exceedingly dear.
O auspicious one, one should renounce yoga, renounce charity, renounce knowledge, and renounce meritorious deeds;
one should renounce austerity, renounce learning, and renounce even spiritual perfection and liberation.
One should not abandon the meritorious twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) during either fortnight;
for in this world, all kinsmen—sons, brothers, friends, and loved ones—are dear.
O Goddess, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is remembered as the means for accomplishment in this world and the next;
by the power of the twelfth day, everything shall become secure.
"I shall cause Dharmāṅgada’s head to be given for the sake of your satisfaction, O auspicious one;
place your trust in my words, O beautiful lady, and be happy. (NarP 2.32.15)
In this regard, O blessed lady, an ancient history is heard;
I shall relate it to you, O blessed one—listen to me with attentive mind.
In former times, there was a Daitya named Virocana who was devoted to righteousness;
his wife was large-eyed and intent upon the worship of the twice-born.
Having worshipped the one eternal Ṛṣi every morning according to the prescribed rite,
O fair-browed one, he drinks his water for the feet with devotion and a joyful mind.
Formerly, when Hiraṇyakaśipu— possessed of fierce splendor— was ruling the kingdom and had died, the gods were filled with apprehension toward the son of Prahlāda.
The two sons of Prahlāda, filled with joy, moved about busily upon the surface of the earth.
Once, those gods, headed by Śakra, having deliberated together, [approached] Vākpati.
They said, "What must be done now by us, who have tormented the enemy?
Having heard those words of the gods, their preceptor spoke.
"Viṣṇu must be informed today by the hosts of gods who have fallen into distress.
Having heard those words of his preceptor of immeasurable splendor, [he departed].
To slay Virocana, they went to the vicinity of Vaikuṇṭha;
having gone there, they praised Vaikuṇṭha, the best of gods, with hymns.
The gods said:
"Obeisance to Viṣṇu, the god of gods, of immeasurable splendor;
obeisance again and again to Vaikuṇṭha, the destroyer of obstacles for his devotees."
To Hari, the wondrous lion, to the dwarf, the great-souled one;
to him in the form of a boar, to the fish, who dwells in the ocean of dissolution.
Salutations to the Tortoise who supported Mount Mandara; to Bhārgava who reclines upon the ocean;
to Rāma, the Lord of all; and to the Lord of the universe, the Witness.
To Dattātreya, the pure one; to Kapila, the remover of suffering;
to the sacrifice, who upholds righteousness; and to him whose nature is that of Sanaka and the other [sages].
To Dhruva, the giver of boons, and to Pṛthu of many deeds;
to the pure Ṛṣabha, whose self bears the horse-headed form.
To Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, who assumes the form of a swan, who holds a jar of nectar, and who bears the body of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Brahmā, and Śaṅkara; salutations to Kumāra, Gaṇeśa, Nandin, and Bhṛṅgin.
Salutations to the one who dwells on Gandhamādana, to Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
to the Lord of the World, to the Protector, and to Rāmeśvara.
Salutations to the dweller of Dvārakā, and to the one who dwells in the forest of Tulasī; salutations to the one with a lotus-navel, salutations to you whose feet are like lotuses.
Homage to you who hold a lotus in your hand; homage to you whose eyes are like lotuses;
homage again and again to Keśava, the protector of Kamalā.
Homage to the one who has the form of the sun and who assumes the form of the moon;
to the one whose very nature is that of the world-protectors and who bears the body of Prajāpati.
Salutation to the splendor whose nature is the collection of beings, whose form is the individual soul,

Salutations to Govinda, the sustainer of the world, the infinite, the primordial one, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
the bearer of the conch, the wielder of the mace, and the holder of the discus.
To the one who wields the sword and the trident, the destroyer of all weapons and missiles,
the refuge, the most excellent, the supreme, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Universal One, whose form is the universe;
salutations to the one with the navel of time, to Time itself, whose eyes are the moon and the sun;
salutations to the Full One, the one worthy of being served, and the one higher than the highest.
To the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the nourisher of the world, and the Ender;
to the deluder, the agitator, the one who assumes forms at will, the Unborn, and the Wise One.
O Blessed One, we, tormented by the Daityas, have come to you for refuge;
therefore, O Support of All, act in such a way that we may indeed be happy.
"We dwell together with our sons, friends, wives, and so forth.
Having heard that hymn of theirs, Vaikuṇṭha was pleased in his mind.
He granted his vision to them, whose souls were tormented by the Daityas;
they, having beheld the Lord of the gods of gods, Vaikuṇṭha, whose mind was full of affection.
Having heard that request for the swift slaying of Virocana,
he, the best among those who know what must be done, [considered] the task of the leaders headed by Śakra.
Having consoled the gods with affection, he dismissed them filled with joy;
and when the hosts of deities had departed, he who was the best among those skilled in all means [reflected].
In the form of an aged brahmin, he who accomplishes all tasks went to the house of Virocana at the very time when the worship of the twice-born was taking place.
But seeing that brahmin, the large-eyed lady, with a joyful heart,
honored him with unprecedented devotion and offered him a seat.
Not accepting the seat offered by her, he said to her: "O auspicious one, O Goddess, I shall not occupy this supreme seat given by you. (NarP 2.32.48)
Listen to my incomparable purpose for which I have come, O proud lady;
having understood that task which dwells within my mind.
"O fair-faced one, I shall accept that worship which he accepts. Having heard those words of the aged brahmin, she who was skilled in speech [replied].

Deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu and exceedingly delighted because of her womanhood, the large-eyed lady said: "O Brahmin, whatever is in your mind, I shall give that; please accept it from me. (NarP 2.32.51)
"Give me a seat and water for my feet, which grant all desired objects.

Right there, in the presence of the twice-born, he had an image fashioned;

Seeing that her husband had arrived at the inner apartments where his large-eyed wife was staying, she, who was devoted to dharma, [welcomed him].
Having risen and bowed to the foremost of brahmins, he offered him a seat again;

Having learned of that incident, Virocana, the king of the Daityas, spoke to the king, the lord of the Daityas, concerning himself.

"Make the words spoken by you true; let us do so, and may you attain joy. Then the Brahmin, his soul delighted, accepted that and the seat.

O tiger among kings, having been born with a desire to conquer the next world, I have become devoid of affection for my son by virtue of upholding my word of truth. (NarP 2.33.8)

Having placed your foot upon their heads, you shall go to the supreme station;
for those who bear devotion to Viṣṇu, even the gods become obstacles.
Blindness will prevail in the world; that very thing has been made manifest.
O King, the gods, together with their lord, have become hostile toward your deeds.
O King, those who destroy the path to liberation are subverters of your certainty;
therefore, becoming firm, put your beloved son to death.
Therefore, fulfill the word of Mohinī by preserving your own truth.
O lord of men, even though the sentence has been revoked, a terrible sin equal to the slaughter of a Brahmin will still be yours;
O King, you shall be known in this world as the Punisher, and your fame will spread across the earth.

"O lady of beautiful hips, the seven continents have now been enjoyed by your son; as an incarnation of Viṣṇu, he shall even surpass his father."

A virtuous son is difficult to obtain, and the day of Hari is difficult to encounter."
The water of the Jāhnavī is difficult to obtain; a mother is difficult to find on earth;
birth in a noble family is indeed rare, and a beloved wife born of a good lineage is hard to find.
The gift of gold is difficult to obtain; the worship of Hari is difficult to obtain;

"O woman of excellent complexion, it is difficult to remember Viṣṇu at the moment of death;

"O lady of beautiful limbs, why should you grant me favor only through my death?

I have placed my foot upon the heads of those who protect the gods, cows, and Brahmins;

"Guard your truth with effort; do as I say. O King, she spoke thus to that slender-waisted Mohinī.

"O father, you must not delay in causing my downfall;

The self must be protected by means of wealth, wives, or even one's own children;

For your sake, my death shall grant me an inexhaustible state;
and for you as well, there will be worlds free from sorrow through the fulfillment of your own word.
Having abandoned the supreme sorrow arising from the slaughter of my son, I shall cast off this body; my undertaking will bear fruit in a human form.
O Lord, who are free from all ailments and equal to Indra,
those who were slain for the sake of their father, as well as those slain for the sake of their mother— [may they find peace].
For the sake of cows, or for the sake of Brahmins, O Lord of the Earth; for the sake of women, or for the sake of land, or for the sake of kings, and likewise for the sake of the deities.
For the sake of children and for the sake of the disabled, they go to worlds of great radiance;
therefore, enough with this distress—slay me with your excellent sword.
"O Indra among kings, uphold the truth; do not eat on the day of Hari.
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of dharma or wealth, one might even slay a son or a wife."
It is heard in the Vedic texts, O King, that one established in the sacrifice may slay his own son during the Aśvamedha, the best of sacrifices; no fault arises from this.
"O protector of the earth, whatever my mother Mohinī says must certainly be carried out by you without hesitation. (NarP 2.33.67)
Be gracious, O Indra among kings, and carry out my words which I have spoken truly for the sake of your own life;
O King, release yourself from this most terrible falsehood of speech resulting from the influence of the deluding power.
"O lord of the earth, by the execution of your son, your fame shall be made manifest;
for from the manifestation of fame, O dear one, eternal renown arises—of this there is no doubt. (NarP 2.33.69)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Speech of Dharmāṅgada," in the account of Mohinī within the latter portion of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.

O tiger among kings, among those three—Meghaśyāma, Nirañjana, and the heroic Rukmāṅgada, son of Dharmāṅgada—[the eldest was Meghaśyāma]. 2,34.4.

Having bowed to the one whose banner is Garuḍa with a mind full of great joy, he seized a stainless sword to slay his son Dharmāṅgada. Seeing his father with the sword in hand, Dharmabhūṣaṇa—
Having prostrated before his parents and likewise the god who wields the discus,
that bull among kings gazed upon his mother’s undepressed countenance.
Then Vṛṣāṅgada fashioned upon the surface of the earth a golden statue of Svagrīva, which was equal to him, with a shell-like neck and very delicate.

O King, when the Lord of the World took up his sword for the sake of giving away his son’s neck, the entire earth, along with its mountains, trembled as his moon-like face overflowed with joy.

and hundreds of meteors, accompanied by thunderclaps, fell upon the earth from the midst of the sky, flashing with lightning.
And Mohinī became pale in appearance, thinking, "The work of the gods has not been accomplished by me.
"Now my birth has become useless, brought about indeed by Fate, the creator of the world. (NarP 2.34.12)
This form is a delusion, a mere mockery, that the protector of the earth did not consume food;

The one with superior merit shall go upon the path to liberation, while I, O evil one, shall go to a most terrible hell.
Then, O bull among kings, as the sword was raised by the monarch,
Mohinī, overcome by delusion, fell to the surface of the earth.
The king also, shining with that sword,
raised it up for the purpose of severing the neck of Vṛṣāṅgada’s son.

While that king, endowed with fortitude and adorned with golden ornaments, was out of extreme joy about to cut off his son’s beautiful, radiant face— which shone like the moon and was graced by earrings— NarP_2,34.17.

"I am pleased, I am pleased; there is no doubt in this. Go to my world, O Lord of the World! (NarP 2.34.18).

Accompanied by his beloved and joined by his son, having established upon the surface of the earth a stainless, pure, and white fame worthy of worship throughout the three worlds, he shall place his foot upon the head of Yama, O King.

"Enter my body, which is known as a dwelling. As soon as he was touched by the hand of that wielder of the discus, the lord of the earth became free from passion, reunited with his beloved and joined by his son.
Approaching with speed, that high-souled king went to the divine body of the god,
leaving behind the prosperity born of the earth, leaving behind his female servants, and leaving behind his treasury of great wealth.
Leaving behind the elephants, horses, chariots, his own wives, and his kinsmen, he entered the body of Madhusūdana; then a shower of flowers fell from the sky.
The kettledrums, struck by the delighted Siddhas and the guardians of the celestial worlds, resounded;
O King, the divine women sang most charming songs and danced filled with joy.
Having witnessed that marvel— the Gandharva maiden pleased by the king's deed— the son of the Sun-god,
erasing his own inscription, saw the lord of the earth, together with his wife and son, enter the body of Hari.

Having made all the worlds grateful for the path to the realm of Hari according to the king’s command, he became afraid; reaching once more the presence of his grandfather, he spoke to the four-faced god while weeping.
"O Lord, O Protector of the World of the Gods, I shall certainly not become a servant devoid of my own command;
therefore, O Father, ordain something else, for I shall carry out that instruction—let there be no punishment upon me."

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Blessed One by Rukmāṅgada, Who was Intent on Killing His Son," in the latter portion of the *Śrī-Bṛhannāradīya-Purāṇa*, within the narrative of Mohinī.
Yama said:

"Your task is certain; let this agitation be abandoned.

like a mortal who has been defeated, or like a flower whose petals have withered.

Like speech that is unrefined, like an army that has been crushed,

Like a house devoid of splendor, like a dense cloud without water, like a seven-flamed fire without smoke, or like the sun without its rays; (NarP_2,35.18)
Like a mortal whose mind has strayed, like a man afflicted by a joint disease,
like a lover unsatiated by his beloved, or like a serpent from which the venom has been removed.
Like a bird with its wings clipped, like a twice-born man deprived of his livelihood,
like a garland fallen from the head, or like a mountain stripped of its minerals.

Those inhabitants of heaven saw that the Sāṃkhya doctrines were devoid of truth, that their dharma was filled with hypocrisy, and likewise that their splendor was lacking, being delusive.
O Lord, she was seen by the people meditating with despondency,
accompanied by the cruel words of reproach regarding the murder of her son.
The assembled gods said to Caṇḍā: "She is immoral, has abandoned the Dharma, is robbed by her own words, and yet she seeks to keep her own word. (NarP 2.35.25)
"Do not grieve for me, O fair-thighed one, for you have indeed displayed manly valor;
for among those devoted to Mādhava, there is no violation of their honor."
O fawn-eyed one, you have come for the sake of the gods' purpose;
yet that has not been accomplished, O lady of beautiful hips, for he has now departed to the state of non-existence.
Indeed, this most meritorious Ekādaśī, which destroys obstacles and is enchanting, was previously observed in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha by Rukmāṅgada.
O large-eyed one, for a year she was honored with the kṛcchra-pāda penance;
her attainment of that goal was incomparable, for she never wavered from the truth.
Indeed, that woman who, in her thoughts, words, or deeds, sets her mind upon the destruction of her son, is proclaimed in the worlds as Vighnarājñī.
Having drawn his sword and cast aside all affection from afar,
the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana subjected him to such a test.
Having observed the disposition of the king toward his beloved son and his own beloved wife, she will not eat on the day of Hari, for she knows he will kill his dear son.
The three, their karma exhausted, were led by Viṣṇu, who was pleased with them, to his own abode in their very bodies,
like charcoal cast into a fire.
O fortunate one, if the goddess does not grant success despite the undertaking of the rite with every effort, what fault is there in you now?
Therefore, O auspicious lady, all the gods have arrived as granters of boons;
whether success or failure is achieved, the performance of the rite shall certainly not be in vain.
A king who desires righteousness must support his circle of dependents; yet, even for one who exerts himself toward this true state of being, if his task does not succeed...
Only the prescribed wage should be given, yet that shall not result in satisfaction; for he who does not grant him the very means of life for the sake of his livelihood [is at fault]. (NarP 2.35.37)
That man incurs the sin of cow-slaughter; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, O most excellent beauty, one should give what is desired.
O fair-faced one, when an obstacle was properly created by you through your true being against the work of the gods, why do the deities not act against you?
Shattered by the splendor of the twelfth day, which the wise call the destroyer of obstacles,
she was thus addressed as the deluder who deludes the world.
Deprived of joy, bereft of her husband, and exceedingly miserable, she said: "Fie upon this life of mine, by which my purpose has not been accomplished! (NarP 2.35.41)
O lords of the immortals, the path of Yama has not been crowded with people;
nor has the day of Hari been neglected, nor has food been eaten on the day of Hari.
That heroic king joyfully carried out the slaughter of his son;
having placed my foot upon his head, Rukmāṅgada went to Hari.
Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable qualities, who is stainless and the stainless refuge;
the swan, the abode of purity, the ether, the syllable Om, the imperishable seed-syllable.
Formless, without appearance, free from conceptual proliferation, and untainted;
empty, having the nature of space, and devoid of both the object of meditation and the act of meditating.
That which they call "it exists" or "it does not exist," which is neither far nor near, the supreme abode, graspable by the mind, designated as the Puruṣa, and consisting of the world— NarP_2,35.46.
When he, who dwells within the lotus of my heart, whose form is splendor and who is eternal,
has attained dissolution therein, what indeed will be the fruit of my life?
But that man who accepts wages for work that has not been completed, and then abandons his master and departs, will certainly go to hell. (NarP 2.35.48)
Those gods who do not accomplish the business of their masters are born on earth as horses that consume their keep while serving as servants. (NarP 2.35.49)
"This matter cannot be accomplished; it would bring destruction to my husband and son.
How then can I accept a boon from you, who dwell in the celestial realm?"
The gods said:
"Speak, O Mohinī; we shall grant whatever is desired in your heart.
Having performed this service for you, we shall be free from our debt."
O Queen, you have exerted great effort for the sake of the king;
therefore, O Queen, you shall partake in the fruit of that which was performed for such a purpose.
O lord of the earth, while the deities were thus being invoked,
the royal priest, radiant as fire, then arrived before the king.
The sage, devoted to breath control, dwelt in the midst of the water;
then, when twelve years were completed, he emerged from the midst of the water.
Having gone out, O King, that tiger among sages heard of the delusive conduct of Mohinī; filled with anger, he approached the assembly of the gods.
She spoke to all the gods who had granted her the boon:
"Fie on me! Fie on this assembly of gods! Fie on this action known as sinful! (NarP 2.35.56)
For the sake of your spiritual cultivation,
may you grant the desired boon to Mohinī, which shall cause the human goal to take root.

O gods, for one who has committed ten thousand murders, who has harmed her husband or children, and whose livelihood is ruined—such a person is like a heap of ashes; there is no purification for her in this world even by falling into a blazing fire.
“Ten thousand killings and the murder of a husband—these are equal and were performed by the best of Brahmins in the past;
nor, O gods, does her purification occur here even by falling into a fire of kindled fuel.”
Having liberated Ukmaṅgada and Dharmavibhūṣaṇa with words consisting of nectar,
and having slain him who was joined by his beloved, he established them in the state of liberation and rendered the earth devoid of kings.
Nor is there residence in the hells for her, O gods; where then could this woman of small intellect have her standing in the third heaven?
Nor is she near a king, O gods, nor shall she attain that imperishable station of Viṣṇu.

One who is reviled by public gossip shall find no dwelling anywhere among the worlds; fie on the life of one who is censured for her actions and always devoted to sinful pursuits, O gods! (NarP 2.35.61)

"O gods, having killed her husband, having killed her son, and having killed her co-wife who was like a mother—whether she kills the entire earth or not—to what destination will she go? (NarP 2.35.62)
O gods, this is most wicked, for it destroys the dharma of Hari; yet she always says, "Let that which was spoken by her be eaten on the day of Hari. (NarP 2.35.63)
For the sake of increasing their vital breath, even they may go to a lower state;
let [the meat] be eaten on the day of Viṣṇu, and let the cow be slaughtered together with the twice-born.
"How can one who drinks what is undrinkable obtain residence in heaven after being released?
This has been declared for the ignorant; for those with knowledge, however, there is no such fixed rule.
If a statement is uttered out of ignorance [prohibiting] "let it be eaten on the day of Hari," purification for that too is indeed declared by means of a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Or else, O dwellers of heaven, by fasting on the eleventh lunar day conjoined with the asterism [Śravaṇā], or by bathing in the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa; ||| NarP_2,35.67 |||
"Even by touching a pig or by worshipping a deity, a man is purified—this has been declared by the Brahmins; yet today it has become utterly cruel. (NarP 2.35.68)
Devoted to evil while eating on the day of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to approach,
she utterly disregarded her husband’s command and caused her beloved son to be killed.
He was skilled in speech, devoted to eloquence, and intent on the welfare of his mothers;
yet this [act] was destructive to the dharma of Viṣṇu and fraught with many evils.
"O lords of the gods, she is not to be touched; how can you, who are devoted to justice, righteousness, and their fulfillment, grant her a boon?"
The gods do not provide protection for one who is joined with evil;
the gods are remembered as the upholders of dharma, and dharma is established in the Veda.
Service to the husband is proclaimed as the duty of women according to the Vedas; whatever the husband says, that should be carried out without hesitation.
"O immortals, one should say 'white' for what is white, and 'black' for what is black;
for that indeed is to be understood as true service, not mere attendance. (NarP 2.35.74)
The gods were overcome by their husband’s command out of a desire to establish his own authority;
therefore, there is no doubt that she was a sinner, a deluder of all women.
For the sake of accomplishing the truth, the king was constrained by oaths.
She spoke various words, but she who had killed her son did not desire [to release him];
and by that means, the king attained liberation after casting his sin upon her.
For this sinful body of hers was indeed possessed by ten thousand killings.
He was a donor of all gifts, devoted to the Brahmins, one for whom Hari was his deity,
whose nature was to delight his subjects, and who observed the fast of Hari’s day.
He was free from passion for the wives of others, devoid of longing for sense-objects,
having renounced desire for the sake of others, and was always devoted to the performance of sacrifices.
A lord of the earth who is always engaged in subduing the wicked on this surface of the world, and who is not overcome by the seven terrible vices; NarP_2,35.80.
Having cast out those of wicked conduct, how can she become worthy of a husband?
For whoever would take her side—be it a god or even a demon—[would likewise be cast out].
O best of gods, O deities, I could reduce to ashes in an instant even him who makes an effort to protect Mohinī.
That sin which resides in Mohinī arises for him.
Having spoken thus, O King, that best of brahmins took up water in his hand and,
looking on with intense anger, cast that which was produced by the ritual upon his head like a blazing fire.
O King, as soon as it was cast into the water, his body instantly burst into flames before the very eyes of the inhabitants of heaven,
like a heap of grass consumed by a mass of fire-tongues.

"O Lord, withdraw your anger! Withdraw it!"—as these words of the gods resounded in the sky, even as he spoke, that fire, cleansed by the words of the twice-born, reduced the woman to nothing but ashes.
