Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Curse," in the *Mohinī-carita* of the latter portion of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having cast off her delusion, Mohinī went to the abode of the gods.
"You wicked woman, you have no place here," was she rebuked by the messenger of the gods.
O you of evil character, of very dull intellect, who are devoted to censuring your husband and who neglect the day of Hari— there is no dwelling for you in the triple heaven.
"And for those who turn their backs on the Dharma, residence in hell is ordained.
Having spoken these extraordinary and cruel words, Vāyu [departed].
And having struck her with a staff, he impelled her toward torment;
thus, O King, was Mohinī beaten by the messenger of the gods.
O King, having been overcome by the staff of Brahmā, she reached hell;
there, by the command of Dharma, she was beaten for a long time by the messengers.
Having gone through all the hells in succession, they were cast down;
there, the son Dharmāṅgada was slain by Pāpa with his own hand.
Therefore, enjoy here the fruit of the deeds you have performed, wherever it may be;
[you shall rule] for the welfare of the subjects, with steady wisdom, like Mahendra and Varuṇa.
Having killed a son who was the lord of the seven islands, she became an enjoyer of such a fruit;
for by the killing of even an ordinary son, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
"How much more so for one who is joined with righteousness and whose limbs are marked by dharma?
Thus was he rebuked by the messengers of Yama, O best of kings.
He experienced all the torments in succession as prescribed by Yama;
however, by the touch of the body of one struck by the staff of Brahma, those torments [ceased].
Their limbs burst into flames and they were no longer able to bear [the heat];
then, O King, those denizens of hell approached Dharmarāja.
Terrified and tormented by the touch of his body, they spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, King of Dharma, have mercy! (NarP 2.36.12)
"O Protector, quickly remove this [woman] from our torments for our sake;
alas, by her mere touch, we have been turned to ashes in an instant! (NarP 2.36.13)
"Therefore, drive her away from these hells!
Having heard those words of theirs, Dharmarāja was greatly astonished.
She replied to her own messengers: "This man or woman who is a thief, and who has been consumed by the Brahman’s staff, must be expelled from my palace. (NarP 2.36.15)
My torment does not desire contact with that sin;
therefore, [punish] this woman of great wickedness who has violated her husband’s command.
"Drive her away from my presence—this slayer of sons, this destroyer of dharma, who has been struck by the staff of Brahmā—for my body burns at the mere sight of her. (NarP 2.36.17)
O King, having been addressed thus by Dharmarāja, those messengers then struck with missiles and weapons and drove [the sinners] out from Yama’s abode.
Then, O King, that sorrowful Mohinī, overcome by delusion,
went toward Pātāla, where she was stopped by those dwelling in Pātāla.
Then Māhinī, the daughter of Brahmā, being exceedingly ashamed,
went into the presence of Janaka and fully reported her own sorrow.
"Father, there is no place for me in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
wherever I go, they hurl me away."
Having been banished by the world and severely struck with weapons,
I took your command and went to Rukmavibhūṣaṇa.
And this which I have resolved upon is censured by the whole world:
having distressed my husband and slain my son with a choice sword.
"O father, having caused Saṃdhyāvalī to be agitated, I have reached this state;
O Lord, there is now no refuge for me, a sinner. (NarP 2.36.24)
Especially due to the curse of a brahmin, I have become a partaker of suffering;
I am struck down by the words of brahmins and consumed by the fire.
O son, the celestial river Ganges grants liberation to those killed by outcasts, those devoured by wild beasts and the like, and those perished by lightning strikes.
If, out of affection for me, you together with the gods propitiate that brahmin who gave the curse, then my purpose will be accomplished.
O King, while she was speaking thus, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
was joined by Śiva, Indra, Dharma, Sūrya, Agni, the lords of the gods, and the sages.
Placing Mohinī at his head, he went into the presence of the twice-born;
having arrived there, O protector of the earth, Brahmā was surrounded by the gods and others.
O King, the Grandfather himself paid homage with great reverence; he is the one to be worshipped and honored by Rudra and the other gods.
For the sake of pleasing Mohinī, the deluded one himself performed an act of homage;
for when a great task has arrived that is indeed unachievable within the three worlds.
O King, the salutation of the youngest brother would not be considered defiled;
for that twice-born man was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, established in asceticism.
Beholding the Creator of the World who had arrived together with the gods,
he rose up and paid homage to Brahmā, to those sages, and to the deities.
He caused [the Lord] to dwell there with devotion and offered praise to the Lotus-born One;
then the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds and the teacher of the universe, was pleased.
They entreated that twice-born man, who was honored by kings, for the sake of Mohinī:
"O father, O Brahmin of virtuous conduct, you who bring benefit to the world beyond! (NarP 2.36.35)
Have mercy, O ocean of compassion; become the one who leads the deluded to their goal.
O Brahmin, I have sent you forth for the purpose of bewildering Rukmāṅgada.
O giver of honor, having seen the world of Yama empty,
and having observed Vaikuṇṭha crowded with all the peaceful worlds, I have heard this.
The goddess, born of the mind, who acts for the welfare of the gods—
listen, O Dharādeva, to what I say before you.

Having examined the extremely subtle course of Dharma, which brings about the welfare of the world, by means of this woman whose limbs are dark as a touchstone, he who was adorned with golden ornaments [realized his error].
O Brahmin, together with his wife and sons, he was led to the abode of Hari by the king through the power of unwavering devotion resulting from the observance of Hari’s day.
The abode of Yama has been rendered empty by the act of erasing the records;
O brahmin-sage, this injury to the gods is not something that can be endured by one born of the arms.
They became the assistants of those who were especially devoted to the Brahmins.
O Brahmin, that which is not attained by one who knows the Sāṅkhya system, nor by the eightfold yoga, but is accessible through devotion—
that has been attained by the lord of the earth for his own son as well as for his co-wife.
Because that conduct of the king who was virtuous and the crest-jewel of monarchs was hostile [to you],
you have been consumed by his curse and have become a mere remnant of ashes, driven away by the force of that sin.
She has set out for the sake of the gods, for the increase of existence, and for the benefit of the king;
she does not desire her own self-interest, so how could she deserve contempt? O twice-born one, forgive this offense.

"Show mercy; resort to tranquility. For grinding what is already ground is not consistent with righteousness. Since she has been struck down by the bestowal of a curse, show her favor; become one who grants her a destination.
O Brahmin, when this is done, may this deluding woman abandon her most cruel disposition toward you."
Thus addressed by the Lotus-Seated One, that best of the twice-born reflected with his intellect and cast off his anger;
he spoke to the god who is the lord of the thirty deities regarding the body created by Vimohinī.
"O Lord, your daughter Mohinī is possessed of many sins;
therefore, she has no place in the worlds crowded with living beings."
"Having reflected for a very long time, I have thought of this for the sake of Maudgalya;
out of affection, I shall give it to you, for you are indeed more worthy of my worship."
O Lord of the Gods, just as your word is true, so too shall mine be;
and the work of the gods will be accomplished through the very act of Mohinī.
For that place which is not overrun by the flood of beings is the abode of the deluding one;
the earth, together with its islands, is always pervaded by moving and non-moving creatures.
The surfaces [of the earth] are occupied by the Daityas and others; the sky by birds and the like;
the celestial realm (nāka) by living beings who have performed meritorious deeds; and the hells by those of sinful karma.
The oceans were filled with fish and other creatures; therefore, no stable footing could be found there.
Then, O best of kings, Brahmā consulted with all the gods.
He said to the goddess Mohinī, "There is no place for you anywhere.
Hearing those words of her father, Mohinī remained obedient to his command.
Having prostrated herself before all the world-witnessing gods who were accompanied by their priest, she, the destroyer of the day of Hari, spoke: (NarP_2,36.55)
O best of the thirty gods, I join my palms in salutation to you;
O deities, even with a hundred prostrations, I do so with a heart full of devotion.
That which is requested by me must be given; it brings joy to all.
By the power of Ekādaśī, there is a destination for all sinners.
O best of gods, it is for the sake of increasing that [merit] that I have this purpose;
I have sent my husband, my co-wife, and my son to Vaikuṇṭha.
"O givers of honor, I remain a widow and so forth in the world of mortals for your sake,
so that the day of Hari may not become defiled for me."
I entreat you, grant this for the sake of your own interest; for it cannot be otherwise.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, in the narrative of Mohinī. Mohinī said:
"O gods, there shall be no other purifier equal to Ekādaśī."
Purified by which, even those of great sin go to the abode of Hari.
"Let it be considered that my abode near her is fitting.
The gods said:
"O Creator, at midnight, for the sake of assisting the gods, [she appeared as] Mohinī."
And at sunrise, Hari ordained for the gods that the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day, which destroys the merit of the fast.
Indeed, those eight Mahādvādaśikās that are mentioned in the Vaiṣṇava Āgama are observed as fasts by Vaiṣṇavas, even though they are distinct from Ekādaśī.
The Ekādaśī vow of the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas is declared to be eternal, performed according to the prescribed rite over three days during both fortnights.

One should gradually abandon meals in the morning and evening during the preceding and following fortnights. When the Ekādaśī is distinct [from the Dvādaśī], it should indeed be observed as a fast on the subsequent day;
for the vow must be performed on the Dvādaśī, fasting completely without even water.
For those who are unable to perform the fast by leaping, it is prescribed that water, vegetables, fruit, milk,
or the food offering (naivedya) of Hari— each measuring one-quarter of their own regular diet— shall suffice.
Those free from desire abandon the Ekādaśī when it is pierced by the Svātī nakṣatra at sunrise;
however, they release it if it is pierced by the Yamya (Bharaṇī) at midnight.
Moreover, O sinless one, the tenth lunar day is known throughout all the worlds; you must observe the established practice regarding that day for Yama.
By this, O beautiful one, the task of the gods is accomplished;
for the movements of the sun and moon and the lunar days have reached the end of the tenth day.
Wander over the sacred fords on earth for the destruction of your own sins,
beginning from the dawn of Aruṇa until the rising of the sun.
Since you have entered into this vow, may you obtain the fruit of Ekādaśī;
for whoever performs the Ekādaśī vow, it has indeed been defiled by you.
O beloved of the gods, he will be a benefactor to you;
however, the dawn here should be understood to last for only two muhūrtas.
Fifteen muhūrtas are traditionally taught for both the night and the day;
they should be understood as short or long according to the method of the three-part calculation (trairāśika).
Having arrived above from the night of the thirteenth muhūrta, bestow the merit of those who observe the fast; be at peace, O lady of pure smiles! (NarP 2.37.15)
For the purpose of establishing Yama, for the destruction of Vaikuṇṭha,
for the increase of heretics, and for the accumulation of sins.
"O Mohinī, this place marked by the time of dawn has been granted to you."
O auspicious one, enjoy the fruit of whatever merit belongs to those who diligently perform the Ekādaśikā vow here; be gracious toward this Brahmin. (NarP 2.37.18)
Thus instructed by Brahmā and the others, that enchanting woman became exceedingly joyful;
she considered her own life fulfilled by having visited the sacred ford of her husband’s sin.

This task of the gods has been accomplished; for even though his body has been reduced to ashes, the path made by the king has been cleared away within this mere consciousness, which is of the nature of wind.
"I have indeed brought about my own words, for that which was uttered by me was done with joy.
Having reflected thus, she bowed to the lords of the earth and to her own domestic priest with delight.

Abiding at the end in a time known as "devoid of the sun," on the tenth day for the delusion of people, she assumes a form of hardship and consumes the day; yet, though her form is most excellent, she leads men to hell.
Seeing her standing at the edge, the son of the Sun, with a joyful countenance, spoke these words:
"O lovely-eyed one, you have once again properly established my preeminence here in this world.
This very loud-sounding drum, mounted upon a rutting elephant and adorned with gold, has been sounded by me."
"For when a result is visible, everyone places their trust in it. (NarP 2.37.24)
For this tenth day, which touches upon the rising of the sun, is always censured;
it will lead to delusion for men who do not perceive that the sun has not yet risen.
Having abandoned that enjoyment of union with her beloved, she too remains at your feet, yet her form is invisible;
truly, O large-eyed one, it is for this reason that people call you "Māyinī" (the Enchantress).
"Having utterly deluded all people, you have caused me to be depicted upon my own canvas.
Having spoken thus, the son of Vivasvat, filled with joy, bowed down to that daughter of Brahmā.
Taking the scribe who had written the script in her hand, she went to the celestial realm with the gods;
when the gods had departed, that deluding woman approached Brahmā, the lord of the gods and asuras.
He made this request: "O Father, this priest of mine is exceedingly fierce in his anger;
O Lord of the World, act in such a way that my body, once burnt, shall attain [rebirth] again. (NarP 2.37.29)
This world, which was utterly deluded by me, has at last reached the appointed time of Yama;
for today the King of Death has been conquered by the King, and he has been made victorious, O dear one, through your power.
This is your task, O Father: that I may once again assume a body, O Lord of the World; therefore, please grant me your blessing, O Brahman.
Having heard those words of Mohinī, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds,
again consoled the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of his daughter.
"O dear Vasiṣṭha, listen to this beneficial advice that I speak for your sake, for her sake, O illustrious one, and for the welfare of the entire world. (NarP 2.37.33)
Out of anger, you reduced this Mohinī to ashes;
O giver of honor, if she should request her body once more, then grant her permission.
"O father, this daughter of mine, who is your patroness for sacrifice, is falling into misfortune;
this ascetic woman must be protected by you and me once her task is accomplished. (NarP 2.37.35)
"If you inform me with pure intent, O giver of honor,
I shall once again produce for her a body, for I am her father."
"But this [night], O best of Brahmins, is hostile to the day of Viṣṇu and is a bringer of evil;
therefore, let it be arranged immediately so that she may be purified. (NarP 2.37.37)
Having heard those words of Brahmā, that domestic priest,
filled with joy, gave orders for the purpose of providing a body for the sacrificer.
Having heard the words of the Brahmins, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
sprinkled the ashes of Mohinī’s body with water from his water-pot.
Sprinkled by Brahmā, the creator of the world, that enchanting woman regained her body;
she bowed to her father, the priest of Vasiṣṭha, and, prostrating herself with humility, grasped his feet.

Then the priest Vasu, filled with joy, spoke these words—clear, wise, and heroic—to that wife of the king, who was enchanting, yet abandoned by her husband’s son: NarP_2,37.41: "O lady, you have been left behind by the son of your master; do not be bewildered."
Vasu said:
"O Goddess, anger has been abandoned by me at the word of Brahmā;
I shall now provide you with a means of deliverance through rites such as bathing in sacred fords."
Having spoken thus to Mohinī, the Brahmin, having bowed with joy to the father of Mohinī and to Brahmā, the Lord of the worlds, took his leave.
Dismissed by Mohinī, Vasu, and Prīti, Brahmā departed for the world beyond darkness by way of the unmanifest path.
That Vasu, the best of Brahmins and the family priest of Rukmāṅgada,
considering Mohinī to be worthy of compassion, reflected upon her within his heart.
Having entered into meditation for a moment, he understood the cause of his departure.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Deeds of Mohinī," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O tiger among kings, that Vasu [approached] Mohinī, who was desirous of having him as her officiating priest.
He who is devoted to the welfare of all the world spoke with gentle words.
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī, I shall describe the characteristics of the sacred fords (tīrthas) individually,
by the mere knowledge of which the highest goal is attained even by sinners.
Among all sacred fords on the surface of the earth, Gaṅgā is the most excellent;
there exists nothing equal to her for the destruction of sin.
Having heard those words of her own priest Vasu,
Mohinī, bowing down and intent upon bathing in the Gaṅgā, spoke.
Mohinī said:
"O Blessed One, O best of the Vāḍavas, please now tell me the supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā,
which is esteemed by all the Purāṇas."
Having heard of the incomparable majesty of the Gaṅgā, which destroys all sins,
I shall afterwards go with you to bathe in the Pāpavināśinī.
Having heard those words of Mohinī, Vasu, who was a knower of all the Purāṇas,
recounted the sin-destroying majesty of Gaṅgā.
Vasu said:
"Those regions, those districts, those mountains, and even those hermitages,
in whose vicinity the holy Bhāgīrathī always flows, [are truly blessed]."
Neither by austerity, nor by celibacy, nor again by sacrifices or renunciation,
can a living being attain that goal which one attains by serving the Gaṅgā.
Those men who, having committed sinful deeds in the earlier part of their lives,
resort to the Gaṅgā in their remaining years— they too attain the supreme goal.
A man who might stand on one foot for a thousand yugas and one who bathes in the Gaṅgā for a single month— both obtain equal fruit.
A man who might stand with his head downwards for ten thousand yugas,
and one who might stay by the Gaṅgā as he pleases— he who stays by the Gaṅgā is superior.
For all beings here whose minds are afflicted by suffering and who are seeking a refuge,
there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā.
The Gaṅgā forcibly rescues even the lowest of men, sinners burdened with terrible and preeminent transgressions, as they are about to go to the impure hell.
Those who constantly go to the Gaṅgā, who is beloved by the gods, are surely equal to the sages and to the gods headed by Vāsava.
The vast Gaṅgā, who possesses all forms, purifies those who are blind, dull-witted, and destitute;
she is constantly resorted to by the gods led by Indra, by sages, and by men for the sake of prosperity.

O Mohinī, during the dark fortnight, beginning from the first day of the lunar phase, she remains present upon the earth for as many days as there are until the meritorious new moon; that is, for ten days.
Indeed, for ten days starting from the first day of the bright fortnight,
she herself manifests her presence in Pātāla.
The ten days beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight up to the fifth— on those days, she is always present in heaven.
In the Kṛta age all sacred fords are supreme; in the Tretā, Puṣkara is the best; in the Dvāpara, Kurukṣetra; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā is distinguished as the most excellent.
In the Kali age, however, all sacred fords naturally release their respective powers into the Gaṅgā, but that goddess [the Gaṅgā] herself does not go anywhere.
Even men of sinful character may attain the supreme goal through contact with the wind that is moistened by droplets of the Ganges water.
That Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, whose nature is consciousness, and who is Janārdana—he alone exists in the form of liquid as the water of the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
The killer of a Brahmin, the slayer of a cow, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—all these are purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whether it be situated in a field, or drawn up from a well, cold or even warm—
Ganges water indeed removes sin until the end of life.
Stale water is to be avoided; stale leaves are to be avoided;
but the water of the Jāhnavī is not to be avoided, nor are the leaves of the tulasī.

It is not possible to state the number of Mount Merus made of gold and all kinds of jewels, nor the number of pebbles or even the waters of the Ganges; likewise, there is no power here to describe the extent of his virtues.
Even that man who does not perform the entire ritual for pilgrimage to sacred sites shall partake in the fruit here, through the majesty of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Moreover, even the drops of water from the Gaṅgā are superior to the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi),
in that they bestow upon devotees the fruit desired by them.
By merely rinsing his mouth once with the water of the Gaṅgā out of devotion,
a man enjoys in heaven the divine flavors produced from the udders of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu).
He who pours the water of the Gaṅgā upon a Śālagrāma stone dispels intense darkness and shines like the sun at its rising.
Even one who is seized by manifold sins born of mind, speech, and body becomes purified upon beholding the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt in this matter.
He who always eats almsfood consecrated by the waters of the Gaṅgā shall indeed become free from sin, like a serpent that has cast off its skin.
Heaps of evil deeds as vast as the Himavat and Vindhya mountains perish through the waters of the Gaṅgā, just as misfortunes vanish through devotion to Viṣṇu.
Merely upon entering the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing out of devotion, the sins of men, such as the killing of a Brahmin, depart completely, crying out, "Alas! Alas! (NarP 2.38.35).
The man who should dwell constantly on the bank of the Gaṅgā and always drink the water of the Gaṅgā shall be liberated from previously accumulated sins.
He who, relying upon the Gaṅgā, dwells there eternally without fear,
is indeed worthy of worship by gods, mortals, and great seers alike.
Of what use is the eightfold yoga, of what use are austerities, and of what use are sacrifices?
Dwelling by the Ganges is indeed superior to everything else.
What is the use of numerous sacrifices, recitations, austerities, or the distribution of wealth,
since Gaṅgā— bestower of heaven and liberation— is present and easily accessible?
One does not obtain that fruit through sacrifices, restraints, observances, gifts, or even through renunciation, which one may obtain by serving the Gaṅgā.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains at Prabhāsa by giving a thousand cows when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that very fruit he obtains at the Gaṅgā in a single day.
He who, having abandoned all other means and being firmly resolved,
desires liberation and dwells happily on the bank of the Gaṅgā, is indeed a vessel for mokṣa.
In Vārāṇasī, the Gaṅgā is especially a bestower of immediate liberation,
always on the fourteenth and the eighth day of every month.
Dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā grants success for as long as one lives;
by performing penances (kṛcchras) at all times, one enjoys the fruit that [others] experience with difficulty.
And on the bank of the Jahnavī, one may obtain the merit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow at all times—
that fruit which is obtained here by one devoted to the service of the Gaṅgā in half a day.
O daughter of Brahmā, that cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices,
nor by all acts of sacrifice, austerity, charity, yoga, Vedic study, or ritual action.
Whatever fruit one obtains by residing on the banks of the Gaṅgā with devotion,
and whatever merit belongs to perpetual celibates through their truthful speech— [one obtains that all].
Whatever merit belongs to those who maintain the sacred fire-fire ritual, that same merit accrues from residing by the Gaṅgā for one’s mother,
father, wife, and for an infinite number of ten million kinsmen.
Devotion to the Gaṅgā certainly delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra;
contentment is supreme sovereignty, and the knowledge of reality belongs to those whose nature is happiness.
The perfection of discipline and conduct arises for one devoted to the Gaṅgā;
a mortal becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done simply by reaching the Gaṅgā alone. (NarP 2.38.50)
He who touches that water with devotion and drinks that water shall become devoted to it and intent upon it, even after death; of this there is no doubt. (NarP 2.38.51)
For by this means, a man easily attains the path to liberation;
he is as one initiated into all sacrifices, drinking the Soma daily.
Those men for whom all their rites are always performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
having cast off the body, rejoice in the presence of Śiva.
Just as the gods, headed by Śakra, partake of the nectars situated within the moon and the sun with their mouths, so too do men partake of the water of the Gaṅgā.

And by the ritual giving away of daughters in marriage according to the rules, by the devout gifting of land, by the giving of food, the giving of cows, and likewise by the giving of gold and other such gifts; // NarP_2,38.55 //
Whatever merit is proclaimed to come from the gift of chariots, horses, and elephants,
a hundred times that merit is gained from drinking a single mouthful of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from a thousand cāndrāyaṇa fasts,
a greater fruit than that is obtained from drinking the water of the Gaṅgā.
By drinking even a mere mouthful, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
for him who drinks the water at will, liberation is held in the palm of his hand.
The water of the Sarasvatī is digested in three months, that of the Yamunā in seven,
that of the Narmadā in ten months, and that of the Gaṅgā in a year.
According to the scripture, for those who have died anywhere else without having performed the water-libation rite,
the attainment of that subsequent fruit occurs through the contact of their bones with the Gaṅgā.
He who might perform a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts for the purification of the body is surpassed by him who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā to his heart's content.
Whoever beholds the Gaṅgā, praises her, bathes in her with devotion, or drinks her water,
attains heaven, stainless knowledge, yoga, and liberation.
But for one who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā heated by the rays of the sun,
drinking from the Gaṅgā is superior to subsisting on cow's urine and barley-meal.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Gaṅgā," in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu.
Vasu said: Listen, O Mohinī, I shall describe the fruit of beholding Gaṅgā.
For that which was spoken in the Purāṇas by the sages who perceive the truth: (NarP 2.39.1)
Just as serpents become venomless when bitten by Tārkṣya,
so too one is liberated from all sins upon seeing the Gaṅgā.
A man saves seven generations of descendants, seven generations of ancestors, and those who come before them,
by beholding, touching, and bathing in the Gaṅgā.
By seeing, touching, drinking [its water], and likewise by chanting "Gaṅgā," a person purifies hundreds and thousands of other men.
Knowledge, incomparable sovereignty, stability, long life, and likewise fame— these,
as well as the fruits of the auspicious stages of life, are the results born from the sight of the Gaṅgā.
The fickleness of all the senses, vices, sin,
and cruelty perish merely by the sight of the Gaṅgā.
Violence toward others, crookedness, observing the faults of others,
and hypocrisy— these of men perish simply by the sight of the Gaṅgā.
If a man desires the eternal, imperishable state, he should look upon it again and again, or even touch it again and again, with devotion. (NarP 2.39.8)
Whatever merit may be obtained elsewhere through step-wells, wells, tanks, water-stations, shelters, and the like, that same merit is attained by the mere sight of the Gaṅgā.
Whatever fruit arises for men from the sight of the Supreme Self,
that very same fruit shall arise from the sight of the Gaṅgā through a state of devotion.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing, touching, and serving at Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, the Narmadā, and Puṣkara— [he obtains that same fruit here]. (NarP 2.39.11)
O queenly lady of the earth, the great sages have declared that in the Kali age, [the merit] comes from the mere sight of the Gaṅgā;
indeed, O lady, it comes even from the remembrance of the Gaṅgā.
I shall proclaim that fruit which is celebrated in the Purāṇas for those who,
joined with inauspicious deeds, are sinking in the ocean of worldly existence.
The Gaṅgā is remembered as that which rescues from afar; that man who remembers the Gaṅgā even from thousands of yojanas away is saved from falling into hell.
For even one who has committed evil deeds attains the supreme goal merely by remembering the Gaṅgā; [she destroys] the cage of the multitude of sins.
He falls apart in a thousand ways, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt—
whether going, standing, sleeping, meditating, waking, eating, laughing, or weeping.
Whoever constantly remembers the Gaṅgā shall be released from bondage;
and those who remember the Gaṅgā with devotion even while standing a thousand yojanas away.
Even those who cry out "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā! are released from their sin;
as are those who remember the Gaṅgā and those who are devoted to the Gaṅgā.
They too are liberated from all great sins without exception; of this there is no doubt.
[They obtain] diverse palaces and women adorned with various ornaments.
Health and the attainment of fearlessness are the fruits of remembering the Gaṅgā;
even a man standing at a distance who remembers the Gaṅgā with his mind [obtains these].
Standing even at a distance of a hundred yojanas, one who chants the name "Ganga, Ganga" certainly obtains the fruit of a thousand cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
One is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
by chanting [his name] one is freed from evil, and by seeing him one obtains auspiciousness.
Having bathed therein and likewise drunk [its water], one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation—
seven ancestors, seven descendants, and seven more beyond them.
The Gaṅgā delivers men even when she is merely mentioned incidentally; indeed, the chanting of the name of the Gaṅgā brings liberation even if done without faith. (NarP 2.39.24)
He who performs [this] becomes a vessel for heaven by means of that which carries merit,
even if he has fallen into every possible state or is devoid of all virtuous qualities.
Merely by chanting the name of the Gaṅgā, one shall attain an auspicious state—
even a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a guru, a killer of a cow, or one touched by all manner of sins.
Having touched the water of the Gaṅgā, a man is liberated from all sins;
when shall I behold that Gaṅgā? When indeed shall I obtain a bath there?
Thus, desired by men, she delivers a hundred lineages.
Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim to you the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
For one who has bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, sin is instantly destroyed.
And for those of purified soul who have bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā, O Mohinī, the attainment of unprecedented merit arises immediately.
That prosperity which comes to men cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices;
it shines forth like the sun at its rising, having dispelled the intense darkness.
O beautiful queen, having thus destroyed his evil, he shines, sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā by means of even this single rite of bathing. (NarP 2.39.32)
A mortal certainly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at the Ganga;
the sins of a man accumulated over many births are utterly destroyed.
Merely by bathing in the Gaṅgā, one immediately becomes a vessel for merit;
sin committed in other places is destroyed on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Sin committed on the banks of the Gaṅgā is destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā,
whether at night, by day, or during the twilight, provided one exerts oneself at the Gaṅgā.
By bathing even at home with water drawn from that [river], one obtains the merit born of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
and whatever merit exists in all sacred fords and in all desired shrines, it is likewise attained.
A mortal obtains that fruit from bathing in the Gaṅgā, there is no doubt, even if he is joined with great sins or burdened with all sins. (NarP 2.39.37)
By bathing in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rites, one is liberated from all sins;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a bath superior to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Especially in the Kali age, the Jāhnavī removes sin,
having destroyed the defects born of desire that arise from body, speech, and mind.
By bathing in the Gaṅgā with devotion, a man who bathes in the Gaṅgā for a year while endowed with faith rejoices in heaven like a god.
That man who bathes daily in the Gaṅgā until death shall undoubtedly dwell for a kalpa in the world of Viṣṇu.
Freed from all sins, joined with his entire family,
and endowed with all enjoyments, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
There is no need for further deliberation here: that mortal who bathes in the Gaṅgā continuously and at all times [attains this], even until the end of two parārdhas.
He is liberated while living, and dying right here, he shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
the merit of bathing at midday is remembered as being ten times that of bathing in the morning.
In the evening, in the presence of Śiva, bathing in the Gaṅgā is indeed superior to the gift of ten million tawny cows; it is a hundredfold and infinite in merit.
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever one bathes in her;
however, at Haridvāra, Prayāga, and at the confluence with the Sindhu, the fruit is even greater.
"O Jāhnavī, those who bathe in your waters heated by my rays pierce through the solar orb and attain liberation"— such are the words of the Sun.
"Even he who, though remaining in his own home, shall glorify you at the time of bathing,
shall indeed go to heaven"— thus did Varuṇa speak to her.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Bathing in the Gaṅgā," within the *Mohinī-carita* of the latter portion of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa*.
Vasu said: Now, I shall describe to you the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā at specific times.
I shall proclaim it, O beautiful-thighed one; listen with attentive mind.
The man who bathes continuously in the Ganges during the month of Māgha shall dwell for a very long time in the world of Śakra, together with his kinsmen.
Then that man who bathes in the Ganges according to the prescribed rule with uninterrupted continuity goes to the city of Brahmā for ten million times a hundred thousand kalpas.
He who eats once a day for six months, eating only once during the entire period of the sun's northern course,
goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, delivering a hundred generations of his lineage.
But by bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā on all the Saṃkrāntis,
a man shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
The fruit is said to be especially great at the equinoxes and during the solstices;
they know that the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā during the month of Kārttika is equal to the merit of ascetic penance.

O Mohinī, those who are preceded by Brahmā (the lotus-seated) declare that the merit of bathing in Māgha at the time when the sun enters Aries, or even on the full moon day of Kārttika, is superior [to other rites].
"Your father said that the fruit arising from bathing for a year is inexhaustible on a specific lunar day, whether in the month of Kārtika or Vaiśākha."

O daughter of the sacrificer, by bathing even for three months, one obtains that same fruit which is proclaimed for bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā at the beginning of the Manvantara and at the beginning of the Yuga.
A bath in the Gaṅgā on the twelfth lunar day under the Śravaṇa asterism, on the eighth day under the Puṣya conjunction, or on the fourteenth day under Ārdrā, is extremely difficult to obtain.
The full moon day in the month of Mādhava, as well as those in Kārttika and Māgha,
and likewise the new moon days of these months— bathing in the Gaṅgā on these occasions is very difficult to attain.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one thousand [times the merit] is gained; on all festival days (parvan), it is one hundred;
and likewise on the new moon and the eighth day when the dark half of the month of Māgha occurs.
Then, when it is slightly less than that *parvan*, it is *mahodaya*.
It is taught that the merit at *mahodaya* is a hundredfold, while at *ardhodaya* it is a hundred thousandfold.
O Goddess, bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā during an eclipse of the moon or the sun yields the fruit of bathing for three months in the months of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha.
If a bath is performed with a spirit of devotion in the Gaṅgā on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa),
all the sin accumulated since birth is indeed destroyed.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, a *vyatīpāta* yoga is difficult to encounter;
and especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a *vaidhṛti* yoga occurs in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
The man who bathes according to the prescribed rite at dawn throughout the entire month of Māgha shall become a rememberer of his past births.
He shall certainly become a knower of the meaning of all scriptures and free from disease on the day of the sun’s transit,
at the end of the two fortnights, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
A man who bathes in the Gaṅgā out of desire shall attain the abode of Brahmā;
it is said that this merit is a hundred thousand times that of [bathing in] the moon, and ten times more than that of the sun.
Ten billion Indus rivers and ten billion Suns have reached the banks of the Gaṅgā when the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Madhu coincides with the Vāruṇa yoga;
if it is found on the Gaṅgā, it is equal to a hundred solar eclipses.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, on a Saturday, under the asterism Hasta, this Gaṅgā descended from the mountain to the world of mortals.
On this lunar day, she indeed removes sins; this is that primordial Daśā-Gaṅgā, who bestows a hundredfold the merit of a horse sacrifice.
O Jāhnavī, whatever multitudes of great sins and other evils exist within me, destroy them all upon the arrival of Govinda-dvādaśī.
When the moon, its orb full, enters into conjunction with Jupiter under the lunar mansion known as Maghā,
that is remembered as the greatness of the lunar day (tithi).
If it were possible for [the merit of] bathing in the Gaṅgā to equal that of a hundred solar eclipses,
then the fruit of bathing according to specific locations shall be described.
Wherever it is submerged, it is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra;
where it is joined with the Vindhya mountains, it is a hundred times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra.
The Jāhnavī at the city of Kāśī is said to be a hundred times superior to that at the Vindhya;
the Gaṅgā is difficult to find everywhere, yet she is most preeminent in three places.
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
those who bathe in these places go to heaven, and having died there, they are not subject to rebirth.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of bathing at Gaṅgādvāra and Kuśāvarta:
it shall be equal to the fruit of seven Rājasūya sacrifices and two Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Having stayed there for half a month, the wise know that one obtains the fruit of six Viśvajit sacrifices and the merit of giving ten myriads of cows.
Then, having bathed in the lakes at the best of sites, at Govinda, and at Rudra situated at Kanakhala, as well as in the Gaṅgā, one shall obtain imperishable merit.
And listen, O auspicious lady, to the account of the highly meritorious tīrtha named Saukara,
wherein in former times Acyuta manifested in the form of a boar.
A person obtains the merit of a hundred builders of fire-altars, of two Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices,
and the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
By bathing at that very holy site of Brahmā, a person obtains the merit of ten thousand Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices as well as three Aśvamedha sacrifices.
O Mohinī, there is the sinless holy site named Kubjā, where all diseases and even the sins arising from all previous births are destroyed.
There is another Kāpila Tīrtha here, O auspicious lady, where a man who bathes obtains a fruit equal to the merit of giving away eighty thousand Kapila cows.
Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, Nīlaparvata, and the sacred site of Kanakhala, one whose sins are shaken off shall go to heaven.
Then, for the sake of purification, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha), the most excellent among all sacred fords;
by bathing there during two Viśvajit sacrifices, a man obtains merit.
Then there is the Veṇī kingdom, a sacred ford where the Sarayū, most meritorious and highly auspicious, has united with the Gaṅgā as a sister with her own sister.
From the washing of Hari’s right lotus-foot arose the celestial river (Ganges),
and from his left foot arose the Sarayū, which was born from Lake Mānasa.
By worshipping Rudra and Viṣṇu at that sacred ford (tīrtha), one attains the state of Viṣṇu;
bathing there is proclaimed to bestow the fruit of five horse-sacrifices.
Next is the Gāṇḍava Tīrtha, where the Gaṇḍakī river joins;
there, the gift of a thousand cows and bathing are equal in merit.
Beyond that is the meritorious Rāmatīrtha, where Vaikuṇṭha is ever present;
and beyond that is the meritorious Somatīrtha, where the sage Nakula resides.
Having worshipped Śiva and meditating upon him, he attained the status of a Gaṇa;
[he reached] the meritorious tīrtha named Campaka, where the Gaṅgā flows northward.
The holy site named Kalaśa, which destroys great sins and is equal to Maṇikarṇikā, is located there; from that Kalaśa, the sage arose.
It was here that Agastya, the best of sages, became a worshipper of Rudra;
this Somadvīpa is a highly meritorious sacred site, equal to Vārāṇasī.
Where Soma, worshipping the Lord, was held by Rudra upon his head;
where the sister of Viśvāmitra met with the Gaṅgā.
O Mohinī, a mortal who bathes there in the great sacred ford of Jahnu’s lake shall become an unreturning guest, dear to Vāsava.
One certainly becomes the savior of twenty-one generations;
therefore, that is the Aditi-tīrtha, where Aditi offered oblations to Hari.
O fortunate one, they say that bathing there at the great sacred ford Śiloccaya, where the progenitors performed austerities after receiving [the lineage] from Kaśyapa, brings great prosperity.
By resorting to the multitude of holy fords (tīrthas), one goes to heaven even with mere blades of grass;
there is a holy ford named Indrāṇī, where Indrāṇī [offered] Vāsava.
Having performed austerities, Viśvāmitra obtained this holy bathing-place, which bestows merit and is worthy of service like Prayāga, while he was practicing penance. 2.40.51.
There, by resorting to that sacred ford, a Kṣatriya attained the status of a Brahmanical seer;
it is there that Pradyumna-tīrtha became famous through the ascetic power of Smara, who [served] Hari.
A son named Pradyumna was born there, which brought about supreme prosperity;
thereafter, from the Gaṅgā to the Yamunā, there was indeed Dakṣaprayāga.
Having bathed there, imperishable merit is obtained, just as at Prayāga.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Bathing at Specific Sites," within the Glory of the Gaṅgā, in the Dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu, in the latter part of the Śrī Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.
Vasu said:
Now, the fruit of actions such as immersion and others shall be described.
Listen attentively, O daughter of Brahmā, beloved of the king!
Those by whom the merit-bearing Gaṅgā has been bathed in even once with devotion— the auspicious goddess delivers a hundred thousand of their lineages from saṃsāra.
O Goddess, because the twilight is worshipped there at its general location, it is capable of making merit a hundred-thousandfold; it is the purifier of the twice-born.
O Mohinī, the waters offered there by sons endowed with faith to their ancestors produce an inexhaustible satisfaction that is difficult to attain.
For as many sesame seeds as are taken for the ancestral rite,
for that many thousands of years do the ancestors dwell in heaven.
Whosoever among all the ancestors residing in the worlds of the Pitṛs,
when being satiated, attain supreme satisfaction through the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā.
O lady of auspicious countenance, he who desires a fruitful birth or a virtuous progeny should go to the Gaṅgā and gratify the ancestors as well as the gods.
Those mortals who are considered to be in an unfortunate state, when they are satiated by their kinsmen with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and the waters of the Ganges, proceed to the abode of Hari.
Whatever ancestors of virtuous conduct reside in heaven, they go to liberation when satiated with the waters of the Gaṅgā; such is the word of the Ordainer.
For one month, by means of mere libations and the offering of rice-balls at the Gaṅgā, all the ancestors, possessing the splendor of the sun, become well-pleased.
[He saw] vehicles joined by throngs of apsarases, adorned with gold and jewels,
covered with nets of pearls, and resounding with the music of flutes and lutes.
[They saw beings] adorned with garlands, possessing the beautiful bodies of Gandharvas, endowed with divine enjoyments, and [emitting] the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and so forth.
Having ascended the most excellent celestial chariots, they indeed go to the world of Brahmā;
so too does the man who, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, constantly worships the Liṅga.
In a single birth, he certainly attains supreme liberation;
[superior] to the Agnihotra rites, the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
They are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of a *liṅga* performed at the Gaṅgā;
one should sprinkle the ancestors or the gods with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
His ancestors, even those residing in hell, shall be satisfied at that very moment.
It is taught that bathing from copper jars is ten times more meritorious than bathing from earthen jars.
The merit is said to be a hundredfold when made with silver and ten-millionfold when made with gold;
this same sequence applies to the water-offering (argha), the food offering (naivedya), the ritual oblation (bali), worship, and so forth.
The fruit increases progressively according to the excellence of the vessel; yet, if one possesses the means, he who out of delusion does not perform the ritual in full detail [reaps no fruit].
He who betrays the gods does not partake in the fruit of that action;
beholding the gods is meritorious, and touching them is better than merely seeing them.
Worship through touch is superior; bathing with ghee is even better than that.
The wise declare that bathing with the waters of the Gaṅgā is equal to bathing with ghee.
Whoever offers the *arghya* even once with a specific substance—namely, water from the Gaṅgā measuring one *prastha* of the Magadha standard—placed within a copper vessel; ||| NarP_2,41.21 |||

One should offer [libations] to the deities together with one's own ancestors, joined by sons and grandsons; he shall indeed attain heaven. Water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, clarified butter, curd, and likewise honey—*NarP_2,41.22*.
Red karavīra flowers as well as red sandalwood—
this offering (argha) consisting of eight ingredients is proclaimed for the Sun.
That best of men who performs the installation of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, Durgā, and likewise Brahmā on the bank of the Gaṅgā; NarP_2,41.24 //
Likewise, he causes shrines for others to be built according to his ability;
by building them for followers of other sects, the merit becomes ten millionfold.
Having fashioned liṅgas according to one's ability from clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
and having endowed them with the proper characteristics, one should install them day after day.
Having worshipped with mantras and with leaves, flowers, and so forth according to one's ability, he should daily cast [the offerings] into the Gaṅgā; his merit shall be infinite.
For that best of men who, with devotion, recites the eight-syllabled mantra at the Gaṅgā, which bestows all bliss, liberation stands within his grasp.
Having restrained oneself with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*, "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) indeed attend upon one who recites it for six months.
He who recites the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya" together with the *tāra* (Om) twenty-four hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite, becomes Śaṅkara himself.
The five-syllabled perfected vidyā is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. Whether impure or pure, one who recites it becomes free from sin.
When the Gaṅgā is worshipped, all the deities are worshipped;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship the river of the immortals.
Four-armed and three-eyed, beautiful in all her limbs,
auspicious, with hands holding a jewel-vase, a white lotus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Clad in white garments, adorned with pearls and gems,
she was exceedingly serene with a beautiful countenance, her lotus-heart moist with compassion.

Having meditated upon Gaṅgā— who is composed of water, who always bathes the surface of the earth with nectar, and who is eternally saluted by the three worlds— one becomes a partaker of merit by worshipping her.
He who worships in this manner continuously for even half a month becomes like a god; over a long period of time, his merit is even greater.
In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Jahnu drank up the Gaṅgā out of anger, but released her again from his right ear.
One should worship that goddess Gaṅgā, the girdle of the sky,
there on the Akṣaya day in Vaiśākha, and also in Kārtika, O lady of auspicious countenance.
Having kept a vigil at night, one should worship Viṣṇu, Gaṅgā, and Śambhu with devotion, using offerings of barley-meal and sesame seeds.
Likewise, with fragrant flowers, with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood,
with *tulasī* and *bilva* leaves and the like, and with fruits such as the *mātuluṅga*, [he should worship].
With incense, lamps, and food offerings, according to the full extent of one's wealth,
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
then, returning to the surface of the earth, he becomes a righteous king.
Having enjoyed various pleasures, endowed with beauty, virtue, and good qualities,
he shall become possessed of knowledge at the end of his body and attain union with Śiva.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, recitation, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods—
all these, when performed at the Gaṅgā, become multiplied ten million-fold.
Listen now to the meritorious fruit of him who, on the Akṣaya Tṛtīyā, gives a cow of ghee according to the prescribed rite on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
he shall possess all desires and shine like a thousand suns.
In a variegated celestial chariot made of gold and jewels and adorned with swans,
he is glorified in the world of Brahmā together with his own ancestors.
Thereafter, he is born as a Brahmin on the banks of the Gaṅgā, endowed with wealth;
and in the end, having become a knower of Brahman, he attains liberation without a doubt.
Likewise, he who bestows a cow according to the prescribed rite is honored in the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on the cow's body.
And later he is born into a family abundant with wealth and grain, filled with jewels, gold, and land, and endowed with virtue, learning, and fame. (NarP 2.41.50)
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures together with his sons and grandsons, he will certainly partake in liberation; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
If a tawny cow is given according to the prescribed rite by one who has mastered the Vedas,
she then leads all the ancestors dwelling in hell to heaven.
He who gives land measuring even a nivartana on the bank of the Gaṅgā transcends Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva for as many years as there are atoms of dust in that land.
And he is born again on earth and becomes the lord of the seven continents,
amidst the resounding blasts of kettledrums and conchs, and the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Awakened by the praises of the Māgadhans,
he, being devoted to all dharmas, attains every happiness here in this world.
Having caused all the ancestors residing in hell to reach heaven,
and having liberated those dwelling in heaven, you yourself, O deluder, shall become a possessor of knowledge.
Having first severed the five-faceted ignorance with the sword of knowledge,
and having attained supreme dispassion, he reaches the Supreme Brahman.
Thirty *daṇḍas* measured by a staff of seven cubits constitute a *nivartana*;
the sacred law itself declares that three parts less than this is the measure of a *gocarma*.
He who indeed bestows a village on the banks of the Gaṅgā upon Brāhmaṇas for the pleasure of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and the Sun; NarP_2,41.59.

Whatever merit is found in all acts of giving, whatever fruit in all sacrifices, and whatever fruit is proclaimed for meritorious austerities and vows— [all that is attained by this]. // NarP_2.41.60 //
That merit of the giver of a village should be known to be multiplied a thousandfold;
he dwells in the city of Viṣṇu upon a Vaiṣṇava celestial chariot that shines like ten million suns.
Or he sports joyfully in the realm of Śaṅkara, praised by the gods and others;
having remained there for a period of time equal in years to the number of dust particles on the earth, he [proceeds].
O Goddess, for one who offers sixteen-month-old gold in Akṣayā, he is born into a family of yogins endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the other superhuman qualities.
He who gives [these] to the foremost of the twice-born is honored in the worlds;
through the gift of food one attains the world of Viṣṇu, and through the gift of sesame seeds, the world of Śiva.
Through the gift of jewels one attains the world of Brahmā; through cows and gold, that of Vāsava (Indra);
through gold and garments, that of the Gandharvas; and through the gift of a maiden, one gains fame.
Having attained through knowledge that wisdom which grants liberation, a man who goes to the bank of the Gaṅgā, which is endowed with various kinds of trees, shall reach the stainless state.
One should devoutly cause a grove to be made, along with a residence provided with gardens,
[planted] with plantains, coconuts, wood-apples, *aśoka*, and *campaka* trees.
It was filled with jackfruit trees, bilva trees, kadamba, aśvattha, and pāṭala trees,
as well as mangoes, palmyra palms, oranges, and other various trees.
Having thus caused a dwelling to be constructed, adorned with flowers, filled with *jātī* blossoms, joined with *vijaya* flowers, and likewise shining with *pāṭala* blooms; (NarP 2.41.69)
Whether to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, or Bhāskara,
he likewise offers [the gift] with devotion, having resolved upon every purpose.
I shall describe the fruit of his merit in brief, and not in detail:
as many flowers, roots, and fruits as those trees possess, [so great shall be his reward].
And their various seeds as well as their roots remain established in those worlds for thousands of kalpas.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Giving Gifts and Other Duties" within the "Glorification of the Gaṅgā," in the dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu, in the latter part of the glorious Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa. Mohinī said:
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life has become fruitful."
That supreme majesty of the Earth which I have heard from the lotus of your mouth.
Aha! There is no sacred ford on the surface of the earth equal to the Gaṅgā, for such merit is said to result from even the mere sight of her.
O best of Brahmins, please describe in due order the ritual procedures for the various types of cows, such as the cow made of molasses; I am always devoted to you.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard those words of Mohinī, her priest Vasu,
who was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Āgamas, spoke with a smile.
Vasu said:
Listen, O Mohinī, for I shall explain to you that which you have asked of me—
the ritual procedure for the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu) as it is proclaimed in the scriptures.
One should carefully spread a black antelope skin with four necks upon the ground that has been smeared with cow dung, after having strewn it with *kuśa* grass.
One should fashion the cow facing east with its feet toward the north and accompanied by its calf;
the most excellent molasses-cow is proclaimed to consist of four bhāras.
One should make a calf with one bhāra; that which is made with two bhāras is remembered as middling;
a calf made with half a bhāra would be the lowest, while one made with a full bhāraka is the best.

The calf should consist of one-fourth [of the milk], according to the extent of the household's wealth; this applies to the master who follows the primary rule, even when he conducts himself by means of a secondary rule.
No fruit of the hereafter arises for that evil-minded one;
these two, a cow and her calf, are covered with white, smooth garments and [full of] ghee.
With ears like oyster shells and feet like sugarcane, their eyes were pure white pearls;
they had veins like white threads and were draped in white woolen blankets.
Those two had backs like copper water-pots, hair as white as yak-tail whisks,
feet like coral, and were endowed with breasts of fresh butter.
Both had bronze milking vessels, pupils fashioned from sapphires,
golden ornaments upon their horns, and hooves of pure silver.
Having thus arranged the two scent-caskets, joined with various fruits and serving as the source of fragrance, one should then worship them with incense and lamps.
May that goddess Lakṣmī, who resides in all beings and who dwells among the gods,
grant me peace in the form of this cow.
May that Goddess, who dwells within the bodies of the Rudras and is ever beloved of Śaṅkara,
dispel my sin in the form of a cow.
May she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu, who is Svāhā in the form of Agni,
and who is the power of the Moon, the Sun, and Indra— may she, in the form of a cow, be for our prosperity.
May that cow which possesses the splendor of the four-faced Brahmā, the splendor of Kubera the giver of wealth,
and the splendor of the world-protectors, grant me boons.
May that cow who is the *svadhā* of the foremost ancestors and the *svāhā* of those who enjoy the sacrifice,
the remover of all sins, grant me peace.
Having thus addressed that cow, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
this is declared here as the ritual procedure for all cows.
O Mohinī, listen as I describe the true nature of those ten cows, which are proclaimed in the scriptures as destroyers of sin. NarP_2,42.21.
The first is the jaggery-cow; then the second is the ghee-cow;
the third is the sesame-cow, and the fourth is known as the water-cow.
The fifth is the milk-cow, and the sixth is remembered as the honey-cow;
the seventh is the sugar-cow, and likewise the eighth is the curd-cow.
The ninth is the jewel-cow, while the tenth is according to its own form;
for the liquid cows there should be jars, but for the others, there should be heaps.
In this regard, some wise men desire even a golden cow;
likewise, certain great seers [prefer one made] of butter or oil.
This very same procedure and these very same ritual implements,
accompanied by the mantras and the invocation, should always be employed on every festival day.
These auspicious [gifts], which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grant the merit of numerous sacrifices, and remove all sins, should be given according to one's faith.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, or auspicious moments; or again, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the beginning of the Yugas and the Manvantaras, and on festival days such as eclipses.
Gifts such as the "molasses-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others should be bestowed by those endowed with devotion and faith,
either at sacred fords (tīrthas), in one's own home, or especially on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Having thus given a cow to an excellent brahmin according to the prescribed rite,
and having circumambulated that brahmin and gratified him with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [one attains the fruit].
Filled with joy, he should dismiss the officiating priests after paying them homage;
thereafter, being well-composed, he should worship Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite.
And having beheld the goddess of divine form, who bears the eightfold manifestations,
[he offered] a prastha of śāli rice along with two prasthas of milk.
Having caused milk-rice (pāyasa) to be prepared and having given honey and ghee,
each weighing one pala, he should do so endowed with a spirit of devotion.
That milk-rice, cakes, sweetmeats, and circular sweets, as well as gold and silver weighing even half a guñjā; NarP_2,42.34 //
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and guggulu;
bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, gorocana, and white sandalwood. NarP_2,42.35 //
And other blue lotuses and fragrant flowers,
one should cast into the Gaṅgā with great devotion according to one's ability.
O fortunate one, indeed by this mantra spoken in the Purāṇas as well:
"Oṃ, salutations again and again to Gaṅgā, to Nārāyaṇī, and to Śivā. (NarP 2.42.37)
O Mohinī, this very same procedure should be performed every month on the full moon or the new moon day, at dawn, by those who are composed in mind.
The man who, for one year, with devotion and joy, worships according to his ability, eating sacrificial food, moderate in diet, and endowed with celibacy; ||| NarP_2,42.39 |||
O Mohinī, whether by day or by night, through such regular practice,
at the end of a year, Gaṅgā appears before him, assuming a divine form.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial jewels,
she stands visibly before one, bestowing boons.
O auspicious lady, having seen with his own eyes that Gaṅgā in her manifest form, possessing a divine body, a mortal becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Whatever desires a mortal may long for, he shall obtain them all;
but a Brahmin free from desire shall attain liberation in that very birth.
This entire ordinance, beginning with the cow made of jaggery, which you asked about, has been declared by me to you;
it is the worship of the Gaṅgā, a vow that grants liberation and indeed brings satisfaction to the Lord of Śrī for one year.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ritual for the Cow of Jaggery" within the *Gaṅgāmāhātmya*, in the dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu, in the latter part of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard the words of Vasu, which indicated the majesty of the Gaṅgā...
Once again, he questioned that brahmin, his own royal priest, regarding the lord of kings.
Mohinī said:
"O Brahmin, I have heard everything regarding the auspicious gift of cows and other such rites;
now I wish to hear about the unsurpassed vow of the Gaṅgā."
O twice-born one, tell me what is the fruit of worshipping the Gaṅgā and other rivers, or of establishing them there? O omniscient one, I have come to you for refuge. (NarP 2.43.3)
"Now you are the one who grants the destination [after death] to me, who have been abandoned by my kinsmen, separated from my husband, and deprived of my son, O best among the wise. (NarP 2.43.4)
"Having sought refuge in you alone out of respect for my father's word, may you, therefore,
speak of the propitiation of the deity along with the majesty of Gaṅgā, hearing which one is indeed liberated from sin."
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, having heard those words of Mohinī, the powerful brahmin Vasu,
the best among the knowers of the Vedas, honored Mohinī and spoke.
Vasu said:
"Well asked by you, O Goddess, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
The entire majesty of the Gaṅgā, which destroys all great sins,
was formerly told out of compassion by Śiva, who bears the bull upon his banner.
Questioned with affection by the goddess, the one dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā said:
"The gods ate in the forenoon, and likewise the sages at midday."
In the afternoon it is for the ancestors, and at night for the Guhyakas and others;
having bypassed all other times, eating at night is the most excellent practice.
Fasting is better than begging for alms; not asking for alms is better than begging; and eating only at night is better than not asking for alms; therefore, one should practice eating only at night.
One who eats at night should practice these six for six months: eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire-rites, and sleeping on the ground.
He who observes the practice of eating only at night on the banks of the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha,
near a temple of Śiva, [should offer] kṛsara mixed with ghee.
Having offered an oblation of *kṛśara* rice to Śiva,
one should eat while observing silence with regard to wooden implements and avoid any greed of the tongue.
Eating from a palāśa leaf, remembering Śiva, and having conquered his senses,
he should offer separate funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the King of Dharma and for the Goddess.
One should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights;
likewise, on the full moon day, one should worship with perfumes and the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed Śiva with milk, honey, clarified butter, and curd separately,
one should likewise scatter golden flowers upon the top of the liṅga.
Then, according to one's ability, one should offer cakes fried in ghee;
having taken an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds, one should then scatter them over the Śiva-liṅga.
One should worship the Lord of All with blue lotuses and also with lotuses;
but if those are unavailable, one should worship Hara with golden lotuses.
In this rite, one should offer milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee, as well as guggulu resin;
likewise, a lamp of ghee and anointment with sandalwood and other fragrant substances.
One should offer leaves and fruits with devotion to Maheśa,
and likewise present a pair of black cows together with their calves.
At the end of the month, he should feed eight Brahmins with sacrificial fees;
during that month, he should avoid honey and meat and remain celibate.
Having performed this vow exactly as prescribed once, being endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), and being devoted to faith and devotion; NarP_2,43.23 //
In this world one obtains enjoyments, and after death, an unsurpassed state,
traveling in celestial chariots resembling sapphire and yoked with peacocks.
Accompanied by all his own kinsmen, he goes to the beautiful city of Śiva, which is composed of divine jewels and endowed with celestial enjoyments.
Having enjoyed all various desired pleasures with his diverse friends, until the dissolution of all beings (the end of the world).
Then he becomes a righteous soul and likewise the lord of Jambūdvīpa;
there, freed from all taint, he enjoys every kind of pleasure.
Handsome, fortunate, and likewise one whose commands are obeyed,
being entirely freed from all diseases, he too shall partake of this fruit.

Or, being composed in mind on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, he who performs the practice of eating only at night (naktabhojana) with rice mixed with milk; ||| NarP_2,43.29 |||
Having worshipped Śiva with flowers and other offerings, and having presented food,
he should eat while observing silence regarding wood, using a wooden vessel for his meal.
Having become restrained through silence, he should indeed perform the cleaning of his teeth;
then, near a Śiva-liṅga or on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he should sleep at night.
On the morning of the full moon, having bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite and having made a formal vow for fasting, one should keep a vigil throughout the night.
Having bathed the Liṅga with ghee, and likewise having worshipped the auspicious Bull with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, as well as with food offerings, incense, and lamps; NarP_2,43.33.
Having adorned it according to the prescribed rite with very white flowers, garments, and the like, as well as turmeric and sandalwood, one should offer it to Śiva.
And one should feed Brahmins with milk-rice according to one's ability;
thus, whoever performs this once with devotion and endowed with faith, [attains the fruit]. (NarP 2.43.35)
Having performed austerities with self-restraint, one undoubtedly obtains the merit of two thousand and a half yugas. (NarP_2,43.36)
With celestial chariots resembling the moon, possessing the luster of swans and jasmine, yoked to very white bulls, and adorned with nets of pearls; NarP_2,43.37 //
Together with his own ancestors, he proceeds to the abode of the Lord,
surrounded on all sides by beautiful women who possess the exquisite fragrance of blue lotuses.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures with beloved women of divine form,
he shall then become endowed with sovereignty upon the earth for an infinite period of time.
That protector of the earth is born endowed with fame and sovereignty;
he rules the earth under a single umbrella along with his command.
Endowed with dispassion at the end, he attains the Gaṅgā once again;
joined with that faith, he meets his death in the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, having regained his memory there, he certainly attains liberation on the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when it is conjoined with the asterism Hasta.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, whether a man or a woman, having performed a night vigil with a spirit of devotion, [should then worship] the Gaṅgā with the ten kinds [of offerings].
Endowed with faith, one should worship her with flowers, perfumes, food offerings, and fruits numbering ten, as well as with lamps and betel leaves.
Having bathed with devotion ten times in the Ganges according to the prescribed rite,
one should indeed cast ten handfuls of black sesame seeds and clarified butter into the water.
One should offer ten balls of parched grain flour and ten balls of molasses;
then, on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā, likewise with gold or silver, [one should fashion images].
Having fashioned an image of the Gaṅgā with the form to be described hereafter,
one should likewise place it upon a lotus marked with a svastika.

Having placed [the image] upon a full water-pot adorned with a garland of garments around its neck, one should worship the Goddess; or, if that is unavailable, [one may use] an image made of clay or other materials.
Now, if one is unable even to do that, one should indeed draw [the goddess] on the ground with flour—
four-armed, with beautiful eyes, and possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons.
She was being fanned with yak-tail whisks and shaded by a white parasol;
she was exceedingly serene, bestowing boons, and her inner heart was moistened with compassion.
Its surface was flooded with nectar, it was praised by gods and others,
it was strewn with divine jewels, and it was adorned with celestial garlands and ointments.
Having meditated upon her in the water as previously described, one should worship her there in the image;
one should perform the worship specifically with the mantra that is about to be taught.
Bathing the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) is especially distinguished;
one should smear the ground in front of the image with cow dung.
Nārāyaṇa, Maheśa, Brahmā, and likewise Bhāskara;
King Bhagīratha and Himavat, the lord of mountains.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth according to one's ability;
furthermore, one should give ten *prasthas* of sesame seeds to ten Brahmins.
One should give ten prasthas of barley, as well as ten [measures] of products derived from cows,
along with fish, tortoises, frogs, crabs, and other aquatic creatures.
Having had [the images] fashioned according to one's ability from gold or silver,
or in their absence from flour, the knower of mantras should first worship them with flowers and other offerings and then cast them into the Gaṅgā while reciting the mantra itself.
On that day of the chariot procession, when such resources are available,
one should have an image of Gaṅgā mounted upon a chariot, facing northward.
For those of evil deeds, a sight [of the goddess] while she wanders in the world is difficult to obtain;
likewise, one should also perform the chariot procession of Durgā here.
Having performed it in this manner according to the prescribed rite, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
one is immediately liberated from the ten sins that will be described hereafter.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules, and consorting with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action]. (NarP 2.43.61)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and idle chatter—this constitutes the fourfold nature of vocal misconduct. (NarP 2.43.62)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—these are recorded as the threefold mental [non-virtue]. (NarP 2.43.63)
By these ten kinds of sins arising from ten million births, one is liberated; there is no doubt here, according to the word of Brahmā.
When worshipped with this mantra, she indeed delivers those ten and thirty preceding ancestors, as well as others, from saṃsāra.
"Oṃ, salutations to Daśaharā; salutations to Nārāyaṇī Gaṅgā.
By this mantra, whichever mortal [recites it] day and night on that day, [attains the fruit]. (NarP 2.43.66)
One should recite it five thousand times; one will obtain the fruit of the ten dharmas and shall deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants from the ocean of existence.
Having accepted this hymn to be recited according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu on that day while chanting it at the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, salutations to Śivā, to Gaṅgā; let there be salutation to you, the bestower of auspiciousness. Salutations be to Gaṅgā, who has the form of Viṣṇu; salutations again and again to you.
Salutations to her who embodies the forms of all the gods, whose very form is medicine;
salutations be to you, O best of physicians, for all diseases of every being.
Homage be to you, the destroyer of poison produced by both stationary and moving beings;
repeated salutations to the life-giver who destroys the poison of saṃsāra.
Salutations again and again to the Mistress of Life, who destroys the threefold suffering;
salutations to You, the embodiment of all forms, the Peace who removes all torment.
Salutations to her who effects complete purification, for the sake of liberation from sin;
repeated salutations to Bhogavatī, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Salutations to you, O Mandākinī; repeated salutations to you, the giver of heaven. Salutations to you whose form is the three worlds; repeated salutations to you, the goddess of the thirty [deities].
Salutations to you who abide in purity; salutations again and again to you, the possessor of well-being.
Salutations be to you who abide on the seat of the thirty gods; salutations to you, the possessor of splendor.
Salutations again and again to Mandā, to Liṅgadhāriṇī, and to Nārāyaṇī;
salutations to you, Viśvamitrā, and salutations again and again to you, Revatī.
Homage ever to you, the Vast One; salutations again and again to you, the Sustainer of the World.
Homage to you, the Foremost of All; salutations again and again to you, Nandinī.
Salutations again and again to Pṛthvī, to Śivāmṛtā, and to Virajā; salutations again and again to you, Tārā, who has attained the state of both the supreme and the mundane.
Salutations to you who abide in heaven; salutations again and again to you who are indivisible. Salutations again and again to you, the peaceful one, the foundation, and the giver of boons.
Salutations again and again to Ugrā, to Nukhajalpā, and to Saṃjīvinī;
salutations again and again to Brahmagā, to Brahmadā, and to Duritaghni.
Salutations again and again to the Mother of the World, who shatters the suffering of those who bow before her;
salutations again and again to you, the skillful one, the destroyer of Durga.
Homage again and again to Maṅgalā, the remedy for all calamities! Homage to you, the supreme, the non-supreme, and the beyond; homage always to the bestower of liberation!
May Gaṅgā be before me, and likewise may Gaṅgā be at my sides.

May the Gaṅgā be mine in every respect; O Gaṅgā, may my stability be in you. You are at the beginning, you are at the end, and you are in the middle; you are everything, O auspicious one who flows toward the ocean.
You alone are the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), for you are the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
O Gaṅgā, you are the Supreme Self and Śiva—salutations again and again to you!
Thus, whoever constantly recites this hymn with devotion,
or even listens to it with faith, through actions performed by body, speech, and mind— ||| NarP_2,43.85 |||
By means of these ten established virtues, one is liberated from all faults;
the sick man is freed from disease, and the one in distress is released from calamity.
One is liberated from the two-fold bonds and from all fears;
one attains all desires and, after death, merges into Brahman.
In whosever home this hymn is written and duly honored,
there shall be no fear of fire or thieves, nor any fear even from evildoers.
On that tenth day, standing in the waters of the Gaṅgā and reciting this hymn ten times, even one who is poor or powerless [attains success].
He too obtains that fruit by worshipping the Gaṅgā with devotion,
