according to the previously mentioned procedure, which has been fully described.
As is Gaurī, so is Gaṅgā; therefore, whatever ritual procedure is correctly prescribed for the worship of Gaurī, that same procedure applies to the worship of Gaṅgā.
As is Śiva, so is Viṣṇu; as is Viṣṇu, so indeed is Umā;
as is Umā, so is Gaṅgā—here no distinction exists.
He who speaks of a difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra, or likewise between Gaṅgā and Gaurī, or between Lakṣmī and Gaurī, is indeed a person of deluded intellect.
In the bright fortnight, by day, on the earth, in the Ganges, during the northern course of the sun—
blessed are those who cast off their bodies while Janārdana dwells within their hearts.
Those men who release their lives in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite go to the world of Viṣṇu, being praised by those dwelling in heaven.
He who dies in the Ganges with half his body submerged in water through fasting does not undergo rebirth and attains union with Brahman.
Whatever destination belongs to the wise person of sattvic nature who is disciplined in yoga,
that same destination belongs to the embodied being who gives up their life-breaths in the Gaṅgā.
The man who, having undertaken a fast unto death on the bank of the Gaṅgā, dies there,
truly attains the supreme world together with his ancestors.
A wise person desires to give up his life-breaths by dying in the Gaṅgā;
for many births have passed away, and wherever one has died, [it is there that liberation is sought].
A great deal of time has passed while we have been wandering here and there; it is not far off, but close at hand, within a distance of two yojanas.
By dying here in the Gaṅgā, there is no need for deliberation;
whether through knowledge or ignorance, or even through intentional desire.
A mortal who dies in the Gaṅgā attains both heaven and liberation;
that man who, while his vital breaths are departing, remembers the Gaṅgā [attains the same].
Even one of sinful character who touches it indeed attains the supreme goal.
Those wise ones who, having gone to the Gaṅgā, have cast off their bodies, have attained equality with the gods;
therefore, setting aside all other things that grant liberation, one should serve the Gaṅgā until the fall of the body.
Whether in the intermediate space, on earth, or in water, even one who is most sinful, upon dying,
attains the imperishable state that is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
He who is righteous, endowed with vitality, self-restrained, and esteemed by the learned,
and who contemplates the Gaṅgā with his mind, shall attain the supreme goal.
Wherever one may die, even when death has arrived,
by remembering the Gaṅgā with devotion, one goes to the city of Śiva or Viṣṇu.
Emerging from the exceedingly harsh mass of matted hair of Śambhu,
she washed away the sins of those born of the city and led them to heaven.
For as many thousands of years as there are bones of a person remaining in the Gaṅgā, for that long he is honored in the heavenly world.
If a person's bones are taken and cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā by men,
their residence shall be in the heavenly world for a period beginning from that very moment.
If the bone of one who has performed auspicious deeds is obtained in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
there is no return for him from the world of Brahmā by any means whatsoever.
If one's bone comes into contact with the water of the Gaṅgā within ten days [of death],
one shall obtain a fruit equal to that of dying in the Gaṅgā itself.
Then, having bathed and sprinkled [the bones] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having combined them with gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
he should place that skeletal mass in a vessel and look toward the direction inhabited by the hosts of departed spirits (pretas).
Having entered the water while reciting "Homage be to Dharma," he should cast [the offering] with the words "May He be pleased with me.
Then, having bathed and seen the inexhaustible [merit] at the holy bathing-place (tīrtha) and the banyan tree, he should then bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
By doing thus, even for one staying in the city of the hungry ghosts (pretapura), there shall be a journey to heaven equal to that of Mahendra.
Taking the current as the boundary for a distance of four cubits, Nārāyaṇa is the master there; no other is ever the master.
One should not accept anything there, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat,
as long as the waters continue to overflow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
One should understand that the depth of the water is the "womb" (garbha), and that which is further than that is called the "shore" (tīra);
up to one hundred and fifty cubits is the womb, and beyond that is the shore.
Such is the opinion of some, O Goddess, which is in accordance with the Śrutis and Smṛtis;
the sacred field (kṣetra) is said to extend for a distance of two gavyūtis all around from the bank.
Having abandoned the bank, one should dwell in the field; dwelling on the bank itself is not desired.
The boundary of the field extends for one yojana from both banks.
Not even all sins together can touch the banks of the Gaṅgā;
upon seeing her, they flee just as forest-dwelling beasts do at the sight of a lion.
O highly fortunate lady, where the Gaṅgā flows through the penance grove of Rāma and Śambhu,
that should be known as a field of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra) extending for three yojanas in every direction.
A man should not accept gifts at sacred fords, nor in holy shrines, nor at any of the prescribed occasions; he should abstain from such things.
For him who accepts gifts at a sacred ford or in holy shrines,
that sacred ford becomes fruitless for him as long as that wealth remains his.
O Goddess, by the sale of the Gaṅgā, there would be the sale of Viṣṇu;
but when Janārdana is sold, the three worlds are sold.
He who bears upon his head the ichor produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā bears the form of the sun solely for the destruction of darkness. (NarP 2.43.126)
Furthermore, that man who, having strewn dust born from the sands of the Ganges, offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to satisfy his ancestors, shall lead them even to heaven. (NarP 2.43.127)
This supreme majesty of the Gaṅgā has been declared to you, O blessed lady;
by reading or hearing it, a person indeed attains that highest abode of Viṣṇu.
O daughter of Vidhi, those who desire the state of Viṣṇu or Śiva should always recite this with devotion, self-restraint, and faith.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Account of Worship and Other Rites," in the *Gaṅgāmāhātmya* within the dialogue between Mohinī and Vasu in the latter portion of the glorious *Bṛhannāradīyapurāṇa*.
